Part XVII — the help system as a graph

297. Seven topics could not be reached from any other help page

The commit before this loop closed a documentation gap it described as “inbound links 71->124”. Measured again, as a graph over man/*.Rd – resolve every \link{} through the alias table and count arrivals per topic, ignoring self-links:

count

The seven: tidy.ggcpt, glance.ggcpt, augment.ggcpt, summary.ggcpt, print.ggcpt, cpt_install_engines, and ggcpt_plot_methods.

The cause is one omission repeated four times: none of the package’s four hub pages had a @seealso at all. cpt_detect() – the central function, the page a reader lands on first – had none, and its prose mentions \code{tidy()} and \code{augment()} in code font without linking either. So the five accessors that exist to get a result out of cpt_detect() were unreachable from the page that produces it. Same for autoplot.ggcpt, ggcpt_methods and cpt_methods.

ggcpt_plot_methods is mine, from §248: I gave it a @seealso pointing out to autoplot.ggcpt and ggcpt_methods and never made either point back. A new page is a leaf until something links it.

Fixed by adding the four missing @seealso blocks, each pointing where a reader would actually want to go next – cpt_detect() to the five accessors, the plot method and cpt_penalty(); cpt_methods() to the installer that fills its installed column; autoplot.ggcpt and ggcpt_methods to each other’s plot documentation. Re-measured: 123 of 123 non-internal topics reachable, 0 unreachable.

Part XVIII — the ... surface, and the example gating

299. Every ... goes where its documentation says

86 exports take .... Six never reference it in their body – alarms, as_tibble, augment, autoplot, glance, tidy – and all six are generics, whose body is UseMethod(): ... travels by dispatch, so not naming it is correct. That leaves 80 functions that actually forward it, and all 80 document it; none has an undocumented ....

Then the harder question: does the documented destination match the actual one? Extracting the \arguments entry for ... from each Rd and the calls that receive ... from each body flagged 16 apparent mismatches – and all sixteen were the extractor’s fault. The receiver pattern required ... to sit inside a call with no nested parentheses before it, which misses every real idiom in this package:

ocp::onlineCPD(data_vec, getR = TRUE, <a multi-line list>, ...)
do.call(ggplot2::geom_rect, c(<...>, full_height_params(mapping), list(...)))
ggplot2::discrete_scale("colour", palette = cpt_pal(), na.value = na.value, ...)

Read directly, all three send ... exactly where the documentation says. Fourth instrument error in five rounds (§268, §289, §292, now this), and the same shape every time: a sweep that cannot represent the thing it is looking for reports its own blindness as a finding. The habit that keeps catching it is reading the code before filing, not a better regex.

300. Example gating is already textbook-correct, with one omission

CRAN reviewers ask specifically about \dontrun, so it is worth knowing exactly where it is used:

mechanism count why

\dontrun 2 topics genuinely cannot run

Both \dontrun uses are the textbook-correct cases: mcp_wrapper() needs JAGS, a system library that no R-package check predicts, and cpt_load_tcpd() downloads from the network, which an example must not do.

mcp_wrapper() explains itself above the block:

Not run by R CMD check: whether this works depends on a system library, and no test of installed R packages predicts that reliably.

cpt_load_tcpd() had no explanation at all – a reviewer would meet a bare \dontrun{} and have to infer the reason. It now says the same kind of thing in the same place: the calls download from the Turing Change Point Dataset’s repository, and an example must not require network access.

Part XIX — guarding the fix that cost five CI rounds

302. Load-time behaviour, measured

S37 is the worst bug in this package’s history to diagnose: cpt_methods() filled its installed column with requireNamespace(), which loads the package, so building a table loaded all 35 engine namespaces – including fabisearch -> rgl, which dies in dyn.load() on macOS for want of libGLU. R CMD check reported it as Vignette re-building failed with no chunk, no line and no message, and it took five CI rounds to find. The fix was find.package().

Measured now, in a fresh session:

value
library(ggchangepoint) 1.09s, 30 namespaces – the Imports and their transitive dependencies, no Suggests engine
cpt_methods() 0.030s, 55 rows, and zero further namespaces loaded
engine namespaces loaded after both 3 of 38, and all three are the Imports engines (changepoint, changepoint.np, ecp)

The fix holds exactly. Nothing in the package loads a suggested engine until a wrapper actually needs it.

302.1 Nothing guarded it, so now something does

The suite had no assertion on this at all – the only uses of loadedNamespaces() were in §290’s need_pkg test. The new test is order-independent, which matters because by the time it runs most engines are already loaded by earlier files: it picks an engine that is installed and not yet loaded, calls cpt_methods(), and asserts both that the row says installed = TRUE and that the engine is still not loaded. That is the S37 lesson stated as an executable property – answering “is it installed” must not load it.

Proved to fire before being trusted, the same way as §290. Reverting engine_installed() to the pre-S37 requireNamespace() form makes the hardening suite fail, and the side effect is visible in the very same run:

hardening: ..........Registered S3 methods overwritten by 'strucchangeRcpp':
══ Failed ══

Building the table loaded strucchange on the way past. Restored immediately; find.package() is back at R/detect.R:457.

303. And the cross-references from §297 validate

The four @seealso blocks added last pass introduced eleven new \link{} targets, which only R CMD check verifies – and getting one wrong is exactly the mistake of §248 (\link[base]{plot.default}, which lives in graphics). Full check on the current tree:

* checking Rd cross-references ... OK

Status 1 ERROR, 2 WARNINGs, 3 NOTEs – the documented environmental baseline – with examples, --run-donttest, tests, the vignette rebuild and installed size all OK.

308. Three of the five recurring warnings were the suite’s own noise

Every pass of this loop has reported “5 upstream warnings” as a constant. Looked at properly, they are two different things.

Three were escaping because the test asserts a different warning. expect_warning() captures the one that matches its pattern and lets the rest bubble up to the report:

site escaping warning now
test-new-infrastructure.R:65 SegNeigh is computationally slow, use PELT instead asserted
test-wrappers.R:31 same asserted
test-040-bugfixes.R:495 Very low number of permuted data sets from kcpRS at nperm = 20 muffled by message text

changepoint advises PELT on every segneigh call, so asserting it both documents the upstream behaviour and takes it out of the report. The kcpRS complaint is about a parameter the test chose for speed, and the block already asserts a different warning it must keep, so a text-scoped withCallingHandlers() muffle is the precise instrument – nothing else is hidden. (The first attempt nested expect_warning(..., NA) around it, which fails: the second warning only occurs for one of the three engines the loop covers.)

Two are staying, because the existing test already argues for them. R52 deliberately does not assert envcpt’s convergence warning, and says why:

whether a given series also triggers an upstream convergence warning is data-dependent, so it is not asserted here; warnings are deferred past the diversion by construction and reach the user unchanged.

That is a substantive point about what the test is checking – the test diverts the message stream and the comment records that warnings survive the diversion. Muffling them for a tidier report would overrule a documented decision to gain nothing.

Suite report: FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 2, down from WARN 5, and both remaining warnings are the ones a reader is meant to see.

Part XXII — what a detection call does to your session

310. Two engines were rewriting the caller’s search path

Instrumenting a full suite run for global state – options, attached packages, the registry, the RNG – turned up four packages on the search path afterwards that had not been there before. Traced per wrapper, in a fresh session each time:

wrapper attached and left behind
bcp_wrapper() package:bcp, package:grid
fabisearch_wrapper() doRNG, rngtools, doParallel, parallel, iterators, foreach, Biobase, BiocGenerics – eight
bocpd_wrapper(), beast_wrapper() none

Nothing in this package calls library(). bcp attaches itself and grid when its namespace loads, and fabisearch needs NMF attached rather than loaded – which the wrapper does deliberately, and documents – so NMF’s Depends and the engine’s own foreach/doParallel/doRNG registration come with it.

The 0.5.0 audit checked this and reported it clean. Its claim was “no option, no attached package, no RNG leak – the fabisearch NMF attach does detach”, and the last clause is exactly what was verified: the wrapper’s on.exit detached package:NMF. What it never checked was what came with NMF. One of eight is a pass if you look only at the package you named.

Both wrappers now record search() and give back whatever the call added, detaching in search() order (most recently attached first, which is the only order that works). Measured after: bcp 2 -> 0, fabisearch 8 -> 0, with the same results as before in each case.

310.1 The first attempt fixed six of eight, and the reason is instructive

fabisearch went from eight to two: Biobase and BiocGenerics survived, and the try() around the detach swallowed whatever refused. In isolation all three of NMF, Biobase, BiocGenerics detach cleanly – so it was not a refusal at all. The baseline was in the wrong place: I recorded search() after need_pkg("fabisearch"), and loading fabisearch is itself what attaches Biobase, so those two were already in the baseline and were never candidates for removal. Moving the record above need_pkg() takes it to zero.

The try() is what made this look like a permissions problem instead of an arithmetic one. A swallowed error is a bad place to keep a diagnosis.

310.2 What was deliberately not done

Loading bcp also prints “Loading required package: bcp” and “Loading required package: grid”, because it attaches them itself. Wrapping requireNamespace() in suppressPackageStartupMessages() does not silence them – they are plain messages from library() calls inside bcp’s own load – and the next tool up, suppressMessages(), would hide anything an engine says at load time for a cosmetic gain. Reverted. §252’s fix targeted a warning, which is louder, appears in R CMD check output, and was about the machine; conventional load chatter is neither, and escalating the instrument to win the point would have been the wrong trade.

311. The rest of the suite’s global state is clean

property after a full suite run
registered methods left behind 0
options changed 45 – all created by loading engines (bfast.*, datatable.*, BioC), none set by this package
RNG seed unchanged

And the timing, since check time matters at submission: 249.6s across 327 blocks. The three slowest are ocd at ~21s each, a quarter of the suite – and they already pass mc_reps = 10 with a comment explaining that mc_reps only calibrates the threshold. The cost is the engine’s per-observation streaming loop, not a test parameter, so there is nothing to trim without shortening the series the assertions depend on. Worth knowing before optimising it.

What was real: nine entries nothing cites anywhere. Eight are cited by no vignette, no Rd and no code – chen2009information, gneiting2006geostatistical, hariz2007classification, lai2005comparative, meinshausen2006estimating, olshausen1997sparse, rigaill2020fpop, wang2022overview. Sparse coding and geostatistical space-time models are not changepoint references; these look like the residue of a broader library. The ninth is vandenburg2020evaluation, a duplicate of van2020evaluation – the same paper, same DOI, in the same file under two keys, one for the vignettes and one for the Rd (which reads inst/REFERENCES.bib, where it also lives, so the Rd path is unaffected).

Removed: 77 entries -> 68, still 61 cited, still 0 broken. The seven that remain uncited by a vignette are all \insertRef’d from the Rd, so the vignette bibliography being a superset of the Rd’s is a maintenance choice rather than dead weight.

cpt_cite() deserves a note: the Demšar (2006) reference behind the critical-difference diagram is uncited in the vignette bib and looked like an attribution gap, but it is named in ?cpt_benchmark’s prose and returned in full by cpt_cite("critical_difference"). The package’s own citation mechanism covers it.

314. “Four rows carry status planned” – the table below says five

vignettes/ggchangepoint.Rmd claimed:

cpt_methods() is the live capability table … Four rows carry status "planned" rather than "available": their engines (gfpop, robseg, FOCuS, hdbinseg) are not on CRAN

planned_methods() has five rows: those four engines plus changeforest. And the chunk on the very next line is print(cpt_methods(), n = Inf) – so a reader is told “four” and then shown five, on the same screen.

vignettes/introduction.Rmd gets it right (“Five more, whose engines are not currently on CRAN”, listing all five including random-forest classification), so the two vignettes contradicted each other. Corrected.

This is the second time this exact claim has gone stale: the 0.5.0 audit’s S30 recorded “a stale planned-engine count” as one of its findings. So it is now guarded – a test extracts the engines named in that sentence and the number word in front of it, and compares both to planned_methods(). Proved to fire: changing “Five” back to “Four” fails the suite.

314.1 A check I designed badly, recorded so it is not repeated

Before that, I compared per-capability engine lists (ci, fitted, posterior, statistic, path) against the registry – using a list I had invented, not one taken from the vignettes. The mismatches it reported said nothing about the package. What the exercise did establish, by accident, is the useful fact: the vignettes do not hard-code capability lists at all. They write subset(cpt_methods(), ci)$method and let the chunk execute, so there is nothing there to go stale. A claim generated by running code cannot rot; that is why §314’s hand-written count is the one that did.

Part XXV — the census, and the 0.4.0 number in the opening sentence

§316 said enumerating the vignettes’ hand-written numbers was “a cheap, finite job”. Done: every number word or numeral in vignette prose (chunks excluded) followed within three words by a package noun – methods, engines, vignettes, rows, families, provenances, geoms, criteria. 50 claims. Most are structural and cannot rot (“one row per changepoint”, “one more row than $changepoints”). Six state a total, and one of those was wrong.

320. The introduction advertised 31 methods

vignettes/introduction.Rmd, third line of the opening paragraph:

a central dispatcher cpt_detect() covering 31 detection methods across six algorithmic families

31 is the 0.4.0 number. It is 50 – and 31 -> 50 is the headline of the release this vignette introduces. The first sentence of the first vignette a reader opens advertised the previous version’s capability.

Corrected. The “six algorithmic families” beside it stays: the vignette’s own §325 sentence enumerates six and §285 verified all eight sections it names, so that number is internally consistent even though the feature tour counts nine methodological families – the two are different groupings, one of the introduction’s sections and one of the registry’s.

Also corrected, and self-inflicted: the tour’s 0.5.0 section said “three companion vignettes develop these properly” while the closing paragraph – which §316 had just changed – lists four. Fixing one count exposed the other.

321. Guarded, after five wrong versions of the guard

The total-method count changes every release, so it is worth a test rather than a proofread. Getting the test right took more attempts than the fix:

  1. Too broad. “Any number before methods” flagged the benchmarks article’s “Ten methods raise zero false alarms” – a measured subset, not a claim about the package. Narrowed to the five totalising constructions the vignettes actually use: covering N methods, all N wired methods, wraps N detectors, N methods share one interface, N methods in this.
  2. [[ on a missing name errors rather than returning NULL, so words[[tok]] %||% NA threw on “wrapped methods” instead of skipping it.
  3. The guard silently never fired. regmatches(m, regexpr(pat, sub(...))) applies the offsets from the substituted string to the original, so it extracted "co" from "covering 31 detection methods" – never a number, always skipped. Replaced with plain sub() calls.
  4. My verification of it was also wrong: sed 's/covering 50 detection/.../' matched nothing, because the vignette has “covering 50” and “detection methods” on different lines. The test reads the file joined with spaces; sed works line by line. Two clean runs looked like proof and were proof of nothing.

Final state, verified in both directions: the clean tree passes, and breaking the count in each of the four vignettes that state a total fails the suite – introduction.Rmd, comparison.Rmd, extending.Rmd and benchmarks.Rmd – while the benchmarks article’s subset counts stay quiet.

Part XXVI — attribution: are the citations pointing at the right work?

The standing instruction asks whether citations are “attributed to the right work”. Keys resolving (§313) is a weaker property than that. The package carries its own answer: cpt_cite(method) returns, per method, the paper the package says introduced it. So the two can be checked against each other.

323. A check that had to be redesigned before it said anything

First attempt: co-location. For each method, collect the @keys on prose lines that mention the method’s name, and compare their first author with cpt_cite()’s. It paired only 4 of 50 methods – method names mostly appear inside chunks, and citations mostly sit in different sentences – and its single flag was ecp “citing” @grundy2020geomcp, which is one sentence mentioning two engines. Useless in both directions.

Second attempt, well-defined: does the paper cpt_cite() names exist anywhere in the two bibliographies – matching on first-author surname and year across all 123 pooled entries? That question has an answer, and it found four.

324. Two founding papers were named in prose and in no bibliography

method cpt_cite() says status
segneigh Auger and Lawrence (1989) absent from both bibs
amoc Hinkley (1970) absent from both bibs
mcp Lindelov (2020) present as lindelov2020mcp; the matcher cannot equate Lindel{\o}v with ASCII
fcov Aue, Rice and Sonmez (2020) absent, and correctly so

introduction.Rmd names the first two as bare parentheticals – “segment neighbourhoods (Auger and Lawrence, 1989), and at-most-one-change (AMOC; Hinkley, 1970)” – in a sentence where every other method carries a real citation ([@killick2012pelt], [@scott1974cluster], [@maidstone2017optimal]). So two of the four changepoint methods the package has wrapped since 0.1.0 appeared in the text and never in the References.

Fixed: both added to vignette_reference.bib with the metadata cpt_cite() already carries – volume, issue, pages – and no invented DOIs – and the parentheticals replaced with [@auger1989segment] and [@hinkley1970inference]. Verified by rendering: 0 unresolved citation markers, each new key appearing twice in the HTML, once as “(Auger and Lawrence 1989)” in the text and once in the bibliography block.

fcov is the interesting non-fix. cpt_cite("fcov") cites Aue, Rice and Sönmez (2020) on covariance operators and adds “See also … (2018)”, while fmean cites the 2018 functional-mean paper – two different papers, correctly distinguished. The 2020 one is in no bibliography because no vignette discusses fcov at all: every “functional” in the vignettes means functional pruning (fpop, cpop, decafs), a different idea. Adding an entry nothing cites would just recreate §313’s dead weight, and cpt_cite() already gives the reference in full – the same conclusion Demšar reached in §313.

Part XXVII — the help pages and cpt_cite() disagreed about seven methods

§324 compared cpt_cite() against the bibliographies. The same oracle compared against the help pages – for each of the 50 methods, the \insertRef keys in its wrapper’s roxygen block versus the author and year cpt_cite() gives – flags 15.

326. Eight of the fifteen are correct by design

pattern methods why it is right
one Rd covers five methods pelt, binseg, segneigh, amoc, np cpt_wrapper() documents all five, so its @references cites the software paper (killick2014changepoint) while cpt_cite() resolves each method paper – Killick 2012, Scott and Knott 1974, Auger and Lawrence 1989, Hinkley 1970, Haynes 2017

That is the division of labour the package intends: the help page names the package you are calling, cpt_cite() names the paper you should cite.

327. Seven wrappers cited nothing at all

fpop_wrapper(), wbs_wrapper(), wbs2_wrapper(), not_wrapper(), mosum_wrapper(), idetect_wrapper() and tguh_wrapper() had no @references block and no \insertRef – seven method help pages with no reference, where the other forty-three have one.

The cause is upstream of the roxygen: none of the seven keys existed in inst/REFERENCES.bib. They were in vignettes/vignette_reference.bib only, and \insertRef{key}{ggchangepoint} reads the installed bibliography, so the reference could not have been inserted even if someone had tried. Copied across – maidstone2017optimal, fryzlewicz2014wild, fryzlewicz2020detecting, baranowski2019narrowest, eichinger2018mosum, anastasiou2022idetect, fryzlewicz2018tail – and each wrapper given the @references block its siblings have.

328. And one help page credited the wrong paper

fcov_wrapper() detects changes in the covariance operator of a functional series. Its Rd cited aue2018fchange – “Detecting and dating structural breaks in functional data without dimension reduction” – which is fmean_wrapper()’s paper, cited from the same file eleven lines above. cpt_cite("fcov") has the right one and always did: Aue, Rice and Sönmez (2020), “Structural break analysis for spectrum and trace of covariance operators”, Environmetrics 31(1), e2617.

So a reader of ?fcov_wrapper was sent to a paper about the functional mean for a method about covariance. Added aue2020covariance to inst/REFERENCES.bib and repointed the reference.

This is the entry §324 deliberately did not add to the vignette bibliography, on the grounds that nothing cited it. That reasoning still holds and this is not a reversal: the entry belongs in the bibliography where it is cited, and it is cited from an Rd, so it goes in the Rd’s bibliography.

Re-measured: 15 flags -> 7, all seven the design cases above. All 58 \insertRef keys across R/ resolve, 0 missing.

Part XXVIII — two bibliographies, one paper, two author lists

330. 47 shared keys, one divergence

The two bibliographies overlap by 47 keys, and a key present in both with different content renders one way in a vignette’s References and another in a help page. Compared entry by entry – author list plus title, journal, volume, number, pages, year, doi, publisher:

file authors

cpt_cite("beast") renders “Zhao, K., Wulder, M. A., Hu, T., et al. (2019)”, which is a citation string and correctly abbreviates – that is a different artifact from a bibliography entry and needs no change.

331. inst/CITATION hard-coded the version twice

citation("ggchangepoint") is reader-visible and the file agreed with DESCRIPTION on every field – title, author, URL, and version 0.5.0. But the version was written out twice as a literal, in note and again in textVersion, so the next bump would leave citation() advertising the previous release. That is §320’s defect (the introduction’s stale “31 methods”) waiting to happen in the citation a user pastes into a paper.

Both now read meta$Version, which is what R passes to a CITATION file and what Writing R Extensions recommends. Verified by bumping DESCRIPTION to 0.6.0 in place: both fields report 0.6.0 and no 0.5.0 remains anywhere in the rendered entry. Restored.

Part XXIX — the lock-step literals, and a guard debugged three ways

§331 ended by asking where the rest of the “must be edited in lock-step” literals are. Answer: two, both unavoidable, now guarded.

333. The own-version thread closes clean

Every 0.5.0 in R/ and tests/ is a historical comment – “0.5.0: diagnostics, selection and influence”, “0.5.0 layers: the objects the package could not draw before” – which stays true forever. The only code that reads a version uses packageVersion(), and the one version comparison (packageVersion("HDCD") <= "1.1", the Pilliat guard) is about an upstream package and documented. 334. Two files state the method total and cannot compute it

file text
DESCRIPTION “a ‘cpt_detect()’ dispatcher covering fifty methods”
R/ggchangepoint.R -> man/ggchangepoint-package.Rd “dispatcher that reaches fifty methods”

Both are correct today. Neither can be computed – DESCRIPTION and Rd are static text – so the literal has to stay, which makes them precisely the shape that goes stale on the next engine wave, exactly as §320’s “31 detection methods” did in a vignette. §321’s guard now covers them alongside the four vignettes that state a total.

335. Three bugs between writing the guard and having one

Extending a working guard to two more files took three fixes, and all three presented as “the guard does not fire”:

  1. Indented continuation lines. DESCRIPTION wraps as “dispatcher coveringfifty methods”, so joining lines with a single space leaves a run of blanks and a pattern written with literal spaces never matches. Fixed by normalising whitespace before matching – which also retires the line-wrap trap that bit §321’s verification.
  2. My verification, again. Breaking the Rd with a plain string replace looked like it had worked and the guard stayed silent, so I concluded the path was unresolved. The path was fine.
  3. The real bug: a half-added pattern. The new reaches ([A-Za-z0-9]+) methods pattern was added to the pattern list but reaches was never added to the alternation that strips the leading word before reading the number. So tok came out as "reaches", which is not a numeral and not a number word, and every match was silently skipped. A pattern and its parser are two edits, and only one of them was made.

Final state: clean tree passes; breaking the count fires in DESCRIPTION, man/ggchangepoint-package.Rd and the four vignettes, with the offending phrase quoted – "ggchangepoint-package.Rd: 'reaches thirty methods' but the registry has 50".

The discipline is cheap – break the input, watch the failure name the input – and it has now caught more defects in the guards than the guards have caught in the package.

Part XXX — CI green, and the one anomaly it surfaced

7ece62f pushed to master. All five R-CMD-check jobs succeeded, plus pkgdown and the pages deployment. macOS carries only the known environmental note (rgl failing to dlopen for want of libGLU).

338. Windows reports WARN 10 where every other platform reports 2

Not a failure, but a platform difference worth reading rather than ignoring. It decomposes cleanly:

count source verdict
9 test-040-polish.R:1050 – NaNs produced from envcpt’s arima fits the data-dependent case §308 deliberately left unasserted; the test’s own comment predicts exactly this
1 test-050-registry.R:275 – JAGS failed ... Returning an mcpfit without samples investigated below

The nine confirm §308’s decision rather than undermining it: the comment there says “whether a given series also triggers an upstream convergence warning is data-dependent”, and a different platform’s BLAS producing nine instead of two is that sentence being right.

339. The mcp/JAGS path is already correct – and its comment says otherwise

The Windows runner installs mcp but not JAGS. So requireNamespace("mcp") succeeds, mcp::mcp() warns rather than errors, and hands back an mcpfit with no posterior samples. That is S35’s trap (“having the package is not the same as being able to run it”) arriving on a platform CRAN tests.

The wrapper handles it. mcp_has_samples(fit) catches the sample-less fit and stops with an actionable message naming JAGS, so cpt_detect(x, method = "mcp") on Windows errors rather than returning a result built from a model that never sampled. My §S-era fitted sweep wraps its call in tryCatch, so mcp is skipped and only the warning escapes.

What was wrong is the comment fifteen lines above the guard:

mcp imports rjags, so a successful requireNamespace("mcp") already implies JAGS is present.

That is false, and it is false in exactly the way the code below it exists to handle – rjags loads on a machine with no JAGS program. A reader trimming “redundant” checks would have deleted the guard on the strength of it. Rewritten to say what the first check is for (the common case, with the install instruction) and why the second is not redundant.

The escaping warning is now muffled by message text in the sweep, the way §308 handled the other three, so the Windows report will show 9 rather than 10 and every remaining warning is one a reader is meant to see.

Part XXXI — are the workarounds still needed, and still right?

§339 found a comment whose premise its own guard disproved. The same question, asked of the comments that encode upstream behaviour: this package carries a dozen workarounds justified by “engine X does Y”, and if X has since changed, the workaround is either wrong or unnecessary. Nothing re-checks them. Tested against the engine versions actually installed – changepoints 1.1.0, ocd 1.1, ChangePointTaylor 0.3, bcp 4.0.4, HDCD 1.1, bfast 1.7.2, binsegRcpp 2025.5.13.

assumption measured
changepoints::thresholdBS() returns cpt_hat = NULL, not a zero-row matrix, when nothing clears class NULL, is.null TRUE – holds

Two of the six needed a second attempt, and both times the probe was wrong rather than the package:

  • The ocd check first passed thresh = c(1, 1, 1), which makes “compare against 1” true by construction and tests nothing. Re-run with the default Monte Carlo thresholds, the arithmetic is visible and the claim is confirmed.
  • The ChangePointTaylor check looked for a field called confidence_interval and got nothing back, which read like a broken workaround. The column is actually named CI (95%) – with the confidence level inside the column name.

341.1 That column name is a trap the wrapper already avoids

change_point_analyzer(x, CI = 0.9) returns a column called CI (90%), not CI (95%). A wrapper that hard-coded the name would break the moment a user passed conf_level. taylor_wrapper() uses grep("^CI", names(fit))[1], and it works: measured at conf_level 0.95, 0.90 and 0.99 the upstream column is CI (95%), CI (90%), CI (99%) respectively, and the returned intervals widen as they should – [60, 60] -> [59, 60] -> [58, 60].

Part XXXII – The upstream claims, enumerated rather than remembered

344. Why the previous pass was too thin

§343 checked six upstream assumptions because six were the ones I could recall. That is not an audit, it is a memory test. Every contiguous comment block in R/*.R that names a package from Imports or Suggests was extracted instead – 323 blocks – and filtered to those making a behavioural claim (a pkg::fn reference, or the package name within 70 characters of errors|warns|returns|refuses|requires|segfaults|silently|...), leaving 105. What follows is what testing them found.

A workaround is a claim about someone else’s code. It is the only kind of claim in this package that can become false without anything here changing, and R CMD check will never say so.

345. Five claims were wrong, and each had justified a workaround

where the comment said measured
wrap-functional.R “two or three columns” are too coarse a grid, so fChange stops only two fail; ncol 3, 4 and 6 all return a fit
wrap-nonparam.R GLRAdjusted/ExponentialAdjusted are both “rejected by cpm’s own dispatch” GLRAdjusted is rejected; ExponentialAdjusted runs and returns changepoints
wrap-highdim.R ocd::ChangepointDetector() fails at dim = 1 with “subscript out of bounds” it fails, but with “‘dims’ cannot be of length 0”, and only under the wrapper’s default thresh = "MC" – given an explicit numeric thresh it constructs fine at dim = 1
broom-methods.R non-Normal test statistics warn “Not changed to be -2*logLik” CUSUM/CSS error (“logLik is only valid for distributional assumptions”); that warning comes from the cpt.range path instead – the two were swapped
wrap-search.R breakfast’s default "lp" “reports spurious changepoints on constant data” not reproducible: "lp", "ic" and the real default (NULL, not "lp") agree on all four series tried – 0 changepoints in constant, near-constant and pure noise, and the single step at 100 in a two-segment series

None of these broke a user’s result – the workarounds are all conservative – but each recorded a reason that was not the reason, which is how the next reader gets sent after the wrong argument.

346. Two real defects in cpm_wrapper()

cpm_type = "FET" could not succeed. It is offered by match.arg() and documented, but cpm::processStream() has no default for lambda, and without one it dies inside cpm with base R’s “only 0’s may be mixed with negative subscripts” – a message about neither the argument nor the method. Confirmed across Gaussian, Bernoulli, integer and 0/1-as-double input, and across six startup/ARL0 combinations: 0 successes. cpm ships FET thresholds for lambda = 0.1 and 0.3 only (swept 0.01-1.0), and with either one the wrapper returns the right answer – 1 changepoint at 154 for a true change at 150.

A lambda problem was reported as an arl0 problem. cpm prints the same “No thresholds available” line for both arguments, and the branch that catches it assumed arl0. So cpm_wrapper(y, cpm_type = "FET", lambda = 0.5) answered `arl0 = 500` is not an average run length that cpm ships thresholds for – about a value the caller had set correctly. The printed line names which argument it means (“selected lambda” vs “selected ARL0”); the branch now reads it.

347. ?cpt_detect promised a list it had outgrown

The help page names the engines whose own signature ends in ..., so that a misspelt argument is discarded upstream rather than reported – which makes it a promise about every other method. Sweeping all 49 installed methods with an impossible argument name found three that swallow it and were not named: fmean and fcov (both ) and bfast. A reader checking the list would have concluded their typo had been caught.

Nine methods swallow, forty error. The sweep is now the test, because a hand-maintained list of upstream behaviour is exactly the thing that drifts.

348. Both bibliographies had drifted, in the direction nothing checked

§342 recorded “7 uncited, all \insertRef’d from Rd” as benign. Six were. The seventh, demsar2006comparisons, was in both files and cited by neither, and the Rd bibliography separately carried two entries (jewell2022testing, londschien2023changeforest) that only the vignettes cite. With no \insertAllCited anywhere in the package, none of the ten rendered anywhere: each was dead weight that read as though an attribution existed. Each bibliography now holds exactly what its own consumer cites – 63 / 63 in the vignettes, 58 / 58 in the help pages.

The R44 test checked only that a citation resolves. It now also checks that an entry is cited, in both files. Proving it fires meant breaking all four directions:

break result
baseline 84 pass, 0 fail
cite a key with no bib entry fails, names zzzmissingkey
add an uncited vignette-bib entry fails, names zzz2099nobodycites
add an unused Rd-bib entry fails, names zzz2098unusedrd
restored 84 pass, 0 fail

The first attempt at that proof proved nothing: skip_on_cran() meant R44 never ran, and the “passing” break was a skip. Under NOT_CRAN=true the guard then failed on the real tree – correctly, because the existing citation regex demanded a four-digit year and so could not see @rcore. Any misspelling of a yearless key had been invisible to this test since it was written. The pattern now matches pandoc’s key syntax with a lookbehind for the email case: 63 candidates across the seven vignettes, every one a real key, zero false positives.

An exactly noiseless series is safe, as documented. The guard refuses both crash cases and correctly passes both safe ones

Part XXXIII – What a documented pass-through actually does

354. Twelve arguments the docs invited and R refused

... is documented on every wrapper as reaching the engine. Eight wrappers also pin one of that engine’s own arguments – and there was no check, so the two promises collided inside R’s argument matcher:

envcpt_wrapper(x, verbose = TRUE)
#> Error: formal argument "verbose" matched by multiple actual arguments

That message names neither the wrapper, nor the engine, nor what to do instead. Sweeping every registry method against every argument its wrapper hardcodes to a literal that the engine also accepts found twelve such pairs:

method argument(s)
wbs2, tguh solution.path, model.selection
smuce jumpint
bocpd getR
beast season, quiet, print.progress
decafs warningMessage
sn plot_SN
envcpt verbose

The pins are all deliberate, so honouring them is the wrong fix. solution.path is what makes tguh tguh; jumpint is what makes SMUCE’s ci_lower/ci_upper columns exist at all; getR is what ggcpt_runlength() draws; plot_SN is what stops SNSeg drawing to the active device; the rest keep engine narration out of the result. So they are refused by name instead, through one shared helper, each with the reason it is fixed:

#> Error: `tguh` sets `solution.path` itself, so it cannot be supplied
#> through `...`: it is what selects the tail-greedy unbalanced-Haar path
#> rather than one of breakfast's others -- a `tguh` result with a
#> different path is not tguh.

Re-swept afterwards: 0 raw collisions remain, all twelve refuse by name, and the five arguments that were legitimately accepted before still are (envcpt_wrapper(x, minseglen = 10) among them). Proved by disabling one guard, which brought the raw message straight back and failed the new test with two expectations naming envcpt verbose.

355. The vignettes disagreed about the package

introduction.Rmd: “50 detection methods across six algorithmic families”. ggchangepoint.Rmd: “50 methods across nine methodological families”. Same 50 methods, same package, two numbers.

“Family” is a prose taxonomy, not a registry column, so neither number can be derived – but the introduction enumerates its six (penalised and optimal partitioning, multiscale and search, Bayesian, nonparametric and sequential, multivariate and high-dimensional, regression-based) and has one section per family plus two for the cross-cutting concerns it names, which is exactly the eight tour sections it has. The nine had no enumeration and nothing in the package counts to it: _pkgdown.yml has eleven wrapper groups, not nine. ggchangepoint.Rmd now says six.

Guarded both ways – the vignettes must agree, and the number must equal the list the introduction spells out. Proved by reintroducing the disagreement (fails, quoting both files) and by deleting one family from the enumeration (fails, 5 against 6). The enumeration parse needed one correction of its own: four of the six names contain their own “and”, so splitting on ,| and read a list of six as ten.

357. Two stale justifications, corrected

EnvCpt’s stderr diversion cited “Error in arima(…): non-stationary AR part from CSS”. That would not reproduce on any of eight series chosen to provoke it – random walk, explosive AR(1), doubly-integrated, scaled to 1e6, numerically constant, exact step, and two ordinary two-segment series – zero stderr lines each. The engine’s only stderr output is its “Fitting 12 models” narration, which this call already suppresses with verbose = FALSE. The diversion is kept (it costs nothing and an upstream try() that stopped being silent would print into the caller’s console) but the comment no longer claims to be fixing an observed leak. What it must not do is swallow real conditions, and it does not: a genuine convergence warning still reaches the user.

The error-message sweep – every backticked name in a stop()/warning() checked against the enclosing function’s formals – found no new defects across 23 candidates. All are column names, aesthetics, or another function’s arguments; n_replicates, the one that looked wrong, is a documented output column of cpt_confint().

The first 4.6.0 run of this pass failed, and the fault was mine. The new managed-argument test ends with expect_gt(tested, 0L) – a tripwire against a sweep that silently tests nothing – but every engine it sweeps is a Suggests one, so against an Imports-only library it correctly tested nothing and the tripwire fired:

── Failure (test-050-registry.R:399:3) ──
Expected `tested` > 0L.

This is the same mistake §353 recorded fixing for the swallow sweep one pass earlier, repeated in a new test written the same day. The condition is now a skip() on “no relevant engine installed”, and the R-devel run confirms it: • none of the engines with a managed argument is installed (1). The lesson worth keeping is narrower than “guard the guards”: a tripwire asserting that a sweep did work is itself environment-dependent, and belongs behind the same availability check as the sweep.

Part XXXIV – Two engines that were mostly broken, and nobody knew

359. The result contract holds everywhere

Before hunting bugs, a baseline: every method’s returned ggcpt was checked against the documented contract on five input shapes each – an ordinary two-segment series, pure noise, a change 8 observations from the start, one 8 from the end, and a 30-point series. 245 cells, zero violations. What was checked, per cell: cp integer, inside , sorted, unique, no NA; cp_value equal to the series at cp; segments tiling contiguously with n = end - start + 1 and one more row than there are changepoints; method and change_in length-one; data with n rows.

That is the invariant the rest of the package is built on, and it is now measured rather than assumed. The sweep is also what surfaced both defects below – not as contract violations, but as errors in cells that should have produced a result.

360. wbsts could not report more than one changepoint

wbsts::wbs.lsw() ends with

OUT = post.processing(...)          # the post-processed breakpoint set
suppressWarnings(if (is.na(OUT)) OUT = NULL)

That suppressWarnings() was the right fix when if on a length > 1 condition was a warning. Since R 4.2 it is an error, and suppressWarnings() does nothing for an error. So the call dies with “the condition has length > 1” exactly when post-processing keeps two or more changepoints – which is to say, whenever the method would report more than one.

Measured on R 4.4.1, before the fix:

series runs failures changepoints reported on success
1 change, n = 120 20 2 0 or 1
3 changes, n = 400 20 19 1
5 changes, n = 600 20 19 0

A wrapper cannot patch upstream, but every piece wbs.lsw() uses – tau.fun, ews.trans, uh.wbs, post.processing – is exported by . So the failure is caught, .Random.seed is restored to what it was before the call, and the body is replayed line for line with the single line corrected to all(is.na(OUT)), which is what the surrounding suppressWarnings() shows was meant.

Restoring the seed is the point. It means the replay draws the identical random intervals, so it does not return a different answer – it returns the one the upstream function had already computed and then threw away. Verified: on 30 runs where wbs.lsw() succeeds, the replay’s cp.bef and cp.aft are identical() to upstream’s 30 out of 30. Afterwards the table above reads 0 failures in all three rows, with counts up to 6 and 8 – the method now finds the multiple changepoints it exists to find. An unrelated upstream refusal (one scale) still propagates untouched.

361. hdcov failed on 44-96% of runs, intermittently

changepoints::thresholdBS.BS() prunes the binary-segmentation tree with

for (i in 2:level_length) { ... 1:table(BS_object$Level)[i] ... }

so a single-level tree makes that 2:1, the body runs with i = 2, table(...)[2] is NA, and 1:NA stops with base R’s “NA/NaN argument”. BS.cov() returns one level whenever the series is short relative to the number of coordinates – and because the threshold comes from a permutation draw, whether a given call lands there is random:

n p failures / 25 seeds
200 10 11
120 8 23
80 5 12
400 20 24
300 10 0

An intermittent opaque error on exactly the shapes a high-dimensional covariance method is for. Refusing would have been wrong – the answer is not in doubt. One level means one candidate split with no ancestors to prune against, so it is a changepoint precisely when its own statistic clears the threshold; on a multi-level tree that same rule reproduces thresholdBS()’s output exactly (checked: locations 156, 218 either way), which is what makes it safe to apply. Multi-level trees still go through thresholdBS() unchanged, so nothing that already worked can move.

After: 0 failures in 125 runs across all five cells.

362. Vignette numbers, checked against the live package

pelt gives 1 changepoint at , 29 at , 138 at introduction.Rmd exact at n = 200, set.seed(1)
"MBIC" is , and is not Zhang-Siegmund’s mBIC introduction.Rmd matches the implementation line for line
CROPS default range is , admits “a handful” of segmentations, and the most parsimonious recovers both true changepoints introduction.Rmd range confirmed in the formals; 2 segmentations; most parsimonious has 2 changepoints at exactly 100 and 200
one hit out of two predictions and two truths gives precision = recall = F1 = 0.5 comparison.Rmd 0.5, 0.5, 0.5
cpm raises about 3.7 false alarms per 2000 in-control observations, edetector about 13 monitoring.Rmd 3.75 and 12.08

363. One vignette number was wrong, and it was load-bearing

monitoring.Rmd claimed a larger run gives median detection delays of “12, 4 and 2” for edetector at shifts of 1, 2 and 3 sigma, against “11, 5 and 4” for cpm. At 150 replicates per cell under two seeds:

shift edetector cpm
1 7, 8 (claimed 12) 10, 10 (claimed 11)
2 3, 3 (claimed 4) 5, 5
3 2, 2 (claimed 2) 4, 4

cpm’s row was right. edetector’s 1-sigma figure was not – and the prose built an argument on it: “the small run above and the larger one disagree about which is ahead”. They do not. The vignette’s own displayed chunk gives edetector 7.0, 4.0, 1.5 against cpm 9.0, 4.5, 4.0 – edetector ahead at every shift – and the larger run agrees at every shift. Only the erroneous 12 made edetector look slower than cpm at 1 sigma. The numbers are now the measured ones, the design is stated (150 replicates, two seeds), and the conclusion says what the data says: the gap is real but modest where the change is small, with inter-quartile ranges of [5, 12] and [7, 15] that overlap almost entirely.

364. ocd’s timing note understated it by 2-3x

The note said, at mc_reps = 5, “about 3 s at , 9 s at and 55 s at ”, extrapolating to “roughly a minute” at the default mc_reps = 100. Measured here: 10.3 s, 21.6 s and 113.4 s, and 189 s at the default – so minutes, not a minute. The shape was right and is what matters (linear in mc_reps: 38 s at 20 against 189 s at 100 is exactly 5x for 5x), and the advice was right, but a reader planning around “roughly a minute” would wait three. Not a threading artefact – unthrottled and pinned to one thread give the same 38 s. The note now carries the measured figures, says they are one machine’s, and points at the linearity as the part to plan around. Its other claim held: monitoring after calibration is cheap, 0.37 s for a thousand observations.

365. A negative result

Every backticked name inside a stop() or warning() was checked against the enclosing function’s formals – 23 candidates, no defects. All are column names, aesthetics, or another function’s arguments.

366. Two things the check caught that I had introduced or missed

An escaped underscore in Rd. The rewritten ocd timing note said x86\_64, which is right in a vignette and wrong in Rd: R CMD check answered

* checking Rd files ... NOTE
checkRd: (-1) ocd_wrapper.Rd:68: Escaped LaTeX specials: \_

a NOTE the baseline does not have. Now x86-64, and a sweep confirms no other \_ anywhere in R/. (Running tools::checkRd() directly on the sources reports “Lost braces” on every \insertRef in 84 files; that is an artefact of checking before Rdpack expands them, which is why R CMD check — which builds first — never reported it.)

A misplaced helper deleted a help page. wbs_lsw_replay() was inserted immediately above wbsts_wrapper <- function(...), which put it between the wrapper’s roxygen block and the function it documents. The block then documented the @noRd helper, man/wbsts_wrapper.Rd was deleted, and git status jumped to 70 files. Moving the helper above the roxygen block restored it. Worth stating as a rule: an internal helper goes above the whole roxygen block of whatever follows it, never between a block and its function.

367. The package sits on CRAN’s 5Mb boundary

One 4.4.1 run reported

* checking installed package size ... NOTE
  installed size is  5.2Mb
  sub-directories of 1Mb or more:
    doc   3.8Mb

and seven other runs of the same tree — three under 4.4.1 and four under 4.6.0 — did not. The tarball grew 7.5 KB this pass, and neither engine fixed above appears in any vignette, so the swing is not attributable to these changes: the installed size is simply within rounding distance of the 5Mb threshold, and what decides it is how large the rendered vignette figures happen to come out. doc is 3.9Mb, 3.6Mb of it the seven HTML files with their base64 figures (ggchangepoint.html alone is 1.2Mb), against 2.0Mb of help and 625Kb of R.

Recorded rather than acted on: the figures already run at dpi = 72, and shrinking them further would change how the vignettes look, which is a choice about the documentation rather than a defect in it. But a reviewer may raise it, and the answer is that it is vignette HTML, not data or compiled artefacts.

New guards this pass, each proved by breaking its input: the managed-argument refusal (12 pairs; disabling one guard brought the raw R message back and failed the test with two expectations naming envcpt verbose), the hdcov single-level route (8 expectations, including one asserting that upstream still fails on that tree, so a future upstream fix is signalled rather than silently bypassed), and the wbsts replay (5 expectations, one of which checks the replay is identical() to upstream wherever upstream can run).

Part XXXV – What the published capability table actually delivers

369. The flakiness that motivated this pass is gone

§360 and §361 were both found because a method failed sometimes. So the first thing this pass did was look for more of that: every method, twelve different random series each, failures counted.

Zero intermittent failures across 45 methods x 12 seeds. The four non-clean rows are all explained and none is stochastic: ocd and fcov exceed the per-cell time limit (§364 measures ocd at 189 s a fit, so twelve of them cannot fit in any sane cap), and hdreg and fabisearch fail all twelve because the sweep hands them a plain Gaussian matrix when one needs a response and the other needs non-negative input – their own errors say so.

Last pass’s two fixes closed the flakiness, and nothing else in the package has any.

370. cpt_methods() published four capabilities it could not deliver

The registry carries one boolean per capability, and cpt_statistic(), cpt_solution_path() and ggcpt_posterior() each build their “these do:” error message from those columns. That makes a wrong flag worse than misleading:

> cpt_solution_path(cpt_detect(x, method = "wbsts"))
Error: Engine `wbsts` does not expose a solution path. These do:
binseg, segneigh, wbs, wbs2, not, tguh, wbsts, binsegrcpp
                                        ^^^^^

The message lists the method it is refusing. Sweeping all 50 methods against the real accessors – posterior_prob_profile(), extract_statistic(), extract_solution_path(), $data$fitted, the changepoints tibble – found four disagreements:

method flag accessor says resolution
wbsts path no path flag -> FALSE
binsegrcpp path no path flag -> FALSE
nsp ci no ci_lower/ci_upper flag kept – see below
bocpd posterior no per-location profile flag kept – see below

fitted and statistic were correct for all 50.

Why two flags stay. cpt_recommend(need_uncertainty = TRUE) is documented as asking for “a confidence interval or significance region” and filters on ci | posterior. nsp reports a region (region_start/region_end plus $regions), so its ci flag is right for the question actually being asked – it was the registry’s own internal comment, which said the flag means “populates ci_lower/ci_upper”, that was too narrow. Same for bocpd: it is Bayesian and does quantify the location, but over run lengths, drawn by ggcpt_runlength(). Both comments now say what the flags mean and name the exceptions.

Why the other two go to FALSE rather than getting an implementation. The data is there – binsegrcpp’s $splits is a textbook nested path (segments, end, loss, depth) and wbsts keeps cp.bef, the candidates before post-processing. Writing the extraction would be a new capability, which this pass is not for, and it would add an untested code path to a release about to be submitted. Nothing that ever worked is lost: cpt_solution_path() has always errored for both. Recorded here so the implementation is a small job whenever it is wanted.

371. ?mcp_wrapper claimed a function that rejects it

the changepoints themselves get full posterior distributions rather than point estimates, which ggcpt_posterior() already knows how to draw.

ggcpt_posterior() handles exactly two fit classes, bcp and beast, and returns NULL for everything else. Handed an mcp result it stops with “No posterior probability profile found on this object.” The help page now says what mcp actually gives – ci_lower/ci_upper from the posterior quantiles, $data$fitted – and that ggcpt_posterior() does not accept it.

And because cpt_methods() sends people to that function, its error message now names the accessor that does work for the method in hand: run-length for bocpd, the interval columns for mcp. A dead end became a signpost.

372. The vignette’s result-contract table was two engines short

introduction.Rmd lists which engines add which optional column. Measured against the live package, ci_lower/ci_upper are populated by six engines, not the four listed: bfast and taylor were missing, and mcp does it too. The table now names all of them and, since a reader comparing it with cpt_methods() would otherwise wonder, says explicitly that nsp reports a region instead.

Everything else in that table checked out exactly: posterior_prob really is bcp and beast alone, detection_time really is only cpm, strength only inspect, declared_at only ocd, mapping only geomcp.

373. Attribution, checked with the package’s own oracle

cpt_cite() records who invented each method; the wrappers carry \insertRef keys. Those are two independent records of the same fact, and R44 never compared them – it only checked that a key resolves and that the two bibliographies agree with each other.

Comparing them: 45 of 50 methods match exactly on year. The five that do not are pelt, binseg, segneigh, amoc and np, which share cpt_wrapper and cite killick2014changepoint – the software paper. That is correct: the help page opens “This function wraps a number of cpt functions from the changepoint package”, so the software paper is the right citation for the wrapper, while cpt_cite() gives each method’s original work (Killick 2012, Scott and Knott 1974, Auger and Lawrence 1989, Hinkley 1970, Haynes 2017) and the vignettes cite those where the methods are discussed. No misattribution.

Bibliographies re-verified: 63/63 vignette entries cited, 58/58 Rd keys resolving, 0 dangling, 0 unused, every entry carrying its required fields.

374. Instrument errors worth recording

The first capability sweep reported 19 mismatches. All 19 were mine: I tested fitted by asking whether segments$param_estimate was finite – which is part of every result’s contract, so it answered TRUE for everything – and statistic by looking for names in $diagnostics rather than calling extract_statistic(). The registry’s own comments say precisely what each flag means (fitted populates a length-n signal on $data); reading them first would have saved the sweep. The corrected sweep found the four real disagreements above.

Also: a bib-field parser that captured four lines per field turned year = 2014 into 2014426 by concatenating it with pages, which is what made all 50 methods look misattributed at first.

Part XXXVI – The whole S3 surface, and 23 arguments the docs invited

376. Every generic works on every result

Nothing had ever checked that. The contract sweep of §359 verified the data; this one verifies the surface: for each method’s result, all ten of autoplot(), plot(), print(), format(), summary(), tidy(), glance(), augment(), as_tibble() and as.data.frame(), with the two plotting ones forced through ggplot2::ggplot_build() so laziness cannot hide a failure.

40 methods x 10 generics, zero failures. hdreg skips (it needs a response, and says so) and fabisearch exceeded the time limit.

377. 23 arguments the documentation invited and R refused

Every wrapper documents ... as reaching its engine. Most also rename that engine’s arguments into this package’s snake_case – n_intervals for wbs’s M, cpm_type for cpm’s cpmType, min_dist for fabisearch’s mindist – or derive them from x. So the engine’s own name is the natural thing for a reader of the upstream help page to pass, and it collided with the value the wrapper already supplies:

> fabisearch_wrapper(M, nruns = 2, mindist = 5)
Error: formal argument "mindist" matched by multiple actual arguments

Sweeping every wrapper against every argument its engine accepts – 86 pairs – found 23 of these, across 14 methods:

method engine argument use instead
ecp min.size min_size
fpop lambda penalty
wbs, wbsts M n_intervals
cpop, decafs beta penalty
bocpd hazard_func hazard
cpm cpmType, ARL0 cpm_type, arl0
kcp RS_fun, RS_name, Kmax running_stat, kmax
sn paras_to_test, ts parameter, x
ocd MC_reps, dim mc_reps, derived
strucchange formula derived
segmented seg.Z derived
fabisearch mindist, nruns, nreps, ncore min_dist, n_runs, n_reps, n_core
bfast max.iter max_iter

§354’s sweep missed every one of them, and the reason is worth recording: it matched name = <literal>, and these are mindist = min_dist – a variable. Testing against the engine’s own formals instead of against a static pattern is what found them, and needs no parsing at all.

Because these are renamed rather than pinned, the answer is a redirection rather than a refusal:

> cpt_detect(x, method = "wbs", M = 200)
Error: `wbs` renames its engine's `M` argument, so passing it through `...`
collides with the value the wrapper already supplies. Use `n_intervals`
instead.

Re-swept afterwards: 0 raw collisions, all 23 redirected, the 12 pinned arguments from §354 still refused, and the 18 legitimately-accepted arguments identical to before.

378. network had the same upstream bug as hdcov

§361 fixed changepoints::thresholdBS()’s single-level-tree failure in hdcov_wrapper(). network_wrapper() calls the same function, and asking the obvious next question found the same failure: 10 of 12 runs for a 20-point sequence of 4-node graphs, the same “NA/NaN argument”, the same cause. It is clean from n = 30 up, which is why one shape per method never saw it.

The route-around is now a shared threshold_bs() helper used by both wrappers rather than inline code in one, so a third caller cannot reintroduce it. Verified: network 10/12 failures -> 0, hdcov unchanged, and on six multi-level trees the helper’s output is identical() to upstream’s – 6 of 6.

379. Vignette pass

benchmarks.Rmd had never been checked as a whole. Every count claim in it is internally consistent with the list or table it introduces: “Nine methods exceeded a 120-second limit” lists 9; “Five of those” lists 5 and is a subset of the 9; “Ten methods raise zero false alarms” matches exactly the 10 all-zero rows in its table; “four provenances” matches its 4-row table. All 25 method names it mentions are real registry methods – no invented ones.

380. Two non-defects, checked so they stay checked

ggcptplot() rejects a one-column data frame while ggecpplot() accepts one. Not an inconsistency: ggcptplot() takes @inheritParams cpt_wrapper, whose data is documented as “A numeric vector”, while ecp_wrapper() documents “a numeric vector (for univariate) or matrix/data.frame (for multivariate)”. Each matches its own contract.

fabisearch writes an NMF_<hash>/ directory into the working directory while it runs, which git status catches mid-sweep and which got copied into two check trees before I noticed. It is NMF’s own scratch space and it is removed on completion – measured: nothing left behind. The lesson is about my own sequencing, not the package: do not start a build while a sweep is running.

The first R-devel run of this pass failed, on the same mistake as §358 and §368. The new renamed-argument test ended with expect_gt(tested, 5L), and against an Imports-only library only one of its seventeen engines exists:

── Failure (test-050-registry.R:616:3) ──
Expected `tested` > 5L.
Actual comparison: 1 <= 5

§358 recorded the lesson (“a tripwire asserting that a sweep did work is itself environment-dependent”) and I then wrote the same assertion again. So the fix is not another note – it is a shape that cannot misfire. Both sweeps now count how many cases could run and assert against that:

available <- sum(vapply(cases, function(z) engine_installed(z$eng), logical(1)))
...
expect_equal(tested, available)

That still catches a sweep which silently tests nothing (available would have to be 0 too, which the accompanying expect_gt(available, 0L) refuses), and it is correct on any library. The capability guard of §370 carried the same > 5L threshold and has been converted too, before it could fail on some future machine.

New guards this pass: the renamed-argument redirection (54 expectations across 17 cases) and network’s share of the threshold_bs() route-around (added to the existing hdcov test, which now also asserts the helper is identical() to upstream on multi-level trees rather than merely equivalent).

Part XXXVII – Argument values, not argument names

382. A new axis

The last three passes swept argument names – typos discarded, pinned arguments colliding, renamed arguments colliding. This one sweeps argument values: every numeric or logical-defaulted argument of every exported non-detector function, probed with NA, Inf, -1, 0, a length-2 vector and a string, asking one question of each result – does the error name the argument the caller passed?

That question is the whole point. An error is only useful if the reader can tell which of their arguments caused it, and a wrapper that forwards a value into an engine or a plotting layer loses that thread by default.

383. Three arguments answered about something else

cpt_power(sigma =) and cpt_min_detectable(sigma =) answered about sd. sigma reaches cpt_simulate() as its sd, and neither caller validated it, so a bad value came back as `sd` must be a single finite number – naming an argument neither function has. Both now check it.

cpt_power(location =) was silently clamped, and reported power for a different changepoint. It is documented as “a fraction of n in (0, 1) or an integer position”, may be a vector (so validate_scalar() cannot express it), and went through nothing at all. The scenario loop clamps with max(2, min(cp, n - 2)), so:

asked for changepoint actually used reported
location = 0.5 100 power 1
location = -1 2 power 0.75
location = 0 2 power 0.75
location = 1e6 198 power 0.75

Every one of those looks like an answer. A new validate_location() enforces the documented contract elementwise – a fraction in (0, 1), or an integer in [1, n-1] – so a position that is not a position is refused, while every documented form, vectors included, still works. The clamp stays: it is right for an extreme fraction (0.001 rounds to 0, and a changepoint needs observations either side).

ggcpt_interactive(width_svg =) answered about width. ggiraph::girafe() reports “width must be a scalar positive number”, its own internal name. Checked now on the ggiraph path only, because that is the only path that uses it – the plotly branch ignores both arguments, as documented, and still does.

And cpt_simulate(df =) used a bare if (df <= 2), so df = NA answered “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed” and df = "a" answered “invalid arguments”. rho, immediately beside it, already went through validate_scalar(). df now does too, keeping its domain message – “must exceed 2 so the t-noise variance exists” is worth saying with its reason.

384. Two contrasts worth keeping

cpt_scenarios() was already right, and shows what “right” is. Its location is fractions-only, it clamps the same way – and it warns, naming the argument and explaining the fraction convention, for every scenario it moved. So it is left exactly as it is. Silence was the defect in cpt_power(), not clamping.

ggcptplot()’s cptline_alpha and cptline_linewidth are not defects. They accept NA, 0 and -1, and a length-2 value fails late with ggplot2’s “Problem while setting up geom” or grid’s “‘lwd’ must be non-negative”. But measured against ggplot2 itself, geom_vline() accepts every one of those five values too – alpha = NA is a meaningful ggplot2 idiom for fully transparent. These are documented aesthetic pass-throughs, and matching the leniency of the grammar they are built on is the correct behaviour, not a gap.

385. Vignette pass

Every `fn()` referenced anywhere in the vignettes resolves to something that exists – the single external one, penaltyLearning::IntervalRegressionCV(), is present at 2024.9.3 and correctly attributed. 386. Two more of the same, found by finishing the sweep

The sweep’s full result over all 83 argument slots: 48 clean, 15 whose base call could not be built generically, and 20 flagged. Of the 20, twelve resolved as by-design (arguments documented as used only on another code path – cpt_monitor’s arl0/patience/mc_reps, cpt_simulate’s rho, cpt_scenarios’s clamping-with-a-warning; new_ggcpt, whose help page says outright that “this constructor does not check its arguments”; and the ggplot2 aesthetics of §384). The rest were the six fixed here.

ggecpplot()/ecp_wrapper()’s min_size answered about min.size. Same shape as sigma->sd and width_svg->width: the value reaches ecp under its own name, so min_size = -1 came back as “min.size must be an integer greater than 1”, and min_size = NA reached an if and answered “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”.

cpt_scenarios()’s seed is used arithmetically – seed + (i - 1) * n_rep + r, to give each scenario its own stream – so a character seed died in + with “non-numeric argument to binary operator” and a length-2 seed silently vectorised.

Both now go through validate_scalar(), which is what the rest of the package uses and what names the argument.

Part XXXVIII – The supports column, verified

388. Every change_in a method claims does work

supports is published in cpt_methods() and drives validate_method_change_in(), which refuses anything outside it. So each listed value is a promise about what the method will do – the same kind of promise the path flag made and could not keep (§370).

Sweeping all 73 (method, listed change_in) pairs: zero fail. The five non-results are all explained and none is a broken claim – mcp x 3 because mcp/rjags are absent here, ocd x 1 on the 189-second fit of §364, and hdreg’s regression because my probe passed y as a vector when y selects a column of x, which its own error says.

That is a clean negative result on a table users read to decide what to run.

389. Six requests are answered with a different change type

The sweep’s other output. A compatible request is sometimes routed to the method’s own native change type, because the engine has no separate estimator for the thing asked about:

method requested detected
not var meanvar
cpm mean, var distribution
kcp mean, var running mean, running var
wbsts mean var

None of it is silent – the result’s change_in records what was actually detected – and each individual case is defensible. not genuinely has no variance-only contrast: its variance contrast is pcwsConstMeanVar, piecewise-constant in mean and variance, and ?not_wrapper’s @return already says the reported value is "mean", "meanvar" or "slope". wbsts detects change in the wavelet spectrum. cpm is a distribution detector; kcp works on running statistics.

What was missing is that ?cpt_detect did not prepare the reader. Its change_in documentation promised only the negative half – “incompatible combinations error rather than silently running something else” – which reads as though a compatible request gets what it asked for. It now names the six routed pairs and says to compare the result’s change_in with the request. Documentation, not behaviour: nothing about what the engines do has changed.

Guarded both ways: every listed change_in must still work, and the routed set must be exactly those six for the methods the test reaches. A seventh appearing means the help page has gone stale.

Part XXXIX – The dimension flags, and nine refusals made to agree

392. Completing the registry verification

ci, fitted, posterior, statistic, path (§370) and supports (§388) have been checked against behaviour. This pass finishes the table: multivariate, univariate and online.

online is consistent, and three different sets explain each other. The registry flags bocpd, cpm, ocd; cpt_monitor()/cpt_replay() accept edetector, cpm, ocd; cpt_recommend(online = TRUE) returns bocpd, cpm. All three are right. edetector is monitor-only – not in the detector registry at all, documented under ?cpt_monitor’s method, and cpt_detect(method = "edetector") is refused with the valid list. ocd is absent from the recommendation because dimension defaults to "univariate", which ?cpt_recommend states, and ocd is multivariate-only; asking for dimension = "multivariate" returns it.

multivariate is accurate for all 50 methods on a 3-column matrix.

393. univariate = FALSE did not mean what it said

The registry’s comment read “FALSE for the engines that need at least two coordinates and error on one”. Testing every one of the fourteen against a plain vector split them in two:

behaviour on a vector engines
errors ocd, geomcp, hdcov, network, var, kwc, hdreg, fmean, fcov
runs, and recovers the changepoint at 110 npmojo, inspect, esac, pilliat

So the flag is not the behavioural claim it was documented as. It is right for its actual consumer – cpt_recommend(dimension = "univariate"), where pointing someone at a sparse high-dimensional projector for one series would be poor advice however well it runs – so the comment is what changed, in both the registry and cpt_recommend(). FALSE now records intent, and names the four engines that tolerate a single column without being meant for it.

394. Four opaque refusals, and a fifth the guard caught

Of the nine that do refuse a vector, five named the requirement and four answered with something a reader cannot act on:

method was now
hdcov “non-conformable arrays” Method `hdcov` is high-dimensional and needs at least two coordinates, but `x` has 1
var “incorrect number of dimensions” same shape
kwc “dim(X) must have a positive length” same shape
network “‘x’ must be an array of at least two dimensions” names the n x p^2 / n x p x p shape it wants

Then the new guard – which requires a refusal to name the method, so a reader with several in flight knows which call failed – caught a fifth: geomcp answered changepoint.geo’s “Univariate changepoint analysis is not supported”, clearer than base R but naming neither the method nor the argument. It now matches the other eight.

That is the guard doing its job on its first run, which is the argument for writing the assertion stronger than the fix.

All nine refusals now name the method; the multivariate paths are unchanged (hdcov, var, kwc, network and geomcp all still work on the input they are for), and a one-column matrix is refused as well as a bare vector.

399. Vignette pass

400. What the fix got wrong, and how the suite said so

The first R 4.4.1 run of this pass failed, on two existing tests – and the failures were right:

Error ('test-040-polish.R:1448'): Error: `arl0` must be a single finite
                                  number, at least 1 (got 0).
Error ('test-050-engines.R:216'):  Error: `frequency` must be a single finite
                                  number, at least 2 (got 1).

Both arguments already had a better guard than the one I added. arl0’s printed-error branch names the average run lengths cpm actually ships thresholds for; bfast_wrapper() refuses a frequency below 2 with a message about the seasonal frequency. My generic validate_scalar(..., min = ) fired first and replaced each with a range complaint – a regression in message quality dressed as an improvement.

The lesson is specific enough to be worth stating: a blanket validation added in front of an existing specific guard makes the message worse, not better. Both now validate type and length only (validate_scalar(arl0, "arl0")), so NA, "a" and c(1, 2) are caught by name while 0, -5, 333 and frequency = 1 still get the message that tells the reader what the legal values are. Verified both ways.

Then the full suite caught a third thing: the “no test reaches a Suggests engine outside a guarded block” check flagged this pass’s own new guards, because they gate per-method work on engine_installed() rather than skip_if_not_installed(). That predicate is the package’s own, and for a loop over methods it is the better guard – it skips the one method instead of aborting the test – so the detector now recognises it. The check was working; it just did not know that spelling.

Full suite after all three corrections: 0 failures.

Part XLI – The extension mechanism, and two side effects a check must not trigger

402. The headline feature holds under abuse

cpt_register_method() is the first thing the 0.5.0 notes describe, and nothing had tested it with a badly behaved detector. Seventeen shapes, each registered and run through cpt_detect():

the registered function returns result
valid indices, or a ggcpt accepted, contract holds
unsorted, duplicated, 0, n, beyond n, negative, containing NA, non-integer, integer(0) accepted, sanitised, contract still holds
a character vector, NULL, a list, a data frame refused, message naming the registered method
the input series back accepted; 7 survive the sanitising
an error propagated verbatim

The sanitising is not a lapse – ?as_ggcpt’s @param cp says exactly “Out-of-range, duplicated and missing values are dropped, and the result is sorted – the same contract every built-in wrapper is held to”, and @param fn points a bare-vector return at that function. So a user’s buggy detector is held to the same standard as a wired one, which is the right call, and it is written down. No defect.

403. HDCD’s power-of-two trap, measured

The pilliat guard is the most consequential upstream workaround in the package, and its claim had only been spot-checked at one dimension. Measured across fourteen:

p 2 3 4 5 7 8 9 15 16 17 31 32 33 64
raw HDCD::Pilliat() cpts on 120 points 119 1 119 1 1 119 1 1 119 1 1 119 1 119
wrapper refuses ok refuses ok ok refuses ok ok refuses ok ok refuses ok refuses

At every power of two the engine reads past the end of its threshold vector and returns a changepoint at every observation; at every other dimension it returns the one real changepoint. The guard fires exactly on the powers of two, with no false positive across eight other dimensions. Without it a user gets 119 garbage changepoints and no indication anything is wrong.

404. Two functions with side effects a check must never trigger

cpt_install_engines() installs packages; cpt_load_tcpd() downloads from the Turing Change Point Dataset’s GitHub repository. Both are currently safe – and nothing was holding them that way:

  • extending.Rmd has a bare cpt_install_engines("bayesian"), safe only because its chunk carries eval = FALSE;
  • ggchangepoint.Rmd’s evaluated chunk passes dry_run = TRUE;
  • cpt_load_tcpd() appears in the vignettes as prose only, and its examples are \dontrun{} with the reason stated.

Deleting one chunk option would make R CMD check install packages while building a vignette. That is now guarded: every evaluated vignette chunk calling cpt_install_engines() must pass dry_run = TRUE, no evaluated chunk may call cpt_load_tcpd() at all, and both help pages must stay \dontrun{} or dry-run. Proved by deleting the dry_run = TRUE, which fails the guard with “ggchangepoint.Rmd:822 installs packages in an evaluated chunk”.

405. Vignette pass

Accessibility, checked properly for the first time: 65 chunks emit a static figure and all 65 carry fig.alt. (The first detector flagged ten of them; every one was a false positive – seven include = FALSE setup chunks, two chunks whose value is a tibble, and one returning an htmlwidget.)

The remaining verbatim-quoted upstream messages both hold: as.numeric() on a character vector really does warn “NAs introduced by coercion” (and the package refuses a character or factor series before reaching it, with its own message), and ggcpt_eval() on an evaluation with no prediction and no miss raises zero warnings, which is what its early return exists for.

Bibliographies re-verified: 63/63 cited, 58/58 keys resolving, 0 dangling, 0 unused, all complete.
