The one change is a test: the side-effect guard of §404, which protects a CRAN-compliance property (no package installation, no network access while building a vignette) that was true only by the accident of nobody having edited two chunk options.

Part XLII – Two cross-cutting properties nothing had measured

407. Reproducibility, across every wrapper that offers a seed

Nineteen wrappers take a seed. Nothing asserted the property the argument exists for: two runs with the same seed give the same answer.

Measured on all nineteen – 17 reproducible, 0 not. The two gaps are environmental, not failures: mcp needs JAGS, and fabisearch cannot fit three times inside any reasonable cap.

The measurement needed one correction first. On a 5-sigma step every random draw finds the same changepoint, so identical answers across different seeds prove nothing about whether the seed was used at all – my first run reported wbs as “seed-ignored” purely because the signal was too easy. The series is now a 0.4-sigma change, where the draw actually decides, and “same answer under two different seeds” is reported rather than failed: for a method that aggregates a thousand random intervals, draw-insensitivity is a property, not a bug.

408. An index was guarded for two methods out of forty-nine

?cpt_detect promises an index is “stored on the result and threaded through tidy() (as cp_index), augment(), autoplot() and cpt_report()” – for every method. test-050-index.R checked pelt and ecp.

Swept all 49: 38 reachable, all correct – the $index slot present, length n, Date class preserved, an index column on $data, and tidy()’s cp_index equal to dates[cp] element for element. (hdreg skipped: its y selects a column, and my probe kept passing a vector.)

Both properties are now guarded, over a spread of eleven methods each – univariate and multivariate, and engines that rebuild the data tibble themselves rather than inheriting it.

Proved by breaking attach_index() out of the dispatcher: the new index guard goes from 67 passing to 55 failing, and the seed guard correctly stays at 11/0, since it tests something else. Specificity as well as sensitivity.

409. Vignette pass

ggchangepoint.Rmd’s index section claims tidy(), augment(), autoplot() and the reporting functions “all speak in the user’s units” and that as_cpt_series() “accepts ts, xts, zoo and tsibble directly” – both now measured across 38 methods and four container classes respectively.

Bibliographies re-verified: 63/63 cited, 58/58 keys resolving, 0 dangling, 0 unused, all entries complete.

410. The new test declared a dependency the package does not have

R-devel came back with an extra WARNING, and it was mine:

* checking for unstated dependencies in 'tests' ... WARNING
'::' or ':::' import not declared from: 'broom'

The index guard called broom::tidy(res). broom is not a dependency of this package at all – it appears only in the DESCRIPTION prose (“‘broom’-style tidy/glance/augment methods”); the generics come from and are re-exported. So the call was not merely undeclared, it would have failed outright on any machine without broom installed, and every other test in the suite already calls the bare tidy(). Mine was the single broom:: call anywhere in tests/.

Fixed to tidy(res); both guards still pass (11 and 67), and the check now answers checking for unstated dependencies in 'tests' ... OK.

Two process notes, both of which cost time here. A pkill that appears to succeed can leave the old run alive, and the symptom was a check tree whose copy still contained the pre-fix line – so verifying the copy (§387) caught a stale run that verifying the source would not have. And several command lists silently short-circuited on &&/||, reporting nothing rather than failing; the steps that mattered were re-run one at a time.

No package code changed this pass. The two new guards convert measurements into checks: reproducibility across eleven seed-taking methods, and index propagation across eleven spanning univariate and multivariate – where the suite previously covered two.

Part XLIII – Parallelism, and the search path

412. A parallel plan does not change the answer

Three functions make a documented claim about parallelism: cpt_batch() “Honours future::plan() for parallel execution when is available, with parallel-safe RNG”, ggcpt_compare() “Respects future::plan()”, and cpt_benchmark() takes a parallel argument. Nothing checked the property that makes those claims worth anything: the answer must not depend on the plan.

That is not a hypothetical. A parallel run that reseeded each worker would still look entirely fine – every result plausible, none reproducible, and nothing in the output to say so.

Measured under sequential and a two-worker multisession:

sequential == multisession
cpt_batch() (via tidy()) identical
ggcpt_compare_table() identical
cpt_benchmark() (F1 to 8 dp) identical

Now guarded. The guard is skip_on_cran(), because spawning workers inside a check is not something to do to a CRAN machine – so it is exercised here and by anyone running the suite with NOT_CRAN=true, which is where a regression in the RNG plumbing would show up.

413. Neither engine leaks into the caller’s session

with_search_path_restored() exists because “two engines mutate [the search path]”: bcp attaches itself and grid when its namespace loads, and fabisearch needs NMF attached rather than loaded, which brings Biobase, BiocGenerics and a foreach/doParallel/doRNG stack with it – eight packages, where the wrapper originally detached only NMF.

Verified by snapshotting search() either side of a real call:

call leaked lost
bcp_wrapper() nothing nothing
fabisearch_wrapper() nothing nothing

And after the fabisearch call, NMF is loaded but not attached – which is exactly the intended end state: attached for the duration because the engine requires it, detached afterwards, namespace left warm. A user’s session is byte-identical either side.

414. Vignette pass

Bibliographies re-verified: 63/63 vignette entries cited, 58/58 Rd keys resolving, 0 dangling, 0 unused, all entries complete.

Four instrument errors this pass, all mine and all worth naming because each cost a run: cpt_batch() has no parallel argument (it honours the plan unconditionally, unlike cpt_benchmark()); its return is a ggcpt_batch tibble with list-columns, not a list of ggcpt objects, so comparison goes through tidy(); fabisearch cannot complete inside a 600-second cap alongside other probes and needed isolating; and R rejects else at the start of a line at top level, which silently turned a whole sweep into nineteen false timeouts before I checked that the probe parsed. Parse-check a generated probe before launching a sweep with it is now the rule.

Part XLIV – Streaming, and the panel layer’s bad members

416. Feeding a monitor one observation at a time

cpt_replay() is documented as doing “in one call” what hand-rolling the update loop does – and it is literally cpt_monitor() plus a single cpt_update(), so that equivalence is true by construction and testing it proves nothing.

The one that is not by construction: does a bulk update equal feeding observations a few at a time? That is what an online detector is for, and a monitor that mishandled its state across calls would give a streaming user different alarms from the batch replay with nothing to signal the difference.

Measured for all three monitors, on a change at observation 100:

monitor bulk one at a time chunks of 5 cpt_replay()
edetector 41, 77 41, 77 41, 77 41, 77
cpm 53 53 53 53
ocd (3 coordinates) 49 49 49 49

Identical throughout. Now guarded, with ocd given an explicit thresh so the test does not pay for its ~189-second Monte Carlo calibration.

417. cpt_batch() accepted a panel of factors

Sweeping the panel functions over collections with one bad member found the gap. cpt_batch() coerced each series with

lapply(x, as.numeric)

where cpt_detect() uses coerce_series_values(). The difference is the whole point of that helper: as.numeric() on a factor returns its level codes – an alphabetical ordering of the labels rather than the data – and on a character vector it returns NAs. cpt_detect() has refused both since 0.4.0. cpt_batch() ran them and reported changepoints:

> cpt_batch(list(a = ok, b = as.character(ok)), method = "pelt")
# a 2-row ggcpt_batch, both series "detected"
> cpt_batch(list(a = ok, b = factor(c("a","b","c"))), method = "pelt")
# accepted

It now goes through the same helper, and the message names the series – Series `b` (2 of 2): `x` is a factor... – because in a panel “which one?” is the question. Everything legitimate still works, including the containers coerce_series_values() deliberately lets through: a plain list, an unnamed list, a matrix, and a ts.

This is the same defect class as the very first finding of this loop (silent factor-to-level-code coercion at eleven call sites) surviving in the one place that reached the engine by a different route.

418. And an empty method set

cpt_benchmark(methods = character(0)) built a zero-row grid and then set an attribute on NULL, so base R answered “attempt to set an attribute on NULL” – nothing about the argument. datasets was already checked immediately above it, for exactly this reason. methods now is too, and NULL takes the same path.

419. What was already right

Worth recording, since these are the cases a panel function is most likely to mishandle: cpt_batch() already refused an empty collection, a too-short member and an all-NA member – each naming the series and its position – and handled a constant series, a single series and an unnamed list. And cpt_benchmark() already tolerated a method that cannot run on the data and truth supplied for only some datasets, scoring the cells it could.

Two package fixes this pass (cpt_batch()’s coercion, cpt_benchmark()’s empty method set) and two new guards (streaming equivalence, panel refusals), with both check trees verified to contain the fixes before the runs were trusted.

The cpt_batch() finding is the one worth remembering: the very first defect this loop fixed was silent factor-to-level-code coercion, at eleven call sites – and it survived here, in the one function that reached the engine through as.numeric() rather than through the helper written to prevent it. A defect class is not closed until every route to the engine takes the same door.

Part XLV – Every route to the engine, taken seriously

Part XLIV closed with a rule rather than a fix: a defect class is not closed until every route to the engine takes the same door. This part executes it against the oldest defect in this loop – silent factor-to-level-code coercion – and finds that the door was open in six more places.

421. Enumerating the routes instead of guessing them

Two sweeps, because one is not enough.

The first enumerated every exported function whose first formal is a series (x, data, series, datasets) – 57 of them – and called each with a numeric control, a factor, and a character vector. The factor was built so the trap is visible rather than theoretical:

fac <- factor(sample(c("10", "2", "30"), 180, TRUE))
levels(fac)                     # "10" "2"  "30"  -- alphabetical
as.numeric(fac)[1:8]            # 3 3 1 2 1 3 1 1  -- level codes
as.numeric(as.character(fac))[1:8]   # 30 30 10 2 10 30 10 10  -- the data

56 of 57 refused. One did not: cpt_replay().

The second sweep is the one that mattered more, and it exists only because the first had a blind spot. cpt_monitor()’s first formal is method, not a series – so the entire monitoring layer was outside the first sweep’s filter. Enumerating exported functions with a series-like formal in any position returned 17 candidates, of which five carry a genuine raw series that the guard on x cannot see.

422. The monitoring layer had three doors and one guard

cpt_replay(), cpt_monitor() and cpt_update() each coerced their series independently:

b <- as.numeric(baseline)                       # cpt_monitor, edetector arm
for (v in as.numeric(baseline)) ...             # cpt_monitor, cpm arm
matrix(as.numeric(new_obs), ncol = 1)           # cpt_update
matrix(as.numeric(x), ncol = 1)                 # cpt_replay

A factor reached two of the three detectors as its level codes, and the monitor then ran, alarmed, and reported delays for a series the caller never supplied. Nothing warned, because level codes are perfectly good numbers.

The first patch fixed the coercion sites one at a time and cpt_monitor() still accepted a factor – the edetector and cpm arms coerce before the arm I had patched. That is the whole lesson of this part in miniature: patching sites is not the same as closing a route. The guard now sits once, before the switch():

if (!is.null(baseline) && !is.matrix(baseline) && !is.data.frame(baseline)) {
  baseline <- coerce_series_values(baseline, arg = "baseline")
}

Placed there it holds for a fourth arm nobody has written yet.

423. cpt_replay(baseline =), which is two arguments wearing one name

baseline is documented two ways – a count of leading observations, or an explicit baseline series – and the explicit-series branch was the subtlest hole in the package:

base_data <- if (is.matrix(baseline)) baseline else {
  matrix(as.numeric(baseline), ncol = ncol(X))
}

It hands cpt_monitor() an already-numeric vector, so the guard added in §422 could never see the factor. A guard upstream of a coercion is not a guard. It also missed data.frame, which now routes through as_mv_matrix() like every other matrix path.

424. The impossible count, silently reinterpreted

Same function, adjacent defect, found by reading the branch condition rather than by testing:

if (length(baseline) == 1L && baseline >= 1 && baseline < n &&
    baseline %% 1 == 0) {          # count
} else {                           # explicit series

A single number that fails any of those tests falls into the series branch and becomes a one-observation baseline. So cpt_replay(x, baseline = 500) on a 180-point series failed with

edetector estimates the in-control mean and scale from baseline, so it needs at least 5 pre-change observations.

which never mentions the 500, and blames the wrong thing. A lone number is now validated as a count, and both documented readings still work: a count sets offset to itself, an explicit series sets it to 0.

425. The learned penalty predicted from the level codes

cpt_penalty(type, series =) ignores series for every named penalty, and uses it for exactly one thing – predicting a learned penalty from the series’ features:

return(unname(stats::predict(type, as.numeric(series)))[1])

A factor here yields a penalty computed from features of the level codes, returned as a bare number with nothing to suggest it is wrong. This route is unreachable by any sweep that passes a type string, which is why source reading and behavioural probing are both necessary and neither is sufficient.

426. The one route where x is not the series

strucchange_wrapper(y ~ t, data = df) reads the response out of data:

data_vec <- as.numeric(data[[response]])

Here x is the formula, so the wrapper’s type guard on x has no series to check. The guard now names the offending column, which is more useful than naming the argument:

y is a factor. Detection needs numbers, and coercing a factor gives its level codes …

That message comes from coerce_series_values(), which grew an arg parameter this round for the purpose – it previously said “x” everywhere, including when the thing at fault was called baseline, new_obs, series or y.

427. What was already right, and left alone

Three findings were not defects, and saying so is part of the audit:

  • new_ggcpt(data = factor) is accepted, and should be. Its own documentation says “as_ggcpt() is the validating way to build one of these from the outside; this constructor does not check its arguments.” as_ggcpt() does refuse a factor. The low-level constructor is allowed to be low-level.
  • cpt_labels(series =) and as_cpt_labels(series =) accept a factor because there series is a series identifier for a panel, not data. A factor is the natural type for a grouping id; refusing it would be the bug.
  • as_mv_matrix() already refused a factor column in a data.frame, at every matrix-shaped entry point. Only the vector paths were open. This is why the fixes above route matrices through it rather than adding a second check.

Six coercion sites closed, one argument-validation fix, one shared helper made honest about which argument it is complaining about.

428. Fixing half the message made the other half wrong

Adding arg to coerce_series_values() in §426 created an inconsistency that had not existed before: vector paths now named the argument at fault, while every matrix path still said “x” whatever it was given. So cpt_monitor(baseline = df) reported a problem with x, an argument cpt_monitor() does not have.

as_mv_matrix() got the same arg parameter – its own comment already said the point of the function’s error was to name “which argument was empty”, so the intent was there and only the parameter was missing.

429. Which column, not just which argument

While there, a longer-standing weakness in the same message. as.matrix() on a data.frame with one non-numeric column returns an all-character matrix, so both front doors said

x must be numeric.

and left the reader to find the culprit in a fifty-column frame. They now say

x must be numeric. Not numeric: b (character), c (factor). Coercing a factor gives its level codes, an alphabetical ordering of the labels, not the data.

validate_data() and as_mv_matrix() are the two front doors a data.frame can arrive through, so the column-naming lives in one helper (nonnumeric_columns_note()) that both call, rather than in two copies that would drift.

430. The seam changepoint

The message work turned up a defect of its own. cpt_batch(list(p = df)) reported

x must be a numeric vector, matrix, or data.frame, not data.frame.

which is self-contradictory, and reading why exposed something worse. A panel is documented as “a list of numeric vectors”, and as.numeric() on a matrix unrolls it column after column. So an 80x2 matrix passed as one panel member became a 160-point series:

M <- cbind(a = c(rnorm(40), rnorm(40, 3)), b = c(rnorm(40), rnorm(40, 3)))
cpt_batch(list(p = M), method = "pelt")   # changepoints at 40, 80, 121
cpt_detect(M, method = "ecp")             # one changepoint

The 80 is the seam where column b was appended to column a. It is not a feature of the data; it is a feature of the concatenation, and it is reported with the same confidence as the real one at 40.

This was not a regression from Part XLIV’s cpt_batch() fix – the old as.numeric() unrolled a matrix exactly the same way, and refused a data.frame member with R’s own “‘list’ object cannot be coerced” message. It has been wrong for as long as the function has existed.

A multi-column member is now refused, naming the member, because cpt_detect() is the multivariate route and making the panel multivariate would be a new feature rather than a fix. A one-column matrix or data.frame is still accepted: unrolling it changes nothing, so refusing it would be strictness with no defect behind it.

The lesson is narrower than §421’s and worth keeping separate: a self-contradictory error message is not merely cosmetic. It is a sign that the code reached a state its author did not model, and the state was worth more than the message.

431. Vignette pass

Bibliographies first, as every round: 63 of 63 \citep/@key citations resolve to vignettes/vignette_reference.bib, all 58 inst/REFERENCES.bib keys are consumed by an \insertRef, nothing dangling, nothing unused, no incomplete entries.

Six sweeps beyond that, all of them checks that would catch drift rather than re-readings of the prose:

  • Function names in prose. Every cpt_*(), ggcpt_*(), geom_cpt_*() and friend mentioned across the eight vignettes resolves to a current export. No stale names.
  • Stated defaults against live formals. arl0 = 500, alpha = 0.01, cpm_type = "Mann-Whitney", patience = 5000, relearn = 20, alpha = 1.01 (sSIC), alpha = 0.5 (SMUCE), layout = "facet" – all match. The CROPS claim of a default range [log n, 10 log n] matches pen_min <- log(n) / pen_max <- 10 * log(n).
  • Structural counts. “Fifty methods” is right, and worth pinning down because cpt_methods() returns 55 rows: 50 available plus 5 planned (gfpop, robust, focus, sbs, changeforest) whose engines are not on CRAN yet. The vignettes count what a reader can actually call. “Six families” is already held by a shipped test; “Ten methods” and “Nine methods” in the benchmark tables match their own rows.
  • Citations per method. All 50 registry methods resolve through cpt_cite() to a dated reference, and the attributions spot-check correctly (pelt to Killick et al. 2012, wbs to Fryzlewicz 2014, mosum to Eichinger and Kirch 2018, ecp to Matteson and James 2014).
  • Figure alt text. 65 of 65 genuinely-drawing chunks carry fig.alt. Five chunks flagged by a first pass turned out to emit tables or printed objects, not figures – supervised.Rmd’s error curve prints the tibble in one chunk and plots it in the next, and it is the next one that needs the alt text and has it.
  • Titles and index entries. All seven package vignettes have a YAML title identical to their \VignetteIndexEntry; benchmarks.Rmd has no index entry because it is a pkgdown-only article, which is what _pkgdown.yml declares it to be. Every _pkgdown.yml topic resolves, and the fourteen exports that are not listed by name are all aliases on pages that are (ggcpt_statistic on cpt_statistic, the scale_* family on scale_colour_cpt, the broom generics on reexports).

Two measured claims were re-measured rather than read:

The false-alarm rates. monitoring.Rmd claims that on 2000-observation in-control streams at the defaults, cpm raises about 3.7 false alarms against the 4 that arl0 = 500 implies, and edetector about 13. Measured over ten replicates: cpm 4.00, edetector 13.80. The claim holds, and so does the reasoning behind it.

The interval widths. benchmarks.Rmd recommends the bootstrap by default and warns that posterior intervals are vacuous, on the strength of mean widths of 11.9, 6.2, 33.0 and 245.5 over 20 replicates. One replicate gives 8.0 (native, via smuce), 4.0 (bootstrap), 20.0 (nsp) and 232.0 (posterior, via bcp) – same ordering, same magnitudes, and the source column reports the four provenance names the vignette uses. A 232-wide interval on a 300-point series is the vignette’s point exactly.

432. length() is not the number of observations

The last defect of the round was found by a test rather than by the package: the 4.6.0 Imports-only check failed on an expectation I had just written,

expect_error(cpt_monitor("ocd", baseline = df), "`baseline` must be numeric")

because need_pkg("ocd") runs before the validation, so on a library without the Suggests the error is “Package ‘ocd’ is required” instead. That is the environment-dependent-tripwire mistake this loop has made before, and the fix is the same one: assert the property where it lives (as_mv_matrix(df, arg = "baseline")) rather than through a route that needs an engine to be installed.

Probing for a Suggests-free route to the same assertion turned up the real defect. cpt_monitor("edetector", baseline = <60-row, 2-column data.frame>) said:

edetector estimates the in-control mean and scale from baseline, so it needs at least 5 pre-change observations.

The baseline has sixty observations. The guard was

if (is.null(baseline) || length(baseline) < 5)

and length() on a data.frame is its column count – 2. The same guard is wrong the other way for a matrix, where length() is rows times columns, so a 3x2 matrix has “6 observations” and passes a test it should fail.

Two changes. The count is now NROW(), which is length() for a vector and nrow() for anything rectangular. And a multi-column baseline is refused outright for the two univariate detectors, because the documented contract is “a numeric vector (or, for ocd, a matrix with rows as time points)” – so a two-column baseline for edetector was never meaningful, and the observation count was only the first thing it got wrong. One column is accepted, as in §430, since there is no reshape to object to.

ocd keeps validating its own matrix, and still names baseline while doing it.

433. The same seam, in the oldest code in the package

§432’s NROW() fix raised the obvious next question: where else does this package take length() of something that might be rectangular? Sweeping the sources for length(x), length(data), length(series) and friends returned 29 sites. Most sit downstream of a validation and see a vector by the time they run, and R/ecp.R was already doing it correctly:

n_obs <- if (is.matrix(data) || is.data.frame(data)) nrow(data) else length(data)

Three sites take raw input. cpt_select() refuses a multi-column series outright (“Method pelt is univariate, but x has 2 columns”). The other two are the oldest functions in the package, and both were wrong:

M <- cbind(a = c(rnorm(60), rnorm(60, 3)), b = c(rnorm(60), rnorm(60, 3)))
cpt_wrapper(M)          # changepoints at 58, 120, 180
cpt_wrapper(M[, 1])     # changepoint at 58
ecp_wrapper(M)          # changepoint at 61   -- ecp is multivariate
cpt_detect(M, "pelt")   # refused: univariate, but `x` has 2 columns

58 is real. 120 is the seam, and 180 is column b’s change displaced by the length of column a. ggcptplot() drew the same 240-point concatenation, and its show_points <- length(data) <= 500 default was computed from 240 rather than 120.

The two got different treatments, each matching its closest counterpart rather than each other:

  • cpt_wrapper() refuses, because it is an analysis entry point and cpt_detect() refuses the same input. An answer computed from a concatenation is worse than no answer.
  • ggcptplot() plots the first column and says so, because ggecpplot() already established that convention for exactly this case, with the reasoning in a comment: “The line plot is univariate; for multivariate input draw the first column (and say so) rather than crashing or silently mis-plotting.” A plot is a presentation, and the sibling functions of a pair should not disagree about what a matrix means.

The reduction happens before show_points is computed, so that default now sees the observation count too.

The multi-column rule was by this point written out inline in three places, so it moved into reject_multicolumn(x, arg, hint) – one sentence about the join, one caller-supplied hint about what to do instead – and cpt_batch(), cpt_monitor() and cpt_wrapper() all call it. That is the same consolidation §422 did for the coercion guard, for the same reason: three copies of a rule are three chances for the fourth caller to miss it.

ggcptplot_internal() was deliberately left alone. It is shared with autoplot() and ggecpplot(), both of which hand it a vector they have already reduced, so a guard there would have been a guard on the wrong side of the reduction.

434. Verification

Both trees were confirmed to contain all nine of this round’s edit markers before either run was trusted – the habit exists because a heredoc that matches nothing leaves a check running against the pre-fix source and reports it as clean.

R 4.4.1, full Suggests library, --as-cran: FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 38 | PASS 3259. Status 1 ERROR, 2 WARNINGs, 3 NOTEs, and every one of the six is an absent external tool or package rather than anything in the package:

item cause
WARNING qpdf not installed
WARNING + ERROR pdflatex not installed
NOTE rjags, mcp not available
NOTE tidy and V8 not installed
NOTE ggchangepoint-manual.tex left behind when the PDF step aborted

R 4.6.0, Imports-only library, --as-cran: FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 157 | PASS 1817. Status 1 ERROR, 1 WARNING, 2 NOTEs – the same missing tools, minus the two Suggests NOTEs that only the 4.4.1 library can raise. Vignettes re-built in 71s with the Imports-only library.

The PDF-manual ERROR was worth one round of actually chasing rather than assuming. module -t avail lists texlive/2022 and texlive/2023, so the tool looked available; with /software/texlive-2023-el8-x86_64/bin on PATH, pdflatex --version reports TeX Live 2023 and then fails on any input with

I can’t find the format file `pdflatex.fmt’!

because fmtutil.cnf has no pdflatex entry and texmf-var is not writable. R_TEXI2DVICMD=emulation gets past the separate texi2dvi incompatibility (texinfo-6.7 against this pdftex) and then hits the same missing format. So the ERROR is environmental in the strong sense – there is no working pdflatex on this machine to be had – and not a latent Rd problem hiding behind a missing binary. (The ~/.texlive2023 tree that attempt created was removed.)

Local full-suite run before the checks: 0 failures, 0 errors across every test file.

435. Where this leaves the class

Fourteen fixes, all of them the same shape: an input that arrives as one thing and reaches the engine as another, with no warning, and an answer returned for a series the caller never supplied.

Two mechanisms, and the round found both by enumerating routes rather than by inspecting the functions it already suspected:

  • as.numeric() on a factor gives level codes – an alphabetical ordering of the labels. Six routes still did this: cpt_replay()’s series and its baseline, cpt_monitor()’s baseline through two arms, cpt_update()’s new observations, cpt_penalty()’s learned-penalty series, and the response column of the formula interface.
  • as.numeric() on a matrix concatenates its columns, inventing a changepoint at every join. Three routes did this: a cpt_batch() panel member, cpt_wrapper(), and ggcptplot(). length() on the same input then counts the wrong thing in both directions – columns for a data.frame, rows times columns for a matrix.

The guards are now consolidated rather than scattered: coerce_series_values() and as_mv_matrix() both name the argument at fault, nonnumeric_columns_note() names the offending column, and reject_multicolumn() holds the single-series rule for its three callers. Every one of them was proved to fire by breaking its input and watching the behaviour change from accept to refuse – not by reading the code and concluding it must work.

What is left unclosed is a question rather than a defect: ggcptplot() and ggecpplot() reduce a multivariate input to its first column with a message, while cpt_wrapper() and cpt_detect() refuse it. Both are defensible, both are now deliberate, and a future round could reasonably decide the pair should agree.

Part XLVI – The other silent coercion: non-finite values

Part XLV closed the factor-and-matrix class by enumerating routes rather than inspecting suspects. The same enumeration applies to a second class that Part XLV noticed in passing without chasing: coerce_series_values() deliberately does not check finiteness – its comment says so – and only validate_data() does. Every route that reaches an engine through the coercion helper rather than the validator was therefore unguarded, and nobody had asked which routes those were.

436. The sweep

57 raw-series entry points, each called with a numeric control and then with one NA, one NaN and one Inf injected at position 95 of a 180-point series whose only real changepoint is at 90. A route “passes” only when the control works and the non-finite version is refused – a refusal on a route whose control already fails says nothing.

42 of 57 refuse. Twelve have controls that fail for shape reasons (a high-dimensional or functional wrapper handed a univariate vector), so their finiteness behaviour needed a separately shaped probe. Three accepted: as_cpt_series(), ecp_wrapper() and ggecpplot().

437. ecp does not refuse a non-finite series; it answers wrongly

This is the finding of the round, and it is worse than a missing guard, because the answer comes back looking ordinary:

input (one real changepoint, at 90) ecp_wrapper() reports
clean 91
one NA 91
one NaN, or one Inf 91
twenty NAs nothing at all
second half all NA 12 and 14

Twenty scattered NAs lose the changepoint completely. An all-NA second half reports two changepoints in the first quarter of the series that the data does not contain, with no warning and no missing values in the output to hint at it. cpt_wrapper() has always refused this input – “data must be finite (no NA/NaN/Inf)” – and so has cpt_detect(method = "ecp"), which validates before dispatching. Only the direct ecp_wrapper() route was open, and ggecpplot() inherited the hole because it draws through it.

ecp_wrapper() now refuses, counting against the series the caller passed (“1 of 180 values are not”), and rectangular input goes through as_mv_matrix() so a non-numeric column is named as it is everywhere else. Clean vector, matrix and data.frame input all return the changepoint they returned before.

That the two original wrappers disagreed is the same shape as Part XLV’s finding about cpt_wrapper() and multi-column input: the modern dispatcher validates, and the 0.1.0-era API it wraps does not. Both times the fix was to bring the old function up to the new one’s standard rather than the reverse.

438. cpt_replay() named whichever argument happened to catch it

cpt_replay(x) did refuse a non-finite series – but downstream, in whichever of cpt_monitor() or cpt_update() received the slice holding the bad value. So the same call reported:

NA at position 20  ->  `baseline` must be finite ...; 1 of 45 values are not.
NA at position 95  ->  `new_obs` must be finite (no NA/NaN/Inf).

Neither argument is one the caller passed, the message changes with where the NA falls, and “1 of 45” counts against the baseline slice rather than the 180-point series. The check now happens in cpt_replay() itself, right after the length check, so the message says x and counts 1 of 180 wherever the value sits. An explicitly supplied baseline still reports itself, with its own count – that one really is a different argument.

This is Part XLV’s §426 lesson recurring: a guard that fires somewhere downstream is not the same as a guard that fires where the user can act on it.

439. as_cpt_series() is a translator, and is right to pass NA through

The third acceptance is not a defect. as_cpt_series() is documented as “the one place that separates the two: it pulls the numeric values out of a ts, xts, zoo, tsibble or data frame and returns the time index alongside them, so cpt_detect() can detect on positions and report on dates.” Validation belongs to the consumer, exactly as new_ggcpt() leaves validation to as_ggcpt() (Part XLV, §427). Refusing here would also break a legitimate workflow: extract values and index from a gappy series, impute, then detect.

What makes that safe is that every route onward refuses, so the test added for this pins down the decision rather than the behaviour of one function: cpt_detect() (bare, with an index, and on a ts), cpt_batch(), cpt_select() and cpt_replay() all reject the values as_cpt_series() happily returned.

440. The twelve routes the univariate sweep could not reach

Twelve of the 57 entry points failed their numeric control, because a high-dimensional, functional or network wrapper handed a plain vector refuses on shape long before finiteness is considered. A refusal on a route whose control already fails proves nothing, so those twelve were re-probed with a 120x6 matrix carrying one NA at [70, 3].

Ten refuse cleanly. ocd_wrapper() also refuses – its control merely times out at the default Monte-Carlo threshold, which takes minutes at this size, and a cheap mc_reps = 2 shows the finiteness guard firing normally.

network_wrapper() was the exception, and the only route in the package with no finiteness check at all: it reaches the engine through network_matrix() rather than validate_data(). One NA produced

replacement has length zero

from inside the engine’s random edge-splitting – base R’s message, naming neither the argument nor the problem. The file’s own comments show this is exactly the failure mode its author had been stamping out (“Forwarded to the engine, which reported a bad value from deep inside itself … none of which names the argument”), so the fix matches its siblings’ wording and counts against the matrix the caller passed.

The regression test for this covers the whole family rather than the one offender, and counts what it exercised: expect_equal(tested, available), where available is however many of the eleven engines are installed. A fixed threshold here is what has bitten this loop twice before – once as expect_gt(tested, 5L) on the Imports-only library, and once last round as a cpt_monitor("ocd", ...) expectation that asserted “Package ‘ocd’ is required” wherever ocd was absent.

441. Two process notes, both from mistakes made this round

flush.console() is a no-op under Rscript, so a long sweep written as one process printed nothing for ten minutes and looked hung when it was merely buffered. The 57-route sweep had not hit this because it runs one process per route and lets process exit do the flushing – which is now the pattern for any sweep whose progress needs watching.

And a pkill -f pattern matched the shell that was running it. The command was pkill -f na_mv2 followed by two heredocs; the pattern matched my own wrapper, killed it, and the heredocs never ran – so the driver script launched a moment later did not exist, and the sweep “failed” with an exit code and no output. pgrep -f matching its own caller is a known hazard here; what was new is that a kill built on it destroyed the work in the same command. Kills now go by PID, in their own call, verified with ps rather than pgrep -c.

442. Seven copies of one sentence, four of them less useful

Closing the class left the message family inconsistent. Seven sites refused a non-finite series; three carried a count and four did not:

`data` must be finite (no NA/NaN/Inf).                                 <- cpt_wrapper
`x` must be finite (no NA/NaN/Inf).                                    <- validate_data, twice
`new_obs` must be finite (no NA/NaN/Inf).                              <- cpt_update
`response` must be finite (no NA/NaN/Inf).                             <- hdreg
`baseline` must be finite (no NA/NaN/Inf); 1 of 60 values are not.     <- cpt_monitor

The count is the part that tells the caller what to do: one stray NA in a 10,000-point series is a bad merge or a sensor dropout to be patched, and half the series missing is the wrong series. “Must be finite” alone does not distinguish them.

All seven now come from stop_nonfinite(x, arg), so every route says the same thing in the same shape with the argument the caller passed and the count against the object it passed:

route message
cpt_detect() vector `x` ... 1 of 180 values are not.
cpt_detect() matrix `x` ... 1 of 720 values are not.
cpt_wrapper() `data` ... 1 of 180
ecp_wrapper() `data` ... 1 of 180
cpt_monitor() `baseline` ... 1 of 60
cpt_update() `new_obs` ... 1 of 120
cpt_replay() `x` ... 1 of 180
network_wrapper() `x` ... 1 of 720
hdreg_wrapper() `response` ... 1 of 120

power.R’s “location must be finite numbers: a fraction of n in (0, 1)” is left alone – it is a different statement about a different kind of argument, not a copy of this one.

Worth recording how the consolidation nearly went wrong: the first version called stop_nonfinite(M, "new_obs") inside cpt_update(), where the matrix is called X and no M exists – so the error handler would have errored, turning a clear refusal into “object ‘M’ not found”. Reading the surrounding lines caught it before any test ran, which is the argument for checking what is actually in scope at a call site rather than trusting the variable name one remembers writing.

443. Vignette pass

Bibliography verification changed method this round, because the round began by re-deriving it with a fresh regex and reintroducing a bug the package had already fixed. test-040-polish.R’s R44 does this check properly and its comment says why:

The pattern deliberately does not require a four-digit year: the earlier one did, so @rcore – the R itself citation – was invisible to this check, and a misspelling of any yearless key would have gone unreported.

My throwaway pattern required a four-digit year, so it reported @rcore as an unused entry and a trailing-punctuation artefact as a dangling key – both false. R44 also checks two things the ad-hoc pass did not: that a key defined in both bibliographies describes the same publication (same year, same journal), and the reverse direction, that no entry is unused. The shipped test is the authority; the round’s job is to run it, not to re-derive it. It passes, as does the rest of that file. Verified state unchanged: 63 of 63 vignette citations resolve, 58 of 58 \insertRef keys resolve, nothing dangling, nothing unused, no incomplete entries.

Three new checks beyond that:

  • Capability claims against the registry. The registry’s capability columns are the source of truth for what a method offers, and the prose agrees with them: inference.Rmd’s solution-path section gates on has_wbs and wbs does carry path; its scale-space section gates on has_mosum and mosum does carry scale_space; the posterior discussion names bocpd and beast, both of which carry posterior; and “engines with no native intervals” is consistent with exactly 8 of 50 carrying ci.
  • Every column name promised in prose. This targets a mistake I made last round – reading ci$lower when the column is ci_lower – so the question is whether the vignettes make that error. 35 backticked snake_case identifiers appear in prose; the 12 that are column names rather than arguments all exist (cp_source in wrap-nsp.R, declared_at in wrap-highdim.R, selection_adjusted in inference.R, region_start/region_end, posterior_prob, data_wide, detection_time, index_value, true_changepoints, true_segments, region_midpoint).
  • The as_ggcpt() contract example. extending.Rmd claims as_ggcpt() runs “sorting, de-duplication, range checks” and demonstrates it with as_ggcpt(c(150, 150, 9999, NA, 50), x) on a 300-point series. It returns 50 150: the duplicate collapsed, the out-of-range 9999 dropped, the NA dropped, the in-range 50 kept, sorted. All four promised checks, in one line.

And a claim verified by an accident of measurement. inference.Rmd says “autoplot(type = "statistic") is a thin wrapper: ggcpt_statistic() is the plotting function itself.” The two figures that follow are byte-identical – 43 KB each, the same MD5 – which is not redundancy but proof of the sentence.

The vignettes are also byte-reproducible: rendering monitoring.Rmd twice gives the same 110,348 bytes, figures included. knitr shares one RNG stream across chunks, so the handful of set.seed() calls governs every later chunk; 83 chunks and two seeds is not the reproducibility problem it looks like.

444. Verification, and one NOTE that is new

Both check copies were confirmed to hold this round’s edits first, and the full local suite was run as a gate before either check started (0 failures, 0 errors) – last round spent three check cycles because defects were found after the runs began.

R 4.4.1, full Suggests: FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 39 | PASS 3291. R 4.6.0, Imports-only: FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 158 | PASS 1849.

The pdflatex/qpdf/tidy items are unchanged and understood (§434). One item is new: R 4.4.1 now reports

* checking installed package size ... NOTE
  installed size is  5.2Mb
  sub-directories of 1Mb or more:
    doc   3.8Mb

The immediately preceding run reported this step as OK, and the tarball grew by only 2,141 bytes between them – this round’s code and test text. So the package sits within a rounding error of CRAN’s 5.0Mb threshold and has crossed it; it is not that anything grew materially.

The weight was profiled rather than guessed. doc is 65 figures totalling 2.25Mb of PNG, which base64 inflates to roughly 3.0Mb of the 3.8Mb; help is a further 2.0Mb of Rd database. The figures are already rendered at dpi = 72 and 576px wide – fig.retina is effectively 1, so that lever is spent – the largest single figure is 96Kb, there is no outlier, and the one byte-identical pair inside a vignette is the deliberate equivalence demonstration described above.

So there is no waste behind the NOTE: every megabyte is documentation this package deliberately ships. Buying margin would mean narrowing or dropping figures, which is content removal rather than polish, so nothing was changed. This is a NOTE to expect and explain at submission, of the kind CRAN accepts routinely for a vignette-heavy package, and it is recorded here with the breakdown so the explanation does not have to be reconstructed later. Worth watching whether the next run reports it too, given how close to the boundary it is.

Part XLVII – Degenerate inputs, and errors written by somebody else

Parts XLV and XLVI closed two silent-coercion classes by enumerating routes. The third input class nobody had swept is the degenerate one: a series with no variation, and a series too short for the engine asked to segment it. Both are cases where an engine can fail in its own language rather than the package’s, and where “it errored” is not the same as “it said something useful”.

445. A constant series is already handled

57 entry points, each given rep(5, 180) – a series whose only correct answer is zero changepoints – with a real two-regime series as the control.

34 return zero changepoints. One refuses. Nine return something the probe could not count (plots, tables). Nothing fabricates a changepoint in a constant series, and nothing produces a cryptic error. The scattered guards found at the start of the round – validate_data()’s three- observation floor, cpt_replay()’s ten, the e-detector’s zero-variability check, esac/pilliat dropping constant columns – are doing their job.

One apparent exception was the probe’s fault, and is worth recording because the reasoning generalises. ggcpt_compare_table() looked like it reported three changepoints on a constant series; it returns three rows, one per default method, each carrying cp = NA:

  method cp cp_value
1   pelt NA       NA
2 binseg NA       NA
3   amoc NA       NA

which is exactly what comparison.Rmd documents – “a method that ran and found nothing contributes a single row with cp = NA”. Counting rows is not counting changepoints.

446. A short series, and seven engines answering in their own words

The other half of the class found the round’s work. Every available univariate method, at n = 3, 5, 10 and 20, classifying each failure by whether this package wrote the message or it leaked from below:

mosum, segneigh and sn refuse properly, and wbsts refuses properly at 5 and 10. Seven do not:

method works from what the user saw below that
wbs 4 “sample size is too small”
not 4 “max.length must satisfy 3 < max.lenght <= n”
wbsts 4 “subscript out of bounds”
taylor 5 “Invalid x argument. ‘x’ must be a numeric vector”
envcpt 12 “Minimum segment legnth is too large to include a change”
strucchange 15 “minimum segment size must be greater than the number of regressors”
bfast 25 “series is not periodic or has less than two periods”

Not one names the method the caller asked for or the length they supplied. Two carry the upstream package’s own typos. And wbsts gives base R’s “subscript out of bounds”, which does not even implicate the series.

This is the failure mode the codebase has been stamping out for several rounds – validate_scalar() exists because engines “reported a bad value from deep inside” themselves – so the gap is in the same family, just for length rather than for arguments.

447. Why the fix translates instead of pre-checking

The obvious fix is a minimum-length guard per wrapper, using the measured thresholds in that table. It would be wrong, and the round nearly did it.

Three of those thresholds are not constants: they move with an argument. bfast needs two full periods, so 25 is the number only at the default frequency = 12. strucchange needs h * n to exceed the regressor count, so 15 is the number only at the default h = 0.15. envcpt needs two segments of minseglen. A constant guard would refuse calls that work:

cpt_detect(short(10), method = "bfast", frequency = 4)   # works
cpt_detect(short(5),  method = "strucchange", h = 0.4)   # works

Both are accepted today and would have been refused by a “needs 25” or “needs 15” check. That is why the guard translates rather than pre-empting: rethrow_short_series() keeps the engine’s own diagnosis – the informative half, quoted so its typos are visibly not ours – and adds the method, the length, and where the threshold comes from:

Method bfast could not segment a series of 10 observation(s). The engine reported: “series is not periodic or has less than two periods”. bfast needs at least two full periods, so at frequency = 12 that is 24 observations.

Method envcpt could not segment a series of 5 observation(s). The engine reported: “Minimum segment legnth is too large to include a change in this data”. Every model must fit two segments of minseglen = 5, so the series needs more than 10 observations; lower minseglen or lengthen the series.

The hints are computed from the arguments in force, so they stay true when the caller changes them, and there is no threshold in this package to go stale against its engine. wbs, not and wbsts already had error handlers for other upstream quirks, so there the translation replaced a bare stop(e) in a branch that was already there.

A companion test pins the property that matters most about a translator: that it re-raises anything it does not recognise verbatim. Otherwise every engine failure would become a story about series length.

448. The result contract, checked against every method

extending.Rmd sets out the whole ggcpt contract for anyone writing a wrapper, and says as_ggcpt() enforces all of it:

  • $changepoints$cp integer, sorted, de-duplicated, in 1..n-1
  • $segments with one more row than $changepoints
  • $data carrying index (positions 1..n) and value
  • $method, $change_in, $cp_convention length-one metadata

That is a claim about every method, not about the one in the example, so it was checked against every installed univariate method on a 200-point series with two real changepoints. 35 of 35 satisfy it, with no violations – including the awkward cases: wbsts finds nothing and still returns one segment for zero changepoints, amoc finds one and returns two, wbs2 finds seven and returns eight.

This is now a shipped test rather than a one-off measurement, because a documented contract that nothing checks is a contract that drifts. It counts what it exercised (expect_equal(tested, available)) rather than asserting a fixed method count, for the reason this loop has learned twice.

449. Vignette pass

The bibliography check is test-040-polish.R’s R44, which runs as part of the suite – last round established it as the authority after a hand-rolled regex reintroduced a bug R44’s comment documents. It passes: 63 of 63 vignette citations resolve, 58 of 58 \insertRef keys resolve, keys shared between the two bibliographies agree on year and journal, nothing dangling, nothing unused, no incomplete entries.

Three computed prose claims were reproduced this round rather than read.

The penalty-scale claim (introduction.Rmd) is the sharpest set of numbers in any vignette: “pelt recovers exactly one changepoint at σ=1\sigma = 1 but returns 29 at σ=3\sigma = 3 and 138 at σ=10\sigma = 10.” Reproduced exactly – 1, 29, 138.

But those numbers move with the series length: the same experiment at n = 300 gives 1, 50 and 203. The prose said “on a single changepoint whose jump is five standard deviations” without saying how long the series was, so a reader could not have reproduced 29 and 138. It now says “on a 200-point series”, and the paragraph was re-wrapped rather than left with the ragged lines the insertion caused.

The CROPS claim (comparison.Rmd): “Over the default range [log⁡n,10log⁡n][\log n, 10 \log n] this series admits only two distinct segmentations, and the two-changepoint solution holds over all but the very bottom of it.” Reproducing the vignette’s RNG state by purling it and evaluating up to that chunk:

Penalty range:  [6.215, 62.15]     <- log(500), 10 * log(500)
Distinct segmentations: 2
  penalty n_cpts  cost
1    9.36      2   468
2    6.21      3   459

Two segmentations; the two-changepoint solution holds from 9.36 to 62.15 and gives way only in the bottom sliver, 6.21 to 9.36. Both halves of the sentence, and the penalty range confirms the [log n, 10 log n] default independently of §431’s source reading.

One warning turned out to be intentional. Evaluating those chunks raised “Dropping changepoint indices outside 1..(n-1): 700”, which looked like a malformed example until the source showed the line above it:

# index 700 cannot be a changepoint of a length-500 series
cpt_metrics(pred = c(100, 700), truth = c(100, 300), n = 500)

The vignette is demonstrating the guard. A warning in a vignette is not automatically a defect in it.

450. Verification

Both check copies were confirmed to hold this round’s edits, and the full local suite ran as a gate before either check started (0 failures, 0 errors).

R 4.4.1, full Suggests: FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 41 | PASS 3295. Status 1 ERROR, 2 WARNINGs, 3 NOTEs – the qpdf/pdflatex/tidy items and the rjags/mcp dependency NOTE, all unchanged and all absent external tools.

R 4.6.0, Imports-only: FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 160 | PASS 1853. Status 1 ERROR, 1 WARNING, 2 NOTEs – the same tools, minus the two NOTEs only the fuller library can raise.

§444’s open question is answered. Last round reported a new NOTE:

* checking installed package size ... NOTE
  installed size is  5.2Mb

This round the same step reports OK, with no change to any figure, vignette or dataset in between. So the reading in §444 was right: the package sits within a rounding error of CRAN’s 5.0Mb threshold, and whether the NOTE fires is a coin flip rather than a trend. For the submission that means the NOTE may or may not appear in CRAN’s own check, and the explanation in §444 – 65 legitimate figures already at dpi = 72, no outlier, no waste – covers it either way. Nothing to fix, and now nothing left to watch.

451. Where the three input classes stand

Three rounds, three classes of input that reached an engine as something other than what the caller supplied, all closed by enumerating routes rather than inspecting suspects:

class routes found open mechanism
factor / multi-column (XLV) 9 as.numeric() on a factor gives level codes; on a matrix it concatenates columns
non-finite (XLVI) 3 coerce_series_values() does not check finiteness; only validate_data() did
degenerate (XLVII) 7 engines refuse a short series in their own words, or not at all

The pattern across all three is the same, and worth stating once more because it keeps paying: the guard has to sit where the user can act on it. A check downstream of a coercion cannot see the original type (XLV, §423). A check in one branch of a switch() does not protect the others (§422). A check inside whichever helper happens to receive the bad slice names the wrong argument (XLVI, §438). And a check the engine performs names neither the method nor the input (XLVII, §446).

What is different about this round is that the fix is a translator rather than a guard. Seven thresholds live in seven other packages and three of them move with an argument, so this package cannot hold a copy of them without holding a copy that goes stale. Quoting the engine and adding the context it lacks is the honest version of a guard you are not entitled to write.

Part XLVIII – A result is not correct until every accessor works on it

Part XLVII verified the ggcpt contract across every univariate method and stopped there. That left the seventeen multivariate ones unchecked, and it left a second question unasked: the contract says what the slots hold, but nothing had confirmed that the ten S3 generics built on those slots all work, for every method. This part closes both.

452. The sweep

Every available method, on input of the right shape for it – a 200-point vector for the univariate ones, a 120x6 matrix for the multivariate – with the contract checked and then all ten generics run against the result: print, format, summary, tidy, glance, augment, as.data.frame, as_tibble, autoplot (forced to build, not merely constructed) and plot.

45 of 50 are clean. Of the five that are not, four are not defects: ocd times out on its default Monte-Carlo threshold, mcp is not installed, and hdreg and fabisearch refused the probe’s input because they need arguments it did not supply – hdreg a response, fabisearch non-negative values, both with a clear message and fabisearch counting the offending entries. A probe that hands a function the wrong input has measured the probe.

The fifth was real, and turned out to be two.

453. Two multivariate results carry no data_wide, and the vignette said all do

introduction.Rmd stated it without qualification:

Multivariate results additionally carry a data_wide tibble with one column per coordinate, which autoplot() renders as faceted small-multiples.

Nine of the eleven multivariate methods do. Two do not, and both for the same good reason: their plotted series is a derived quantity rather than the coordinates.

  • network takes a sequence of adjacency matrices. A network has entries per time point, so one facet per coordinate would be unreadable; the wrapper reports mean edge weight (rowMeans() of the vectorised matrices). The changepoints are still estimated from the networks themselves – the summary is for display only.
  • hdreg regresses a response on the covariates and plots the response, which is what a reader of a regression-break plot expects.

hdreg already documented this at the function level (“The plotted series is the response”); network documented only its change_in value, so its @return now says what the series is, why there is no data_wide, and that the estimation does not go through the summary. The vignette sentence now names both exceptions instead of asserting a rule with two holes in it.

Neither is a code change: the behaviour was right and the description was wrong. What the sweep produced is the knowledge that it is exactly these two, which is now a shipped test rather than a fact somebody measured once.

454. augment()’s help had gone stale by three methods

Checking principle P2 – “stable column names across all methods” across sixteen methods spanning every family: tidy() and glance() hold it exactly, with the core columns always present, always leading, and in the same order, and engine extras (ci_lower, ci_upper, cp_source, detection_time, posterior_prob, region_start, region_end) purely additive.

augment() differs for five methods, which is where the finding was. Those five carry an extra fitted column, inserted between value and seg_id – so the names are stable and the positions are not, which is what P2 claims and no more. But the same measurement showed fitted and .fitted holding identical values for all eight available engines that supply a signal, which looked wrong for decafs in particular, whose fit has drift.

It is not wrong. augment.ggcpt() deliberately prefers the engine’s signal:

# Prefer the engine's fitted signal when the object carries one.
engine_fitted <- x$data[["fitted"]]
if (!is.null(engine_fitted) && length(engine_fitted) == nrow(data)) {
  data$.fitted <- as.numeric(engine_fitted)

so .fitted becomes fitted for those engines, and the raw column rides along from $data. The help documented that precedence – and enumerated the engines it applies to as “SMUCE, DeCAFS, cpop, segmented, bcp, beast”. Six. The registry marks nine: that list had lost hsmuce, mcp and bfast.

The help now points at cpt_methods()’s fitted column as the source of truth and lists all nine. The guard added for it checks the behaviour rather than the prose – every flagged engine really does produce a fitted column and really does use it for .fitted, and an unflagged engine does not acquire one – and then checks the enumeration against the registry, so the list cannot drift again without a test failing.

455. Verification

Both check copies were confirmed to hold this round’s edits, and the full local suite ran as a gate before either check started (0 failures).

R 4.4.1, full Suggests: FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 43 | PASS 3295. R 4.6.0, Imports-only: FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 162 | PASS 1853.

Statuses are the documented baselines – the qpdf, pdflatex and tidy items plus the rjags/mcp dependency NOTE, every one of them an absent external tool. checking installed package size reports OK for the second round running, which settles §444’s marginal NOTE: it fires or does not at the 5.0Mb boundary and nothing about the package has changed.

Two things about the new tests are deliberate and worth stating, because they look like gaps otherwise.

The sweeps do not run under R CMD check. Every heavy test added in Parts XLVI-XLVIII carries skip_on_cran(), so NOT_CRAN=false skips them – which is why PASS is unchanged at 3295 while SKIP rose from 41 to 43. They run locally, where the gate that precedes each check exercises them with NOT_CRAN=true. The check’s own test stage already takes 348s; a contract sweep over 50 engines does not belong in a CRAN reviewer’s run, and the pure unit test on rethrow_short_series() – which calls no engine and takes no time – correctly does not skip.

fabisearch is excluded from the multivariate contract test. Its non-negative matrix factorisation exceeds five minutes on a 120x6 matrix, which is too slow for a test that runs on every local gate. Its contract was verified by hand while building the sweep. The test counts what it actually exercised (expect_equal(tested, available)) so the exclusion cannot quietly become a hole.

456. Two rounds of contract work, and what it was worth

Part XLVII checked 35 univariate methods against the documented contract and found no violations. Part XLVIII checked the 11 multivariate ones and 10 generics across all 50, and found no violations either – the code was right everywhere.

What the two sweeps actually produced was documentation that was wrong in three places: a data_wide rule with two unstated exceptions, an augment() enumeration that had lost three of its nine methods, and a network return value that never said what series it carries. None of these would fail a check. All three would mislead a reader who trusted the text over the object.

That is a different yield from the previous three parts, and worth naming. Parts XLV-XLVII found code that did the wrong thing quietly. This part found prose that described the code inaccurately – which is the failure mode a package accumulates once the code is actually correct, and the reason the standing instruction to verify the vignettes every round earns its place.

457. An artifact that was mine, not the package’s

Cleaning up after the sweeps turned up an untracked directory in the test tree:

tests/testthat/NMF_9bfa82e3d99e5/
  fit.midway3-0200.rcc.local.648441.rds
  fit.midway3-0200.rcc.local.648442.rds

NMF’s own scratch, created in the working directory – which for a test_file() run is tests/testthat. A wrapper that writes into the caller’s working directory would be a real side-effect defect, and one this package already guards against in a related form (fabisearch_wrapper() carries a comment that “NMF alone left eight packages on the caller’s search path”, and a shipped test checks the search path is restored).

So it was chased. fabisearch_wrapper() was run from an empty scratch directory three ways: small input with explicit n_runs = 2, n_reps = 2, small input with the defaults (n_runs = 50, n_reps = 100, n_core = 1), and finally the exact 120x6 input that had produced the artifact. That last run took 454 seconds, returned its one changepoint, and left nothing behind. Neither did the others.

The explanation is that NMF creates the directory during a fit and removes it on normal completion. The run that stranded it was the one my own test_file() invocation killed at its timeout – fabisearch was the reason that log was truncated with no result row. An interrupted fit cannot run its cleanup.

Not a defect, and the wrapper needed no change. Recorded because the negative result is the useful part: NMF’s scratch is self-cleaning, so an NMF_* directory surviving in a working tree means some fit was interrupted, not that a wrapper leaks. (fabisearch is excluded from the routine multivariate test for exactly the runtime this measured – 454s for one call.)

Part XLIX – Stale enumerations, and a gate that could not fail

Part XLVIII’s yield was documentation describing the code inaccurately, and §456 named that as the failure mode a package accumulates once the code is correct. This part sweeps that class deliberately instead of stumbling into it, and finds that the one defect fixed last round had three siblings – including two the earlier fix walked straight past.

458. Two mechanical sweeps that came back clean

Every documented default against its formal. 125 Rd pages, 166 “Defaults to X” claims extracted from \item{arg}{...} blocks and compared with formals(). 19 apparent disagreements, all artefacts of the check:

  • Most are arguments whose formal is NULL and whose documentation states the effective default computed inside the function (pen_min = NULL documented as log(n)). Documenting what the caller gets is better than documenting NULL, and every one of these was correct.
  • ggcpt_runlength(prob_floor) is documented 1e-3 against a formal 0.001 – the same number.
  • cpt_crops looked like it documented log(n) for both pen_min and pen_max. It uses a combined @param pen_min,pen_max naming both defaults in order (“log(n) and 10 * log(n)”) and the check read only the first.

Zero real disagreements.

Every @return claim of a change_in value against the live object. Nine wrapper pages claim one; all nine agree with what cpt_detect() actually puts in the slot. Two apparent failures were the check reading the usage signature (cpt_wrapper(data, change_in = "mean_var", ...)) and a @param sentence telling the reader how to request a variance change, neither of which is a return claim.

459. The stale list had three siblings

Part XLVIII corrected augment()’s enumeration of the engines whose fitted signal replaces .fitted: it named six where the registry marks nine. The sweep for enumerations of registry capabilities found the same list, and lists like it, in three more places:

where claimed registry
augment() (fixed in XLVIII) 6 9 fitted
autoplot(show_fit) the same 6 9 fitted
autoplot(show_ci) 2 (strucchange, segmented) 7 drawable of 8 ci
cpt_confint("native") 4 7 drawable of 8 ci

autoplot(show_fit)’s list was character-for-character the one fixed last round, in a file the fix never opened. That is the input-sweep lesson transposed: fixing the instance you found is not fixing the class.

The omissions were confirmed against behaviour before being written down. bfast and taylor really do return source = "native" from cpt_confint(), so their absence from the “native” list was wrong; nsp is marked ci but returns source = "nsp_region", and it carries region_start/region_end with a $regions slot rather than ci_lower/ci_upper – so excluding it from show_ci is right, and now said out loud, with a pointer to show_regions.

All four now name the registry column as the source of truth, so the next reader can check the list themselves rather than trusting it.

460. The same lists had been copied into the vignettes

Three of four again:

  • introduction.Rmd’s fitted list: the stale six.
  • ggchangepoint.Rmd’s show_fit: the stale six.
  • ggchangepoint.Rmd’s show_ci: three engines.
  • introduction.Rmd’s ci_lower/ci_upper list: already correct – all seven, and it was the only place in the package that already spelled out the nsp exception. It became the model for the other three.

461. A guard for the class, not the instance

Last round’s test checked augment.ggcpt.Rd. That is why the identical list next door survived. The replacement scans every Rd page and every vignette for the phrase

… marks in its <column> column: a, b, …

and checks both directions against the registry: nothing named that the column does not mark, and nothing marked that the page fails to mention. The second direction is what caught my own first correction – autoplot(show_ci) omitted nsp without explaining why, which is exactly the silence that made the original lists untrustworthy. A page may leave an engine out, but it has to say so.

Any future page written to that convention is covered without touching the test, and the test asserts the convention is in use (at least three Rd pages, at least one vignette) so it cannot pass by matching nothing.

462. A correction: the local gate could not fail

Worth recording against myself, because it changes what several rounds’ “suite clean” actually meant.

Since Part XLVI each round has run the full local suite as a gate before starting the checks, and the gate script decided pass/fail with

grep -qE "^[0-9]+\. (Failure|Error)" "$SP"/suite.log

testthat’s summary reporter does not print failures that way. It prints

── 1. Failure ('test-doc-coverage.R:215:3'): no test reaches a Suggests engine

with a box-drawing prefix, so the pattern never matched and the gate reported “suite clean” unconditionally. It was not a gate; it was a formality.

Two things limit the damage, and both should be said plainly rather than used as cover. The real verification in every round was R CMD check’s own [ FAIL 0 | ... ] line, which is authoritative, ran on both R versions, and read 0 every time – so the conclusions those rounds reported were correct. And the same broken pattern is why I read this round’s doc-coverage run as clean when it had a failure in it; the failure was found only because a later run happened to print it where a different grep caught it.

The gate now matches ^── [0-9]+\. (Failure|Error), and the failure it would have caught this round was a real one.

463. The failure the gate should have caught

The package ships a guard requiring that no test reach a Suggests engine without an availability check, and it names the acceptable spellings – skip_if_not_installed, requireNamespace, skip_if(, or the package’s own engine_installed. Part XLVIII’s multivariate contract test used none of them: it called thirteen Suggests wrappers inside

r <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(calls[[nm]]())),
              error = function(e) NULL)
if (is.null(r)) next

which is safe against an absent engine but conflates it with a call that failed for a real reason – so a genuine breakage in an installed engine would have been silently skipped, and the test would still have passed.

The guard’s own comment had already explained why engine_installed() is the right tool here (“for a loop over methods it is the better guard – it skips the one method rather than aborting the whole test”). The test now looks the engine package up in the registry, skips only what is genuinely absent, and lets any other error be the failure it is. A shipped guard caught a weakness in a test written to check the docs, which is the kind of thing the guards exist for.

Both check copies were confirmed to hold all six of this round’s edits individually, and the local suite ran as a gate – this time with a pattern that can actually fail (0 real failures).

465. What four rounds of sweeping have actually produced

part class swept code defects documentation defects
XLV factor / multi-column input 9 0
XLVI non-finite input 3 0
XLVII degenerate input (constant, too short) 7 0
XLVIII result contract and accessors 0 3
XLIX documentation against behaviour 0 7

The crossover is the point. The first three parts found code that quietly did the wrong thing; the last two found none, because those sweeps had already been run. What they found instead was text that no longer described the code – and the two rounds of it produced ten corrections, every one of which a reader would have believed.

Both halves needed the same method, and it is the only method that has worked in this loop: enumerate the routes and check each one, rather than inspecting the thing you suspect. The augment() list was found by accident in XLVIII and fixed in one place; the deliberate sweep in XLIX found the same list next door, two more like it, and three copies in the vignettes. Fixing an instance is not fixing a class – which is exactly what §422 said about a guard in one branch of a switch(), in a part that was about code.

The guards now reflect that. Three of this round’s four defects are covered by one test that scans every Rd page and every vignette for a shared convention and checks it against the registry in both directions, so the class is closed rather than the instances.

Part L – NEWS.md, and the accepted values nobody had counted

Part XLIX closed the stale-enumeration class for capability lists. The obvious next question is whether the release’s own front matter is accurate, because NEWS.md is what a CRAN reviewer reads before anything else and it had not been checked once in this loop.

466. NEWS.md holds up

Every checkable claim in the 0.5.0 section was verified against the live package:

  • “Engine wave #2 – 19 new methods.” Counted from the section’s own bullets: nsp, mcp, esac, pilliat, hdcov, network, var, hdreg, fmean, fcov, kwc, fabisearch, pettitt, buishand, snht, taylor, bfast, wbsts, binsegrcpp. Nineteen exactly.
  • “cpt_detect() reaches 50 wired methods.” The registry has 50 available.
  • “New change_in levels "covariance", "network", "regression" and "seasonality".” All four route. The last one took a second look: bfast_wrapper(x) on its own reports change_in = "mean", which looked like the level did not exist – but change_in is a documented argument of that wrapper with "mean" as its default, and cpt_detect(x, method = "bfast", change_in = "seasonality") puts "seasonality" in the slot. Both routes honour the same argument; there was nothing wrong.
  • 161 function names appear in backticks across the file. The 43 that are not package exports are base R, other packages, S3 method names written out, and this package’s own internals (need_pkg, validate_data, build_segments) – all legitimate in a file that describes internal fixes.

467. Two more clean sweeps, and one worth keeping

Every documented default against its formal and every @return change_in claim against the live object both came back clean (§458 in the previous part covers the method; the counts were 166 and 9).

@family changepoint engines: 43 of 43 engine wrapper pages carry it, so the “See also” list on every engine page is complete.

Reproducibility. Each of the 50 methods was run twice in the same session, without a seed, and the changepoints compared – a stochastic method consumes RNG state and so answers differently on the second call, which is what makes this a real test rather than a tautology.

44 of 50 are stable (28 of them deterministic with no seed argument at all, 16 stable and offering one anyway); 5 could not be called with the probe’s input shape. Exactly one varies: taylor, a bootstrap method, which is supposed to. Its contract holds where it matters:

no seed:      70,94,140  |  70,140  |  70,140
seed = 1:     70,94,140  |  70,94,140  |  70,94,140
seed = 2:     70,140
cpt_detect(seed = 1):  70,94,140  |  70,94,140

so the seed controls the answer, gives a different answer for a different value, and works through the dispatcher as well as the wrapper. Every method in the package is either deterministic or has a working seed.

468. The four accepted values the vignettes never mentioned

The defect of the round, and it is user-facing rather than cosmetic. Both vignettes told the reader what change_in accepts:

the change_in argument accepts "mean", "var", "meanvar", "slope", and "distribution".

Five values. The registry’s supports column routes nine:

value methods
mean 37
var 10
distribution 6
meanvar 6
slope 6
covariance 3 (hdcov, fcov, kwc)
network 2 (network, fabisearch)
regression 2 (var, hdreg)
seasonality 1 (bfast)

The four missing are precisely the ones NEWS credits to wave 2 – so the release notes announced them, cpt_detect()’s own @param listed all nine correctly, and both vignettes still described the pre-wave-2 package. A reader of either would not have known they could ask for a covariance or a network change at all.

That is the same split Part XLIX found twice: the function documentation right, the vignette stale. Nineteen new engines were added and the vignettes’ sentence about what the argument accepts was not revisited.

Both now list all nine and point at cpt_methods()’s supports column, and a guard checks every enumeration of four or more quoted change_in values – in any vignette or in cpt_detect.Rd – against unique(unlist(reg$supports)), in both directions. It requires at least three such enumerations to exist, so it cannot pass by matching nothing.
