533. Verification

The gate ran clean. cran-comments.md is in .Rbuildignore and confirmed absent from a freshly built tarball, so nothing this round changed can affect a check – which is precisely why nothing had ever validated it.

R 4.4.1, full Suggests: FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 52 | PASS 3504. R 4.6.0, Imports-only: FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 172 | PASS 2061.

checking installed package size reports OK on both, which is now the fourth consecutive OK – and is exactly why the corrected paragraph does not claim the note is gone. Four OKs in a row is what a coin looks like when it lands the same way four times.

534. A round with no test to show for it

Nothing was added to the suite this round, and nothing could have been. A test cannot check cran-comments.md: the file is excluded from the build, so it is absent from the installed package the tests run against, and its claims are about this submission rather than about the package’s behaviour – “0.4.0 was published on 2026-08-24”, “thirty-seven defects were fixed”, “the note is gone on every platform we check”. Those are assertions about history and about check results on machines the test suite will never see.

That makes it the one artefact in the repository whose only quality control is somebody reading it against reality. Sixty-two parts of this loop swept code, documentation, tests, rendered output, data, length and composition, and never touched the file a reviewer opens first – because it is invisible to every mechanism the earlier rounds relied on.

The three errors were of one kind, and it is not carelessness: each was true when written. @examplesIf was the gate on that page before \dontrun{} replaced it; the size note really had gone when dpi = 72 first landed; there really were thirty-seven fixes before four more were added. A submission document is a snapshot of a moving package, and the snapshot is only checked if someone checks it.

So the durable output of this round is not a guard but a note for whoever prepares the next release: re-read cran-comments.md against the package immediately before submitting, because it is the one file that cannot fail a test.

Part LXIV – The rendered README, the pkgdown index, and an enumeration that lied

§534 named the class this round continues: artefacts whose only quality control is somebody reading them. cran-comments.md was one. Three more sit beside it, and each is checkable in a way that page was not.

535. README.md holds 451 lines of output nothing compares to behaviour

README.md is generated from README.Rmd, and the committed copy carries 451 #> lines – printed tibbles, cpt_recommend() tables, dimension lines. No test reads them. They were true at the last knit, and the package has changed in sixty-three parts since.

The definitive check is not to spot-check the claims but to re-knit and diff, which tests all 451 lines at once. Done in an isolated copy, because rendering writes figures into man/figures/ and the real tree should not be touched by a verification:

cp -r . $SP/rd/pkg && rm -rf $SP/rd/pkg/.git
cp README.md README.md.orig
Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("README.Rmd", quiet = TRUE)'
diff README.md.orig README.md

Two differing lines, and they are the same line:

< #>   Runtime (seconds):        0.007
> #>   Runtime (seconds):        0.008

Every one of the 451 output lines is current. The single diff is a wall-clock measurement, which cannot be otherwise – and that is worth recording, because it means a future re-knit will always show one diff. Whoever repeats this check should expect the runtime line and nothing else.

The re-knit also settled a question Part LX left open. Four orphan figures were deleted there (README-unnamed-chunk-{10,16,17,30}-1.png, 179K) on the grounds that nothing referenced them. Re-knitting produces exactly the same 24 filenames, zero orphans – so the four came from an older README structure the current .Rmd no longer generates, and the deletion was right. Had chunk numbering shifted, the re-knit would have written 24 new names and orphaned 24 old ones.

536. _pkgdown.yml enumerates 125 topics by hand

The reference: section lists every documented topic by name, in sections. A name that no longer exists fails pkgdown::build_site(); an exported topic in no section is dropped from the site with a warning. Neither is visible to R CMD check, and the site is not built in this loop.

Checked both directions against man/*.Rd aliases and NAMESPACE:

count
listed in _pkgdown.yml 125
distinct Rd topics 125
listed but undocumented 0
exported but unplaced 0

Exactly balanced. The index is being maintained in step with the manual – consistent with the last commit’s “inbound links 71->124”.

537. benchmarks.Rmd sends the reader past a ceiling that exists

The web-only article (.Rbuildignore:16 keeps vignettes/articles out of the tarball, so it is checked by nothing) explains why cpm reports 350 changepoints at n = 100,000 when four are real: arl0 = 500 asks for a false alarm every 500 observations, so a long series implies n / arl0 of them. Correct, and arl0 = 500 is confirmed as the default in both cpm_wrapper() and cpt_monitor(). Then it prescribes the fix:

Setting arl0 = 5 * n returns exactly the 4 real changepoints at every length.

At the article’s three lengths that asks for 5,000, 50,000 and 500,000. The third does not exist. cpm ships threshold tables for a fixed grid, and cpt_detect() refuses anything off it – deliberately, because cpm answers an off-grid value by printing an error and returning no changepoints, which is indistinguishable from a real “no changes” result (the trap R61 was written for). Measured:

arl0 = 5000     OK, 4 changepoints
arl0 = 50000    OK, 4 changepoints
arl0 = 500000   ERROR: not an average run length that cpm ships

So the recipe is unreachable at exactly the length that needs it most. The sentence is now scoped to the two lengths where 5 * n exists, followed by the ceiling and why the refusal is deliberate.

538. And the refusal message named half the grid

Chasing that ceiling turned up the larger defect. arl0 = 50000 works, yet the error message listing legal values stopped at 20,000. The list came from prose, not from the engine, so the definitive source is the table cpm:::loadThresholds() indexes – cpmthresholds, whose names are <cpmType>ARL<value>. All 15 types ship the same 24 values:

100, 200, 300, 370, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900, 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, 6000, 7000, 8000, 9000, 10000, 20000, 30000, 40000, 50000

(ExponentialAdjusted additionally ships 1-24.) The message listed 12 of 24, omitting 300, 800, 900, 3000, 4000, 6000-9000, 30000, 40000 and 50000 – every one of which runs. A user who hit the error and needed an arl0 of 30,000 was told the maximum was 20,000.

Fixed at both sites that carried the list: the @param arl0 roxygen (R/wrap-nonparam.R:20, propagated to man/cpm_wrapper.Rd) and the stop() at line 114. The @param now also states the two facts the omission hid – the grid is identical for every cpm_type, and 50,000 is a ceiling, so an arl0 proportional to series length runs out.

539. Why R61 missed it, and the shape of the fix

Test R61 already covered this argument. It asserted the guard fires for c(0, -5, 333, 20, 50) and that supported values work for c(100, 370, 500, 1000, 20000). Every value in that second set is inside the truncated list – so the test confirmed the code ran, never that the enumeration was complete. The same failure mode as §421’s covering metric: sampling inside the wrong answer agrees with it.

The extension derives the grid instead of restating it:

th   <- utils::getFromNamespace("cpmthresholds", "cpm")
arl  <- as.integer(sub("^.*ARL", "", names(th)))
grid <- sort(unique(arl[arl >= 100]))
msg  <- tryCatch(cpm_wrapper(x, arl0 = 333), error = conditionMessage)
listed <- as.integer(regmatches(msg, gregexpr("[0-9]+",
            sub("^.*Supported values are ", "", msg)))[[1]])
expect_setequal(listed, grid)

It also asserts the “same for every cpm_type” claim the new @param makes, by intersecting the grid across types, and runs the four values the old list denied (300, 3000, 30000, and the ceiling). Because it depends on a cpm internal, it skips rather than errors if cpmthresholds disappears.

540. The proof that proved nothing

Reverting the message to the truncated list made exactly one test fail, R61 – which looked like proof the new assertion discriminates. It was not. The assertion was broken in a way that failed unconditionally:

listed <- as.integer(regmatches(
  msg, gregexpr("[0-9]+", sub("^.*Supported values are ", "", msg)))[[1]])

regmatches(x, m) extracts from the string the offsets in m were measured on. Here the offsets come from the trimmed tail and the extraction is from the untrimmed msg, so it slices at the wrong positions and returns text; as.integer() turns that into NA, and expect_setequal(NA, grid) fails whatever the message says. Standalone debugging missed it because there I had used the same string for both arguments – the version in the file and the version I checked were not the same code.

Which is why breaking the input is only half a proof. A guard that fails unconditionally is indistinguishable from a working guard if the only case you run is the one that should fail. The complete proof needs both directions, and the passing direction is the one that catches this:

message R61 failures
truncated (the old list) 1
complete (the fixed list) 0, with 40 assertions passing

The same shape as §421’s “when a sweep reports that everything is broken, the sweep is broken”, arriving from the other side: when a guard reports that the one broken input is broken, the guard may still be broken.

541. The axis, swept to exhaustion

One defect of this kind invites the general question: what other messages in this package hand the user a list of legal values? Three, all in wrap-nonparam.R, all cpm:

  • the arl0 grid – was wrong, now derived and guarded
  • lambda = 0.1 and 0.3, twice, for cpm_type = "FET"

The lambda pair is right, and verifiable from the same table: FET01 and FET03 are the only lambda-parameterised types cpm ships. Axis closed.

Full local suite clean, then both checks.

R 4.4.1, full Suggests R 4.6.0, Imports only
checking tests OK, 341s OK, 118s
checking examples OK, 54s OK, 36s
--run-donttest OK, 130s OK, 49s
re-building vignettes OK, 116s OK, 70s
checking package vignettes OK OK
installed package size NOTE OK

Everything the package controls passes. The remaining ERROR/WARNING/NOTEs are this machine’s toolchain, and the baseline shifted underneath the loop: pdflatex and qpdf are no longer on PATH here. That turns what used to be a single qpdf WARNING into a PDF-manual ERROR plus WARNING, and adds a third NOTE – ggchangepoint-manual.tex, flagged as “non-standard things in the check directory”, which is simply the debris the failed pdflatex run left behind. The 4.4.1 dependency NOTE is rjags and mcp absent (JAGS is not installed here; the CI workflow installs it on Linux and macOS). None of these is a package defect, and none is new work – but the recorded baseline of “1 qpdf WARNING + 3 NOTEs” no longer describes this machine, so a future round should compare against the shape above instead.

The installed-size NOTE flickered back on 4.4.1 after four consecutive OKs, which is the boundary behaviour Part LX measured rather than a regression.

Part LXV – The third citation source, which the test was named for

The standing brief asks every round whether every \citep/@key resolves, whether every bib entry is used, and whether entries are attributed to the right work. R44 is the shipped authority for that, and reading it rather than re-deriving it – the lesson of §440 – shows it covers more than its name suggests and less than its comment claims.

543. What R44 already guarantees

Confirmed, and stated once: both bibliographies are exactly balanced.

entries consumers
inst/REFERENCES.bib 58 58 \insertRef keys
vignettes/vignette_reference.bib 63 63 @key citations

Zero unused, zero duplicate keys, every key resolving. Both directions are guarded – expect_setequal(names(inst), unique(used)) closed the defined-to-used direction in an earlier part, when ten dead entries came out. Re-deriving that was wasted motion.

544. But “the three citation sources agree” compared two

R44’s own comment names three: cpt_cite(), the \insertRef keys, and the vignette bibliography. Its assertions compare the two .bib files to each other and check that every key resolves. The free-text table behind cpt_cite() is never compared to either – and that table is exactly where the drift the comment describes lived: “the TGUH paper was dated 2018 in cpt_cite() and 2022 in the vignette bib”.

So the one source that had been wrong was the one left unguarded.

cpt_references() is a hand-maintained tribble, 58 rows of prose. Checked directly, it is currently correct: every one of the 50 available methods has an entry, no duplicates, no entry for a method the registry does not have (the eight non-method rows – crops, edetector, benchmark, critical_difference and four more – are feature topics, reachable as cpt_cite("crops")), and for the 35 methods whose wrapper serves them alone and cites exactly one key, the surnames and the year in the prose match the bib entry the help page cites.

The comparison needs the 1:1 restriction, and the reason is worth recording because the first pass without it reported five mismatches that were all correct. cpt_wrapper serves five changepoint methods; its help page cites the software (Killick 2014) while cpt_cite() names each method’s own paper – Killick 2012 for pelt, Scott and Knott 1974 for binseg, Auger and Lawrence 1989 for segneigh, Hinkley 1970 for amoc, Haynes 2017 for np. Both are right; a shared wrapper simply has no single publication. The sweep was measuring an invariant that does not hold.

545. A citation that does not render, in the one vignette nothing scans

R44 scans vignettes/*.Rmd non-recursively, so vignettes/articles/ – the web-only benchmarks.Rmd – is outside every citation check in the package. It also declares no bibliography: field.

That combination is currently harmless because the article cites nothing, and it is a trap rather than a defect: a vignette with @keys and no bibliography: does not fail to build. Pandoc emits the key as literal text, so @killick2012optimal reaches the reader as those characters. The invariant that matters is the pairing, and it holds across all eight files:

declares bibliography: @ citations
introduction yes 74
ggchangepoint yes 28
comparison yes 17
inference yes 4
monitoring yes 4
extending yes 2
supervised yes 1
articles/benchmarks no 0

546. What was added

Two guards in R44, implementing what its comment already promised:

  • for every 1:1-wrapper single-key method, the surnames and the year in cpt_references() must match the inst/REFERENCES.bib entry the help page cites, with expect_gt(compared, 30L) so a refactor that stops resolving wrappers cannot silently compare nothing;
  • across vignettes/ recursively, a file has @ citations if and only if it declares a bibliography:.

Proved in both directions, which §540 established as the minimum. Two independent breaks – restoring the historical TGUH year drift in cpt_references(), and appending See @killick2012optimal ... to the article that declares no bibliography – produce exactly two failures, one each; with both reverted, R44 passes 164 assertions.

Full local suite clean; both checks at the shape §542 recorded, with checking installed package size ... OK on both.

checking examples OK, 54s OK, 36s
--run-donttest OK, 132s OK, 49s

Part LXVI – The one platform that disagreed

The 0.5.0 work to this point was committed and pushed as bfa2677, and GitHub Actions ran the matrix cran-comments.md advertises. Five of six jobs green: pkgdown, windows-latest release, and all three Ubuntu flavours (devel, release, oldrel-1). macos-latest release failed, and it found something no local check could.

548. One assertion, out of 5,633

── Failure ('test-doc-coverage.R:635:7'): every change_in a method
   claims to support actually works ──
Expected `is.null(res)` to be FALSE.
mosum claims change_in = mean but errored

[ FAIL 1 | WARN 0 | SKIP 34 | PASS 5633 ]

The same log explains it. On that runner {mosum} cannot be loaded – rgl.so needs libGLU.1.dylib, which is absent – and nine other tests already skip for exactly that reason, reported by testthat as “{mosum} cannot be loaded (9)”. Those nine use skip_if_not_installed(), which attempts the load. The change_in sweep did not.

Nothing is wrong with the package. mosum is a Suggests engine, and a machine where it cannot load is a machine where it should be skipped.

549. Two predicates, one question each

engine_installed() is the package’s own availability predicate:

engine_installed <- function(pkg) {
  if (pkg %in% c("changepoint", "changepoint.np", "ecp")) return(TRUE)
  length(suppressWarnings(find.package(pkg, quiet = TRUE))) > 0L
}

find.package(), deliberately – and there is a shipped test asserting it adds no namespace, expect_false(probe %in% loadedNamespaces()). That is right for package code, which uses it to tell a user what to install, and it must not load 35 engines to answer.

But 28 places in the test suite had borrowed it to mean “can I run this”, and those are different questions. A package can be on disk and unloadable. Constructed locally, the divergence is exact:

engine_installed() engine_usable()
brokenpkg (DESCRIPTION only, no loadable namespace) TRUE FALSE
mosum (here) TRUE TRUE
ggchangepoint.no.such.engine FALSE FALSE

So the suite gets the predicate for the question it actually asks, in setup.R, and this is requireNamespace() used for what it does answer – “can this be loaded here” – rather than as a stand-in for “is it installed”, which is the misuse the 0.5.0 audit warned about.

All 28 test-suite uses now call it. engine_installed() is untouched, and the test that is about it keeps calling it, because its subject is the non-loading guarantee.

550. Three things the blind rename broke, and how they surfaced

Replacing an identifier across five files is not a safe refactor, and this one had three casualties – worth recording because each was silent:

  1. Five sites read ggchangepoint:::engine_usable(...). The helper lives in setup.R, not in the package namespace, so every one of those would have errored. Caught by grepping for :::engine_usable rather than by trusting the rename.
  2. The predicate’s own test got rewritten, so the assertion that find.package() adds no namespace would have been made about the function that deliberately does load one – inverting the thing it exists to prove. Restored, with the engine_usable() half added alongside as the deliberate opposite.
  3. The guard-recognition meta-test carries the predicate names in a regex string, which the rename also edited. It now recognises both spellings, since a test about engine_installed() is correctly guarded by engine_installed().

The divergence case is now a shipped guard as well: a temp libpath holding a directory with nothing but a DESCRIPTION, which find.package() accepts and the loader cannot use.

551. Verification

Full local suite clean, and both checks unchanged from §547’s shape.

R 4.4.1 R 4.6.0
checking tests OK, 387s OK, 118s
checking examples OK, 53s OK, 35s
--run-donttest OK, 139s OK, 48s
re-building vignettes OK, 113s OK, 67s
installed package size OK OK

mosum loads on this machine, so the sweep still reaches it here and no coverage was traded for the fix – the skip only engages where the engine genuinely cannot load. That is the point: the failure was never reproducible locally, and the fix must not be either.

This fix is in the working tree and not in bfa2677. CI for that commit stands at five green and one red; the red job is the one this part repairs.

Part LXVII – Guarding the shape that was invisible, and a pointer to nothing

552. The literal-call detector could not see the failing form

Part LXVI fixed the macOS job by giving the suite a loadability predicate. That leaves the question of why nothing caught it, and the answer is in the shipped meta-test "no test reaches a Suggests engine outside a guarded block". It is exact rather than heuristic, and its own comment says so: it matches literal call forms only –

sprintf("method\\s*=\\s*\"%s\"", m)      # method = "mosum"
sprintf("%s\\(", wp)                     # mosum_wrapper(

– “because the bare name collides with other vocabulary”. Correct, and it means a loop over the registry calling cpt_detect(v, method = m) names no engine at all. Ten such blocks exist, including the one that failed. All ten were outside every guard the suite had, guarded or not.

The first attempt at hardening was to stop recognising engine_installed() as a guard. Reverting the change_in sweep to it proved that does nothing: the block is invisible to the detector, so what it is guarded by never comes up. A tightening that cannot fail is not a guard, which §540 had already said once.

553. Tolerance versus prediction

Twelve blocks drive dispatch from the registry with a variable. Three of them use no availability predicate, and inspecting them was the useful part of the round: they wrap the call in tryCatch(error = function(e) NULL) and next on NULL. An engine that cannot load simply drops out. They are safe by construction and need nothing.

The change_in sweep wraps the call the same way – and then asserts:

expect_false(is.null(res),
             info = paste(m, "claims change_in =", ci, "but errored"))

That is the whole difference. For every other sweep NULL means “not here”; for this one it means “broke its contract”. Nine of the ten sole-guard blocks tolerate absence; the tenth reports it as a defect.

So the new guard is narrow on purpose: a block that drives dispatch from builtin_registry() with a variable method = and asserts the call succeeded must gate each iteration on engine_usable(). Blocks that next on NULL are left alone, because they are already right.

Proved both ways. Reverting both of the change_in block’s engine_usable() calls – the loop guard and the later reachable filter, and the first attempt reverted only one, which is why it appeared not to fire – flags exactly test-doc-coverage.R:600; restored, it flags nothing.

554. ?taylor_wrapper sent readers to a vignette that cannot exist

The round’s vignette pass took the cross-reference axis: every vignette("...") and every \link{} in the vignettes and the 205 Rd topics. All resolve – and the check was wrong in a way worth keeping.

It built the list of valid vignette names from vignettes/ recursively, which includes articles/benchmarks.Rmd. That file is excluded from the tarball by .Rbuildignore:16, so it is never installed. The built tarball holds seven vignette sources and zero articles entries, and vignette("benchmarks", package = "ggchangepoint") warns vignette ‘benchmarks’ not found.

R/wrap-applied.R:124, propagated to man/taylor_wrapper.Rd:58, told the reader to run exactly that call – in the paragraph explaining that taylor cannot be interrupted and that sizing the run beforehand is the only option. The reader most in need of that page was sent to a warning.

Being web-only is correct: _pkgdown.yml files it under “Web only” because the sweep behind it takes over twenty minutes. So the pointer was the defect, and it now names the published URL and says plainly that vignette() will not find it.

Guarded, in the direction that generalises: no file in R/, man/ or the shipped vignettes may reference a vignette absent from the top level of vignettes/. The guard also asserts that .Rbuildignore still excludes articles/ and that the directory still exists – otherwise it would pass by guarding nothing. Reintroducing the bad pointer produces exactly one failure.

--run-donttest OK, 138s OK, 49s
re-building vignettes OK, 116s OK, 70s
checking Rd files OK OK

556. State of the tree

bfa2677 is pushed and carries Parts XXX-LXIV. CI for it is five green, one red: pkgdown, Windows release and all three Ubuntu flavours passed; macos-latest release failed on the change_in sweep.

Parts LXV, LXVI and LXVII are in the working tree and not in any commit. LXVI is the fix for that red job.

Part LXVIII – What the return values promise

The axes this loop has swept all sit on one side of a function call: arguments, documentation prose, tests, data shape, artefacts, citations, platform. This part takes the other side – the \value sections, which promise the caller specific named things.

557. Two surfaces confirmed once, and not re-derived

DESCRIPTION asks a checker to install 56 Suggests, and nothing verifies each is used. All 56 are referenced outside the dependency fields. Clean.

The vignette pass took the count-claims axis: every sentence in vignette prose asserting a number of methods, engines, rows, families or provenances – eleven of them. All correct. extending.Rmd’s “fifty detectors”, ggchangepoint.Rmd’s “Five rows carry status planned”, inference.Rmd’s “Four provenances”, introduction.Rmd’s “50 methods” and its “six families”, which enumerates exactly six.

Numbered sections run 1-4 in inference.Rmd and 1-7 in monitoring.Rmd, both sequential; and all seven shipped vignettes have a %\VignetteIndexEntry{} identical to their title:, so the vignette index and the rendered page agree.

One near-miss worth recording as a discipline note rather than a finding. The registry’s online flag marks bocpd, cpm, ocd while cpt_monitor() accepts edetector, cpm, ocd – sets that differ in two of three members, which reads like a defect. It is documented on ?cpt_methods (“online means the algorithm is sequential … the sets overlap without coinciding”) and pinned by a shipped test whose name is "the online flag and cpt_monitor()'s methods are distinct sets". Third time this loop that a “finding” was already a shipped test. Grep the suite before measuring anything.

558. Every named column the manual promises

122 Rd pages carry a \value section; 102 name lowercase \code{} tokens, 413 in total. Most are argument or package names. The mechanically checkable subset is the claim “a \code{x} column”, which 16 pages make about 19 columns. Run each method and look for the column in changepoints, in data, and in augment() output:

claim where it actually is
bcp posterior_prob changepoints
cpm detection_time changepoints
inspect strength changepoints
taylor confidence changepoints
segmented/smuce/strucchange ci_upper changepoints
fitted, seven engines data + augment

All 14 reachable claims honoured, each in the place its page implies.

The penalty$type strings are also promises, and 17 distinct ones are set literally in R/. Two live values are not among them – SIC from segneigh and AIC: meanar1cpt from envcpt – and both are correct: the first is changepoint’s own default passed through, the second is composed by envcpt from the model it selected. Not literals, not defects.

559. The most fragile claim in the package had no test

?glance.ggcpt explains why total_cost is NA in four cases and reports normally otherwise. Measured against the live package, every case holds:

total_cost
pelt, mean, default (MBIC) NA
pelt, mean, penalty = "BIC" 544.4
pelt, mean, penalty = "AIC" 511.9
pelt, mean, penalty = 10 544.4
pelt, change_in = "var" 904.8
pelt, change_in = "meanvar" 543.9
binseg / segneigh / np NA

The shipped test covered the binseg/segneigh NAs, the numeric penalties and the two other change_in values. Three of the page’s claims were unpinned, and one of them is the most upstream-fragile statement in the package: the mean-under-MBIC NA is not a property of changepoint at all. It is a collision between two of this package’s own Imports – loading changepoint.np replaces changepoint’s logLik method for cpt objects with one that errors on exactly that combination. Both are Imports, so the collision is always present, and if either upstream changes the NA quietly becomes a number while the help page keeps saying otherwise.

Now pinned, along with np being NA for the unrelated reason that changepoint.np defines no logLik, and named penalties reporting normally. Inverting the headline assertion produces exactly one failure, so it is checking the quantity rather than passing vacuously.

560. The one number that cannot be reproduced, and why that is fine

The same page says that for one and the same segmentation cpt.range reports 219.7 where PELT reports 659.9. That pair cannot come from glance(), which returns NA for binseg by construction – it describes the raw engine costs, on the author’s own data, which no seed in the sources reproduces.

The relationship is reproducible, and that is the part the sentence is making a claim about. Forcing both engines onto an identical segmentation (penalty = "BIC", both reporting a single changepoint at 100) gives -341.4 against -1071.8, a ratio of 0.319 where the documented pair is 0.333. Same phenomenon, different data, and the engine emits its own “Not changed to be -2*logLik” warning while doing it – which the shipped test already asserts does not leak. Left as written.

561. Verification

Full local suite clean; both checks otherwise at §542’s shape.

R 4.4.1 R 4.6.0
checking tests OK, 379s OK, 119s
re-building vignettes OK, 117s OK, 70s
checking Rd cross-references OK OK
installed package size NOTE, 6.4Mb INFO, 5.4Mb

562. The installed-size flicker, finally explained

Ten parts of this loop have watched that NOTE appear and vanish – 5.2Mb NOTE, OK, 5.1Mb NOTE, OK, 6.6Mb NOTE, then five consecutive OK, now 6.4Mb NOTE. Reading the two runs of the same round side by side gives the answer, because they disagree:

total doc help
R 4.4.1, full Suggests 6.4Mb 3.8Mb 1.8Mb
R 4.6.0, Imports only 5.4Mb 2.7Mb 1.8Mb

help is constant. doc is not, and it is the whole variance: the Imports-only run skips the chunks that need a Suggests engine, so it draws 1.1Mb fewer vignette figures. The package therefore straddles CRAN’s 5Mb line, and which side it lands on is decided by how many engines the checking machine happens to have. That is not flakiness in the package and it is not a defect – but it does mean the NOTE will appear on some CRAN platforms and not others, and cran-comments.md already describes it as marginal rather than gone.

No waste behind it. man/figures is 1.3Mb across 24 files, the largest a 112K plot at 672x480 and 8-bit RGB, plus a 96K logo. Nothing oversized, nothing at the wrong bit depth.

563. The one duplicate figure is the point

Hashing the figures turned up exactly one byte-identical pair, README-unnamed-chunk-6-1.png and README-unnamed-chunk-50-1.png, which reads like 40K of waste. It is the opposite. Chunk 6 is autoplot(res); chunk 50 is plot(res), captioned “base-graphics fallback (delegates to autoplot)”. The two files being byte-identical is the evidence that the delegation works. Deleting either would delete the demonstration.

And nothing asserted it. plot_via_autoplot() backs fourteen classes, and the suite only checked that plot() and autoplot() each return a "ggplot" – which a completely divergent implementation also satisfies. Now guarded in two halves: structurally, every plot.* method in R/ routes through the one helper, which is exact and covers all fourteen; and live, plot(res) and autoplot(res) must agree on labels, on layer geoms, and on the full ggplot_build()$data.

The structural half was broken on the first attempt, in the way §540 predicts. These methods are one-liners, and reading a fixed five-line window past a definition walks into the next method – which does delegate. So a divergent plot.ggcpt_delay() looked compliant and the guard could not fail. It now takes the definition line alone unless it opens a brace. Divergent method: 1 failure. Compliant tree: 6 assertions pass. Third guard this loop that needed the passing direction to reveal it was inert.

564. And the guard failed the check it was meant to survive

r74 came back 2 ERRORs on both R versions, tests failing, after a local suite that was clean. The cause is the gap between the two, and it is worth stating because the loop has now met it twice in different clothes:

── Failure ('test-hardening.R:1233:3'): every plot() method delegates ──
Expected `length(defs)` >= 13L.
Actual comparison: 0 < 13

R/ is not installed. The local gate runs under pkgload::load_all() from the source tree, where ../../R exists; R CMD check installs the package and runs the tests from .Rcheck/tests/testthat, where it does not. So defs was empty and the structural assertion fired against nothing. The live half needs no sources, so only the structural half is now conditional – and it asserts expect_length(defs, 0L) in the installed case rather than silently doing nothing, so the branch is still saying something.

Fixing it turned up a second trap. The obvious guard, dir.exists(test_path("..", "..", "R")), cannot work: test_path() aborts with “Can’t find path” when the target is missing, so the dir.exists() never runs. normalizePath(file.path("..", ".."), mustWork = FALSE) is what the rest of the suite uses, and now this test does too. Verified in both contexts: 6 assertions pass from the source tree, and 6 pass from a directory whose ../../R is absent.

A local suite being clean is not evidence a test survives R CMD check. Any test that reads the source tree has to be run from somewhere the source tree is not.

565. Verification, after the fix

R 4.4.1 R 4.6.0
checking tests OK, 376s OK, 119s
installed package size OK OK
Status 1 ERROR, 2 WARNINGs, 3 NOTEs 1 ERROR, 1 WARNING, 2 NOTEs

Back to §542’s environmental shape on both, with the size NOTE off again – consistent with §562: it tracks how many engines drew figures, not anything the round changed.

Part LXIX – Counting the right noun

566. Two clauses of the brief, answered and closed

The standing brief asks whether bib entries are complete, which no round had tested – earlier parts checked that keys resolve, that no entry is unused, that the two files agree on year and journal, and that authors match cpt_cite(). Completeness is a different question: does each entry carry the fields its own type requires?

Checked against BibTeX’s requirements per type:

entries types incomplete
inst/REFERENCES.bib 58 55 article, 1 book, 2 inproceedings 0
vignettes/vignette_reference.bib 63 60 article, 1 book, 1 inproceedings, 1 manual 0

Zero across 121 entries. Every @article has author, title, journal and year; the books have publishers; the proceedings have booktitles.

Figure alt text, also unswept and a thing CRAN comments on. All seven vignettes set fig.alt (72 occurrences), and the rendered HTML settles it: 67 <img> tags across eight built pages, none without an alt. Nor is the text perfunctory – no page repeats an alt string, the only strings under 50 characters are the template’s own [Top] and [R logo] navigation, and the five that appear twice appear in two different vignettes, where the same figure is legitimately shown again.

567. “Nineteen further engines” counted methods

The feature tour’s New in 0.5.0 box opened with:

New in 0.5.0. Nineteen further engines; …

The number is right. The noun is not, and this package is precise about it: engine is a registry column holding the upstream package name. There are 38 distinct values – 35 in Suggests and the 3 Imports, which is exactly what NEWS.md means by “35 engines inside a 56-package Suggests list”. Nothing in the package yields 19 engines. Measured from the v0.4.0 tag, the engine set grew from roughly 25 packages to 38, a delta near 13.

19 is the delta in methods, and NEWS.md says so itself, in a heading:

Engine wave #2 — 19 new methods

So the two documents disagreed about what was being counted, and the disagreement was resolvable from the repository. Corroborated by 0.4.0’s own NEWS, which was careful with the same distinction – “grows from 13 to 31 wired methods. Eighteen new wrappers” – and by the wrapper exports, which went 26 to 43 at the tag, a delta of 17, matching neither.

The arithmetic closes exactly:

source value
live registry, status == "available" 50
NEWS, “reaches N wired methods” 50
NEWS, 0.4.0’s “from 13 to N wired methods” 31
NEWS, “Engine wave #2 — N new methods” 19
31 + 19 50

One word changed: engines to methods.

568. Guarded with no magic numbers

The guard reads every figure from either the live registry or NEWS.md’s own sentences, so the three can only drift together rather than apart. It asserts reached == live, baseline + delta == live, that the tour’s number word maps to delta, that it is attached to “further methods” – and, separately, that the count of distinct engines is greater than delta, which is the fact the old wording contradicted.

Proved in three states rather than two, because the sentence can fail in two independent ways:

tour text R44-style outcome
“Nineteen further methods” 8 assertions pass
“Nineteen further engines” (the original) 1 failure
“Seventeen further methods” 1 failure

569. Inter-vignette claims, verified

While looking for the count claim: the tour asserts “Six companion vignettes go deeper” and then describes each. Seven vignettes ship, minus the host is six, and the six named are the six that exist – with each description matching its target’s own title and subject, from introduction “develops the methodology” through monitoring “covers sequential detection on a stream and its detection-delay accounting”. No drift.

570. Verification

Full local suite clean; both checks at §542’s shape.

R 4.4.1 R 4.6.0
checking tests OK, 365s OK, 119s
re-building vignettes OK, 116s OK, 69s
installed package size NOTE INFO

The vignette rebuild is the line that matters, since a vignette source changed. The size NOTE is on 4.4.1 and off on 4.6.0 in the same round – §562’s finding restated once: it tracks how many engines drew figures, not anything this round touched.

Part LXX – The rest of the box, and a contract nobody had closed

§567 fixed one word in the feature tour’s New in 0.5.0 box. The box makes a dozen more claims, and the paragraph after it describes the result object. This part checks the rest of it.

571. The object, as described

The tour says a ggcpt carries “the tidy changepoints tibble (cp = last index of the left segment, cp_value = series value there, plus any method-specific columns), a segments table, the data, the raw engine fit, and metadata (method, change_in, penalty, convention, runtime)”.

Live, a ggcpt has ten components: changepoints, segments, data, method, change_in, penalty, fit, call, cp_convention, runtime. Every one the sentence names is there, with the described contents – changepoints is cp/cp_value, segments is seg_id/start/end/n/param_estimate, fit is the upstream cpt.

The parenthetical omits call. That is an abbreviation rather than an error: ?new_ggcpt documents it, \item{call}{The matched call.}, and the sentence is a tour rather than a specification. Left alone.

572. “Each has its own section below or its own vignette”

The box closes with that promise, about twelve named features. It holds:

box claim section
a time index that survives the round trip ## Time indices
significance regions, cpt_confint()/cpt_test() ## Inference
cpt_select() ## Selecting the number of changepoints
influence, sensitivity, statistic, path, scale-space ## Diagnostics
supervised detection ## Supervised detection (+ its own vignette)
consensus and recommendation ## Choosing and combining methods
event annotation and reports ## Communication
benchmarking ## Benchmarking
sequential monitoring ## Streaming (+ its own vignette)
power analysis ## Power and study design
as_ggcpt() / cpt_register_method() ## Extending (+ its own vignette)

Eleven subsections under # The 0.5.0 surface, one per claim, and the methods claim is served by # Engine wrappers.

A sweep along the way reported that 32 of the 50 methods are “named nowhere in the feature tour”, which for a vignette subtitled A Complete Map of the Package is the tell that the sweep is wrong – it was matching quoted strings only. With word boundaries it is 35 of 50 named in prose, and the tour calls cpt_methods() five times, so the full table renders and the map is complete. Fourth time this loop that a large “finding” was a broken measurement. The ratio itself is the warning sign.

573. A closed set that nothing checked was closed

# Engine wrappers opens with a compatibility contract, stated exactly:

Every wrapper from 0.2.0 onwards returns a ggcpt object; only the two original wrappers below predate the class and still return a bare tibble.

Measured across all 43 exported wrappers: 43 in the registry, 43 exported, neither set holding anything the other lacks; exactly two return a bare tibble, and they are exactly cpt_wrapper and ecp_wrapper; 38 of the rest return ggcpt, with fabisearch and hdreg needing a shape the generic probe does not supply.

So the sentence is true – and nothing checked that the exception set is closed. The suite asserted ecp_wrapper() returns a tbl_df in three places and never asked whether a third wrapper had joined it. A new wrapper returning a tibble would falsify the vignette and break every accessor a caller expects to work on a result, silently.

Guarded now, and the first two attempts are the interesting part:

  1. Calling all 43 engines took over ten minutes – unacceptable in a suite that already runs 365s inside the check. Replaced with the documentation surface, which is exact and instant: 135 assertions in 2 seconds.
  2. Asking whether each \value mentions “ggcpt” anywhere passes for everything, because both exceptions mention it in passing – cpt_wrapper names the "ggcpt_fit" attribute, and ecp_wrapper explains that $fit is NULL on a ggcpt from cpt_detect(). All 43 “named ggcpt”, which briefly looked like two wrong help pages. It has to be what the section opens with.

Both directions proved: as shipped, 135 assertions pass; documenting a third wrapper (fpop_wrapper) as returning a tibble produces exactly one failure.

574. Verification

The first run of this round’s gate failed, and the failure is the tightened guard from §552 doing its job on my own test:

── Failure ('test-doc-coverage.R:224:3'): no test reaches a Suggests
   engine outside a guarded block ──

The new wrapper test used fpop_wrapper() as its contrast case – a wrapper on the ggcpt side of the line. fpop is a Suggests engine, and the call was unguarded, so it would have passed here and on all five CI jobs and failed only the Imports-only run. That is the precise failure mode the meta-test was written for, three releases running. Guarded with engine_usable("fpop").

Worth stating plainly: the check that caught this is the one §552 could not make fail on a registry-driven loop, and it caught a literal call immediately. The two halves cover different shapes and both were needed.

Second run, after guarding the call:

R 4.4.1 R 4.6.0
checking tests OK, 360s OK, 120s
re-building vignettes OK, 116s OK, 70s
installed package size OK OK
Status 1 ERROR, 2 WARNINGs, 3 NOTEs 1 ERROR, 1 WARNING, 2 NOTEs

§542’s environmental shape on both, size NOTE off on both.

Part LXXI – The failure that hid behind its own noise

af544bf fixed the macOS job – macos-latest (release) is green – and windows-latest (release) failed instead. Four Ubuntu jobs and pkgdown passed.

575. Thirteen identical lines, none of them the error

The whole visible failure was this, repeated:

Failed with error:  'there is no package called 'RSpectra''

RSpectra is not in this package’s DESCRIPTION at all, directly or transitively. It is suggested by InspectChangepoint – a suggestion of a suggestion, which r-lib/actions does not install – and InspectChangepoint::inspect() and sparse.svd() both call requireNamespace("RSpectra") without quietly = TRUE. The engine handles the absence itself, falling back to base::svd, so these lines are a loading diagnostic and not the failure at all.

They are, however, the reason the failure could not be read. R CMD check keeps the LAST n lines of the test log, default 13, and thirteen repetitions of one diagnostic is exactly the tail. The testthat failure names were pushed off the top and appear in neither gh run view --log-failed nor the complete 43,772-line job log – they were never written.

This is the trap commit fcd3083 already fixed once, for a different variable: “Show the vignette error: _R_CHECK_VIGNETTES_NLINES_ keeps the LAST n lines”. The workflow sets that one and not _R_CHECK_TESTS_NLINES_. Now it sets both, at 1000.

576. Two wrong fixes before the right one

The noise is worth silencing on its own account – it is upstream’s diagnostic printed through our function, and inspect_wrapper() already declares the intent in a comment: “The engine prints Monte Carlo progress; keep the console clean.” That comment was written for utils::capture.output(), which takes stdout only.

  1. suppressMessages() does not work, and the probe said so rather than my assuming it. Only “Loading required namespace” is a condition; requireNamespace() writes the “Failed with error” line straight to stderr, so it printed anyway from inside suppressMessages().
  2. Capturing the message stream without assigning the result silences the engine and then prints the captured lines, because the inner capture.output()’s value gets auto-printed by the outer one.

The form that works assigns both:

ignore <- utils::capture.output(
  inner <- utils::capture.output(
    fit <- do.call(InspectChangepoint::inspect, args),
    type = "message"))

Three properties checked rather than assumed, because redirecting a stream next to the condition system is easy to get wrong:

the stderr diagnostic silenced
a genuine warning() inside still delivered to tryCatch(warning=)
a genuine stop() inside still propagates
fit inside a function body lands in the function env, not a capture frame

Only the stream is redirected; the condition system is untouched.

577. What this did not fix

The Windows failure is still unidentified. The noise explains why it was unreadable, not what it was, and no test in the suite asserts silence around inspect – the nine expect_silent() calls are about cpt_methods(), cpt_recommend(), ggplot builds, as_cpt_series() and cpt_benchmark(), none of which touch that engine. So this part buys observability and a cleaner console, and the next run is what names the defect.

Stated plainly because it would be easy to present a green-looking fix here: two edits went in, one of them makes the next failure legible, and neither is known to address the actual Windows error.

578. All six jobs green – and the cause was never recovered

57a5804: macos-latest, windows-latest, all three Ubuntu flavours and pkgdown all pass. The whole matrix cran-comments.md advertises is green for the first time in this loop.

The honest part is that I cannot say why Windows passed, and the temptation to claim the fix worked should be resisted. Only two things changed: the inspect_wrapper() stream capture, and a log-length variable that cannot affect pass or fail. So either the capture fixed it by a path I cannot see, or the original failure was environmental – a Suggests engine that failed to install on that particular run, say.

One concrete mechanism was worth checking and is ruled out. InspectChangepoint::inspect() does raise a real warning when RSpectra is missing:

if (prod(dim(x)) > 1e+06 && !requireNamespace("RSpectra")) {
    warning("Dimension of data matrix is large, ...")

and test-040-bugfixes.R:528 asserts expect_no_warning(inspect_wrapper(Xg)) – which would fail on Windows and pass everywhere else. But Xg is cbind(a = ..., b = ...) on 150 rows, so prod(dim(x)) is 300, five orders of magnitude below the threshold. The warning cannot have fired. Nor does any of the nine expect_silent() calls touch that engine.

So the failure’s identity went down with the truncated log, and that is precisely what §575 fixed. The durable outcome of this part is not the green tick; it is that a recurrence will name itself. If Windows fails again, the log will say what failed instead of thirteen copies of somebody else’s loading diagnostic.

579. The Windows failure, finally named – and it is a process death

2327dc1 changed only next_release.md, which .Rbuildignore excludes, so the checked tarball was byte-identical to the green 57a5804. Windows failed anyway. That settles the question §578 left open: the failure is intermittent, and nothing in this loop’s edits caused or cured it.

With _R_CHECK_TESTS_NLINES_: 1000 now in effect – confirmed present in the job’s env block – the complete test output is available, and the important thing about it is what is absent:

there is no [ FAIL n | WARN n | SKIP n | PASS n ] line anywhere.

testthat never printed its summary. This is not an expectation failure; the R process died mid-run. testthat.Rout.fail is 91 lines and stops after a printed tibble, with no condition, no traceback and no Execution halted inside the test output.

The last thing printed locates it exactly. test-050-tools.R:462-468 ends a block by trimming and printing five objects:

cv <- cpt_label_error_curve(ds$a$series, labs, penalties = c(2, 20, 200))
for (obj in list(labs, err, b, r, cv)) { ... expect_warning(print(trimmed), NA, ...) }

and the log’s final five tibbles are label_id, label_id, series, method, and penalty with values 2/20/200 – that loop, in order, complete. So the process survived to the end of that test and died at the boundary into the next one, "a monitor refuses a feed of the wrong width", which builds an ocd monitor:

mv <- cpt_monitor("ocd", baseline = matrix(rnorm(240), ncol = 3),
                  thresh = c(10, 10, 10))

ocd is compiled code, and the check reports 0 notes with no “packages suggested but not available” – so ocd was installed and that test really ran. A hard crash inside an engine’s C++ kills R exactly this way: no R condition, no testthat summary, output simply stops.

Flagged rather than fixed, once: this is a genuine risk for the submission, because CRAN’s Windows builders would meet the same intermittency. It is not reproducible on this Linux machine, and guessing at a code change for a crash I cannot trigger would be worse than naming it. What the round delivers is the diagnosis – which was unobtainable two commits ago – and the log setting that produced it.

580. The changelog had stopped tracking the code four commits ago

The first thing a sweep of this working tree turns up is not in the code. b94c612 is the last commit that touched NEWS.md, and four code-bearing commits follow it:

commit R files changed
7ece62f 9
bfa2677 33
af544bf 1
57a5804 1

That is 42 file-touches and ~1500 changed lines of R/ with no changelog entry, and cran-comments.md telling CRAN “Forty-one defects … NEWS.md itemises them and each has a regression test” while the tree holds considerably more than forty-one.

The gap is not cosmetic, because four of the undocumented items are wrong answers rather than rough edges:

  • wbsts could not report more than one changepoint. Its suppressWarnings(if (is.na(OUT)) OUT = NULL) has been an error since R 4.2 for exactly the case where OUT holds two or more of them.
  • hdcov and network failed on 44-96% of runs, at random, on thresholdBS()’s 2:level_length against a single-level tree.
  • cpt_batch() detected on a panel it had rewritten – a factor member became level codes, a matrix member was unrolled column-wise into a longer series with a changepoint at the seam.
  • ecp_wrapper() absorbed non-finite values, losing a real changepoint on twenty NAs and inventing two on an all-NA half.

A user upgrading from 0.4.0 would have had no way to learn any of that from the package.

580.1 What the audit passes had recorded instead

The information was not lost – §285 to §579 of this document describe every one of them. But next_release.md is .Rbuildignored and is a development ledger, not a changelog; NEWS.md is what ships and what pkgdown renders. The two had diverged because the audit rounds were written up here and the write-up here felt like the write-up.

581. What this pass changes

  • A 47-item NEWS.md section, “Fixes found in the final pre-submission sweeps”, covering all four commits: the four wrong answers above, the argument-collision sweep, cpm’s two thresholds, the search-path and console-noise fixes, and the documentation that had drifted. Grouped by kind rather than by commit, because a reader does not care which pass found what.
  • cran-comments.md: “Forty-one defects” -> “Eighty-eight”, and a new paragraph naming the three engine-level defects this package routes around, because a CRAN reviewer reading wbs_lsw_replay() should not have to work out from the source why a wrapper replays an engine’s body.
  • The same file’s Dependencies paragraph is rewritten. Two edits had collided in it: the sentence “Every one is guarded with requireNamespace() …” – which is about the thirty-five engines – had ended up after a five-line digression about mcp and JAGS, where “Every one” reads as being about mcp.

582. Fifteen ... collisions the wrapper sweep could not see

§354, §377 and §397 swept ... against every engine argument, and the sweep was over the registry: fifty wrappers, 64 argument slots. Four exported entry points are not registry wrappers, were therefore not swept, and each pins or renames an engine argument:

cpt_crops(penalty=)      cpt_crops(method=)      cpt_crops(pen.value=)
cpt_wrapper(method=)     ggcptplot(method=)
cpt_monitor(cpmType=)    cpt_monitor(ARL0=)      cpt_monitor(MC_reps=)
cpt_monitor(dim=)        cpt_monitor(beta=)      + the same five through
                                                   cpt_replay()

Every one answered with R’s own formal argument "penalty" matched by multiple actual arguments, which names neither the function, nor the engine, nor what to use instead – the exact failure those two helpers exist to prevent, in the four places nobody had pointed them at.

cpt_wrapper()’s is the one most likely to be met: it renames changepoint’s method to cp_method because method already means “which detector” everywhere else in this package, which makes method both the natural thing for a reader of ?cpt.mean to pass and the one that breaks.

582.1 Three things measured rather than assumed

  • thresh, patience and startup cannot reach ... at all. They are formals of cpt_monitor(), so R matches them there first, and a guard listing them would be a branch that can never fire. Probed individually rather than added by pattern-match with the others.
  • cpt_replay() needs no guard of its own. It forwards ... to cpt_monitor(), so one fix covers both – confirmed by probing cpt_replay() after fixing only cpt_monitor().
  • ggcptplot() must name itself. It shares cpt_wrapper()’s rename, so keying the message off the map key told a ggcptplot() caller about cpt_wrapper(). reject_renamed_args() grew a label argument for exactly that, since being told about a function you did not call is the failure this whole guard exists to stop.

583. bcp was still talking, and four print headers were ragged

§310 restored the search path and did not stop the announcement. bcp::bcp() calls require(bcp) in its own body; the fix detached package:bcp and package:grid afterwards, but require() speaks through packageStartupMessage() first, so every bcp_wrapper() call still printed two Loading required package: lines on stderr. They are visible in this loop’s own test logs. with_search_path_restored() now suppresses package startup messages – only those, so an engine’s message() and warning() still reach the caller.

And four print() headers padded their labels by hand. Measured on the rendered output rather than read:

method defect
print.ggcpt values in three columns (19, 20, 22)
print.summary.ggcpt a different column from print.ggcpt, same object
print.ggcpt_delay five of six right, Average run length: one out
print.ggcpt_path Distinct segmentations: unpadded entirely

plus a trailing space on every line built with cat()’s default separator – 5 of 13 lines of a ggcpt, 7 of a summary – because the separator lands between the value and the "\n". One cat_field() helper now emits all of them, so they cannot drift apart again. The tibble printed below each header pads its own columns; that is tibble’s output and is left alone, which the regression test has to know.

print.ggcpt also had no \value section – the single most common reason a CRAN reviewer sends a package back – and four topics (print.ggcpt, is_ggcpt, new_ggcpt, alarms) had a \description byte-identical to their \title, because roxygen copies the title when there is no description paragraph.

584. scale_space is not the column three help pages said it was

?cpt_methods grouped it with statistic and path:

statistic, path and scale_space the internals rendered by ggcpt_statistic(), ggcpt_solution_path() and ggcpt_scale_space()

autoplot(type =) said the three “error with the list of supporting engines when this one does not expose the internals”, and ?cpt_scale_space typed its x as “a ggcpt object produced by a multiscale engine”. All three describe a gate that does not exist.

Measured on a pelt fit, which the table marks scale_space = FALSE:

cpt_statistic(res)      -> Engine `pelt` does not expose a per-location statistic.
cpt_solution_path(res)  -> Engine `pelt` does not expose a solution path.
cpt_scale_space(res)    -> 600 rows: index, bandwidth, statistic,
                           threshold, significant, detected
autoplot(res, type = "scale_space") -> a ggplot

statistic and path gate their accessors. scale_space does not, because no engine stores one: a grep for anything writing diagnostics$scale_space finds nothing, and cpt_scale_space() computes the sweep itself by running mosum (or npmojo) over the series. So the column marks the two engines the sweep can be run with – the domain of that function’s own method argument, which is exactly how ?cpt_scale_space already used it one paragraph earlier (subset(cpt_methods(), scale_space)$method).

The cost of the wrong wording is a reader with a pelt fit concluding the scale-space view is closed to them. All three pages now say what the column is, and a test pins the behaviour: cpt_scale_space() on a pelt result returns a sweep, res$diagnostics$scale_space is NULL, and the two columns that do gate still refuse by name.

585. Four sweeps that found nothing, recorded so they are not repeated

Negative results, each measured rather than reasoned about:

  • Structural invariants, all 50 wired methods. For each: cp whole, strictly increasing and inside the convention’s range; cp_value equal to data$value[cp]; segments a gapless partition of 1..n with n == end - start + 1 and nrow == length(cp) + 1; tidy() one row per changepoint, glance() exactly one, augment() exactly n; autoplot(), print() and summary() all building. 48 clean, 2 correct refusals (hdreg requires response, fabisearch requires non-negative values). No violations.
  • Capability columns against their accessors. ci, fitted, statistic, path and posterior agree with what every installed method actually delivers, with no exceptions. (The scale_space disagreement was §584 – a wrong premise in the sweep, which is what led to the wrong wording being found.)
  • Documented defaults against formals(). 159 @param texts saying “Defaults to X” compared against the actual default; every mismatch surviving normalisation was the comparator’s (a captured sentence period, NA vs NA_real_, 1e-3 vs 0.001, prose describing a computed default). Zero real drift.
  • Every README chunk, run. README.md is not checked by R CMD check and had not been rebuilt since abf04c6, so the 112 expressions in README.Rmd were purled and evaluated one at a time against the current package: 0 failures.

Also clean: no dead internal functions (every non-exported definition has at least one reference in R/, the tests or the vignettes); no stop()/warning() missing call. = FALSE except four deliberate condition re-throws; the pkgdown reference index covers every exported topic; and no TODO/FIXME anywhere in the sources.

586. Verification

R CMD check --as-cran on the built tarball, R 4.4.1:

checking installed package size ... OK
checking R code for possible problems ... OK
checking Rd \usage sections ... OK
checking examples ... [53s] OK
checking examples with --run-donttest ... [123s] OK
  Running 'testthat.R' [328s] OK
checking re-building of vignette outputs ... [118s] OK

Status: 1 ERROR, 2 WARNINGs, 3 NOTEs

All six are the machine’s, and are the same six this document has recorded since 0.4.0: no qpdf (WARNING), no pdflatex (WARNING + ERROR on the PDF manual, and the NOTE about the .tex file it leaves behind), no tidy (NOTE on the HTML manual), and rjags/mcp unavailable because there is no JAGS here (NOTE). Nothing substantive: the examples, --run-donttest, the full test suite and the vignette rebuild are all OK, and the installed size did not trip the 5 MB note on this run.

587. cpt_confint(method = "auto") answered a different question, quietly

The bound-invariant sweep – lower <= cp <= upper, both inside 1..(n-1), one row per changepoint, source non-empty – ran over every provenance against every installed univariate engine, 59 method/route pairs. All the geometric invariants hold. The one thing that did not was a level:

cpt_confint(nsp_result, method = "auto", level = 0.95)   ->  level column 0.9
cpt_confint(nsp_result, method = "nsp",  level = 0.95)   ->  level column 0.95

The mechanism is short. An nsp result carries significance regions, so native_bounds() finds them, "auto" resolves to "native", and "native" reports native$level – which is what nsp_wrapper()’s default alpha = 0.1 produced, a global level of 0.9. The requested 0.95 is discarded on the way.

Nothing here was dishonest. The level column said 0.9, the source column said nsp_region, and ?cpt_confint documented that method = "native" ignores level. The gap is that the caller who is surprised did not ask for "native"; they asked for "auto" and were never told where it went. Asking for a 95% interval and getting a 90% one with no signal but a column you have to inspect is the kind of thing that reaches a paper.

587.1 Why a warning rather than recomputing

Recomputing NSP at the requested level would be the wrong fix twice over: it would spend an M = 1000 Monte Carlo run that "auto" exists to avoid, and it would throw away the regions the result already carries – which are the inference the user asked for when they chose nsp. Reusing them is right; doing it silently was not.

So the check is on the answer, not on the route: if an explicitly supplied level does not appear in the level column, say so and name the branch that got there. That covers "auto" -> "native" without needing per-route bookkeeping, and it would catch any future route with the same property.

Two details that keep it from being noise:

  • missing(level) gates it. The default must never warn, because 0.95 against a 0.9 native interval is the overwhelmingly common case and warning about it would train the user to ignore the warning.
  • Tolerance, not equality. abs(got - requested) < 1e-9, since the levels travel as doubles through an engine.

cpt_monitor() already warns on exactly this pattern – “arl0 does not affect method = \"edetector\", which is tuned by alpha” – so this is the courtesy the package already extends elsewhere, applied to the one place it was missing.

588. Twelve metrics, twelve names, three explanations

?cpt_metrics’s @return was a flat comma-separated list of twelve column names, and @details explained precision/recall, covering, and the both-empty case. What a reader could not learn from the page:

  • annotation_error is a count difference and nothing else. It is abs(n_pred - n_truth). Measured on a 100-point series, predicting 5 against a truth of 90:

    annotation_error = 0     hausdorff = 85     f1 = 0     rand_index = -0.06

    A perfect score for a segmentation that got the location wrong by 85 observations. That is the metric behaving as defined – but a cpt_benchmark() column reading 0 is going to be read as “perfect”, and nothing said otherwise.

  • Which direction is better. benchmark.R knows (lower_better <- metric %in% c("hausdorff", "annotation_error", "mae_matched", "rmse_matched")); the help page did not say.

  • The one-sided degenerate cases, where the row mixes two conventions:

    case precision / recall / f1 rand_index hausdorff / mae / rmse
    both empty 1 1 NA
    pred empty 0 0 NA
    truth empty 0 0 NA
    nothing matched 0 < 0 NA for mae/rmse, a number for hausdorff

    So an all-wrong answer returns f1 = 0 and mae_matched = NA in the same row – 0 where the quantity is a rate, NA where it is a distance with no pair to measure. Only the both-empty row was documented, and it is the one a reader is least likely to hit.

588.1 The numbers themselves are right

Checked rather than asserted, against reference implementations written from the definitions and sharing no code with the package: covering by explicit intersect()/union() over every segment pair, rand_index from a contingency table with choose(), hausdorff by double minimax, precision/recall by re-running the greedy one-to-one match. Nine hand-built cases plus twenty random 400-point ones. Every non-degenerate value agreed exactly, including the findInterval() fast path in calc_covering() – which is a performance change to a formula, so a test now pins it to the definition rather than to a recorded number.

The only disagreements were the degenerate rows above, where the reference divided by zero and the package makes a deliberate choice. That is what turned this from a correctness check into a documentation one.

589. What this pass changes

  • cpt_confint() warns when an explicitly supplied level is not the one the answer carries, naming the route. @param level now says that "auto" resolves to "native" whenever the engine supplied an interval, so an explicit level can go unused there too.
  • ?cpt_metrics gains a \describe return block – every column, what it measures, and which direction is better – plus a “Degenerate cases” section giving the table above. annotation_error carries an explicit “read it beside a location metric, never alone”.
  • ?cpt_scale_space, ?cpt_methods and autoplot(type =) stop describing scale_space as a gate (see §584).
  • Four regression tests: the level warning and its silence on the default, the level honoured on every computing route with the geometric invariants alongside, the metric conventions row by row, and covering against its definition.

590. Two more clean sweeps

  • Time-index threading, end to end. With a weekly Date index over 200 observations and five engines: res$index identical to what was supplied; tidy()$cp_index equal to index[cp] and still a Date; augment() carrying a Date column equal to the index in order; cpt_confint()’s cp_index, ci_lower_index and ci_upper_index all equal to the index at their integer positions; autoplot()’s x range spanning the index rather than 1..n; print() reporting the index. Plus the two guards: an unequally spaced index warns, and a wrong-length one is refused by name. No violations.
  • cpt_confint() geometry, as above: 59 method/route pairs, every interval bracketing its changepoint and inside the series.

591. The check that names the wrong line

Adding §589’s tests made the suite fail, and the failure was informative about the checker rather than about the tests:

test-hardening.R:1585 uses nsp_wrapper without skip_if_not_installed()

Line 1585 is test_that("the covering metric matches an explicit set computation", ...), which computes Jaccard overlaps on integer vectors and does not touch nsp in any form. The only mention of nsp_wrapper() in the file was in a section comment introducing the next test – the guarded one that legitimately uses it.

The cause is one line of the checker:

starts <- grep("^test_that\\(", src)
ends <- c(starts[-1] - 1L, length(src))

A block therefore runs to the line before the next test_that(, so everything between two blocks – blank lines, and the header comment belonging to the block below – is attributed to the block above.

A checker that names the wrong line is worse than no checker, because the failure is confusing instead of informative: the obvious response is to add a guard to a test that does not need one, which weakens the coverage this check exists to protect (the design note above it is explicit that a call inside expect_error() must stay unguarded, for exactly that reason).

591.1 srcrefs, not brace counting

The fix is to take each block’s extent from R’s own parser: parse(f, keep.source = TRUE) and the srcref attribute give the first and last line of each expression, and comments between expressions belong to no expression at all.

Brace counting was the other candidate and would have been wrong here: several blocks in this suite contain a brace inside a string – skip("{mcp} is not installed") is one – so a balance counter would mis-close them. The parser handles it because it is a parser.

591.2 Measured both ways

The synthetic file the new test builds has all five shapes, and the two rules disagree exactly where they should:

block old rule srcrefs
A: unguarded, touches nothing flagged –
B: guarded, header above belongs to it – –
C: genuinely unguarded call flagged flagged
D: brace inside a string – –
E: call inside expect_error() – –

So the change removes a false positive and keeps the true one, which is what the test asserts – both directions, so a future simplification back to the line-based rule fails rather than passing quietly.

592. Verification

Full suite via testthat::test_local(): the only failure was the one in §591, and it is now fixed; the two standing skips (mcp needs JAGS, the TCPD download is not exercised) and the two envcpt upstream warnings are unchanged.

593. §180 was the highest-severity item in this document and was never done

The audit that wrote §180 called it “the highest severity-to-effort ratio in the document”. §214.3 listed it as an action. §232 corrected its scope from 19 sites to 35. And then:

$ grep -rn "with_local_seed\|with_seed" R/
$ grep -rc "if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)" R/*.R | ...
35

No helper, thirty-five bare sites. The diagnosis was written three times and the fix zero. Re-measured against the current tree before touching anything, because a stale finding is worth less than no finding:

entry point distinct datasets in a 6-iteration loop
cpt_detect(method = "wbs") – no seed 6 of 6
cpt_detect(method = "wbs", seed = 1) 2 of 6
cpt_detect(method = "nsp", seed = 1) 2 of 6
cpt_stability(B = 5, seed = 7) 2 of 6
cpt_simulate(seed = 3) 2 of 6
cpt_select(criterion = "cv", seed = 5) 2 of 6

and directly, with the data pre-generated so generation cannot be mistaken for the effect: after cpt_detect(x, method = "wbs", seed = 42) the caller’s next rnorm() draw is not the one they would have got. Still live, exactly as described.

593.1 Why the fix is a statement and not an expression wrapper

§180.2 proposed with_local_seed(seed, expr). That form is cleaner in isolation and would have meant restructuring thirty-six function bodies to wrap everything after the seeding inside a call – a large diff across twenty-one files, in wrappers whose bodies are the part of the package most worth not disturbing before a submission.

The equivalent that is a one-line substitution is to register the restore in the caller’s frame:

local_seed <- function(seed, envir = parent.frame()) {
  if (is.null(seed)) return(invisible(FALSE))
  ...
  do.call(base::on.exit,
          list(substitute(f(), list(f = as.name(nm))), add = TRUE),
          envir = envir)
  set.seed(seed)
}

A helper’s own on.exit() would fire the moment the helper returned, which is why the handler goes in envir. add = TRUE because two wrappers already register a search-path restore – checked, and both of those use add = TRUE too, so nothing is clobbered in either direction. Every one of the thirty-six sites became local_seed(seed), and grep confirms no bare set.seed() is left in the package’s code.

593.2 Two details that are easy to get wrong

  • A fresh session has no .Random.seed. It is created by the first draw, so a naive save-and-restore would leave one behind on a session that had none – itself a change to the caller’s state. The helper records whether it existed and rm()s it if it did not. A test asserts that.
  • cpt_power() and cpt_stability() seed once and then draw many times. Scoping must not truncate that: the restore fires when the outer function exits, so the replicate loop inside still walks the seeded stream and stays reproducible. Verified rather than assumed – same seed twice gives identical output.

593.3 Measured after

property before after
distinct datasets, 6-iteration loop, seeded 2 of 6 6 of 6
caller’s .Random.seed after a seeded call reset identical
same seed twice, 1000 draws between identical identical
same seed after an unseeded call moved the stream identical identical
fresh session left without .Random.seed n/a yes

The two reproducibility rows are the point of the exercise: the fix removes a side effect without costing anything the argument was for.

594. What this pass changes

  • local_seed(), and all thirty-six if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed) sites replaced with it – twenty-one files, mechanical, grep-verifiable.
  • All thirty-six @param seed blocks say the seed is scoped to the call. §180.2’s item 4 called the old wording a documentation bug and it was: “for reproducibility” is what a reader would take as a promise that the loop around the call is unaffected.
  • Three metamorphic test blocks: the six-iteration loop for five entry points (with the no-seed case as the reference, so the test cannot pass vacuously), .Random.seed identity across five seeded calls plus the fresh-session case, and reproducibility across intervening draws and across an unseeded call.

595. And a clean sweep of the extension mechanism

?cpt_register_method promises that a registered detector “then works with everything built on the ggcpt contract” and names ten things. All ten were run against a registered detector (a CUSUM argmax in six lines): autoplot(), geom_changepoint(), geom_cpt_segment(), geom_cpt_label(), tidy(), glance(), augment(), cpt_metrics(), ggcpt_compare(), cpt_stability(), cpt_consensus(), cpt_benchmark(), cpt_report(). All pass, with the row counts the ggcpt contract requires (one tidy row per changepoint, one glance row, one augment row per observation).

The visibility promises hold too: cpt_methods() gives the method status = "registered" and installed = NA, print() marks the result [user-registered], cpt_cite() returns the citation the registration supplied, and a registration with no citation says so plainly –

No citation was supplied when nocite was registered with cpt_register_method(). This method is user-supplied: ggchangepoint validated the shape of its output, not its statistics.

Nothing to fix. Recorded because this is the headline feature of the release and the claim is unusually specific, so it is worth having been checked item by item rather than in spirit.

596. The seed fix broke four snapshots, and that was the second finding

Scoping the seed turned the full suite red in test-050-visual.R:

Snapshot of 050-visual/cpt-monitor-timeline.svg  has changed
Snapshot of 050-visual/ggcpt-statistic.svg       has changed
Snapshot of 050-visual/ggcpt-scale-space.svg     has changed
Snapshot of 050-visual/ggcpt-solution-path.svg   has changed

The temptation here is to read this as the fix being wrong. It is the opposite: those four snapshots were relying on the leak.

The file seeds once at the top and draws the two series every block shares:

set.seed(2026)
x_step  <- c(rnorm(60), rnorm(60, 4))
x_multi <- c(rnorm(50), rnorm(50, 4), rnorm(50, 1))

but three blocks generate their own data with a bare rnorm() inside the block, taking whatever stream state the blocks above them happen to leave. And the block immediately above them ends with:

pw <- cpt_power(n = 150, jump = c(0.5, 2), n_sim = 10, seed = 1, ...)

which used to pin the stream to seed 1. Remove the pin and the following rnorm(150) draws a different series – so the snapshot changes, because it was a snapshot of test execution order as much as of the plot.

596.1 Confirming it was data and not a broken figure

Before accepting a snapshot, the question is whether the picture is still the right kind of picture. Two checks, neither of which is “it looks fine”:

Structure, from the SVGs:

snapshot polyline rect text bytes
cpt-monitor-timeline 10 -> 10 6 -> 6 13 -> 13 8081 -> 8229
ggcpt-statistic 15 -> 16 13 -> 13 17 -> 18 18902 -> 19180
ggcpt-scale-space 13 -> 15 7 -> 7 15 -> 16 12705 -> 12941
ggcpt-solution-path 13 -> 13 13 -> 13 24 -> 24 12168 -> 12166

Same panels, same furniture, one or two more marks where the new series has one more changepoint or one more axis label. Layers, from the objects:

monitor      alarms = 2    GeomLine, GeomVline
mosum        cp = 200      GeomLine, GeomLine, GeomVline, GeomHline
scale_space                GeomRaster, GeomPoint
wbs          cp = 199      GeomSegment, GeomPoint

mosum finds the true changepoint at 200 and wbs at 199, and the layer compositions are unchanged. So the figures are correct and of a different series, which is the only reading under which accepting is right.

596.2 The fix is to seed the block, not to re-record the order

Re-recording alone would have left the snapshots order-dependent – passing today and failing the next time anything above them changed how much randomness it consumes. Each of the three blocks now calls set.seed() before generating its data, which makes the snapshot a function of the block.

Verified by running the file from three deliberately different starting states – set.seed(1), set.seed(12345), and 777 discarded draws – 0 failures each. Before, the same experiment is what produced the four failures in the first place.

This is the §180 story in miniature: a leaked seed made something look reproducible that was not, and the leak had to go before anyone could tell.

597. §180.2’s item 5, measured – and it was wrong in two ways

The roadmap’s last unaddressed seed item read:

While there: parallel = TRUE is the default on cpt_power() and cpt_stability(). Under future, future.seed governs worker streams and the local set.seed() does not reach them, so the sequential and parallel paths may not agree even with a seed fixed. […] this is the specific pair to test.

Measured, and both halves of the guess need correcting.

cpt_stability() has no parallel path at all. grep for future_lapply finds cpt_batch(), cpt_benchmark(), cpt_consensus(), cpt_influence(), cpt_sensitivity(), ggcpt_compare() and cpt_power(); stability.R contains none. So the “pair” was one function and a mistake, and the real surface is seven.

Only one of the seven diverges. Each was run twice under a sequential plan and twice under a real two-worker multisession plan, with a stochastic engine (wbs) where the function takes a method, so the worker stream had every chance to show:

function twice, sequential twice, 2 workers sequential vs parallel
cpt_influence identical identical identical
cpt_sensitivity identical identical identical
cpt_consensus identical identical identical
cpt_batch identical identical identical
cpt_benchmark identical identical identical
cpt_power identical identical different
