The reason is not the plumbing but what the tasks do: six of the seven farm out work that is deterministic given its input – refit with this perturbation, score against that dataset – so no random number enters the answer and the worker stream is irrelevant. cpt_power() farms out simulation replicates, which is exactly the case future.seed exists for. One and the same seed = 11 on two scenarios at n_sim = 8:

sequential   power = 0,     1
2 workers    power = 0.125, 0.875

597.1 Why this is documented rather than “fixed”

Both answers are correct estimates of the same quantity and both are deterministic; they differ because the numbers come from different (equally valid) streams. Making them agree would mean either abandoning parallel-safe streams – which is what future.seed is for and would be a genuine correctness regression across workers – or generating every replicate’s data in the parent and farming out only the detection, which changes the numbers for the default path, is a real behaviour change, and still would not close the gap for a stochastic detector.

So ?cpt_power gains a Reproducibility under a parallel plan section stating the guarantee that does hold – same seed and same plan, same answer – how to pin a figure that has to be reproducible by someone else (parallel = FALSE, or state the plan with the seed), and that the gap is Monte Carlo error, which mc_se already quantifies. It also records that the other six are plan-independent, because “is this affected?” is the first question a reader of that section will have.

Two tests pin it: all four testable entry points reproduce within a plan under both plans, and the three deterministic ones give identical answers across plans while cpt_power() is only required to stay a valid rate. The parallel plan is restored with withr::defer() so a failure cannot leave one set for the rest of the suite.

598. Eleven vignette chunks drew data nobody had seeded

The same defect as §596, in the vignettes. vignettes/ggchangepoint.Rmd seeds at line 90 and line 345 and then has four chunks that generate fresh data with a bare rnorm(); monitoring.Rmd has six and supervised.Rmd one. Their rendered output is therefore a function of how much randomness every chunk above them consumed.

And several of those upstream chunks are conditional. ggchangepoint.Rmd gates them on engine availability (eval = has_cpop, eval = has_idetect, …), so on a machine without cpop the chunk at line 258 does not run, and every unseeded chunk after it draws different data. The vignette’s numbers and figures already differed between machines with different optional packages – before this loop touched anything.

Each of the eleven now seeds itself. No prose claim depended on the old values, checked chunk by chunk, so this changes the rendered output and nothing that is said about it.

599. Verification

R CMD check --as-cran on the tarball built after the 36-site seed change: checking examples ... [54s] OK, --run-donttest ... [123s] OK. The seed scoping reaches every example and every \donttest block, so those two lines are the ones worth quoting.

600. as_ggcpt() was losing changepoints quietly, and the docs said it should

?as_ggcpt’s @param cp read:

Out-of-range, duplicated and missing values are dropped, and the result is sorted – the same contract every built-in wrapper is held to.

So the dropping was a decision, not an oversight. Measured on a 200-point series:

as_ggcpt(c(50, 500), x)  ->  1 changepoint at 50
as_ggcpt(c(0, 50), x)    ->  1 changepoint at 50
as_ggcpt(c(50, 200), x)  ->  1 changepoint at 50
as_ggcpt(50.5, x)        ->  1 changepoint at 50    (truncated, not rounded)
as_ggcpt(c(50, 50), x)   ->  1 changepoint at 50    (deduplicated)
as_ggcpt(c(50, NA), x)   ->  1 changepoint at 50

The x side, by contrast, is validated exactly as cpt_detect() is – a factor, a character vector, an NA, an Inf, a two-point series and a NULL are all refused with the same messages, verified side by side. It is only cp that was unguarded.

The justification in the docs is sound for a wrapper: the indices come from an engine, some of which legitimately emit a boundary value (ecp reports n), and normalising a machine’s output is what a wrapper is for. But as_ggcpt()’s documented use cases are “a published paper’s reported breaks, an analyst’s annotations, another package’s output” – human transcription, where one mistyped index vanishing without a word leaves a result that looks complete and is short a changepoint.

600.1 Warn, not refuse – and why that is the right scope

Refusing was implemented first and then backed out. It is the better behaviour in the abstract and it is the wrong change here: the dropping is documented, so refusing would break code that works today, and the brief for this pass is polish rather than behaviour change. What is not defensible under any reading is the silence.

So the return value is byte-identical to before, and each of the five now warns – with the values, the range they had to fall in, and the sentence that makes the range make sense:

`cp`: 1 outside 1..199 (200). 2 location(s) supplied. A "left" changepoint
is the last index of the segment before it, so 200 would leave no segment
after it.

Sorting stays silent, because reordering loses nothing. An integer-valued double (150.0) is not a truncation and does not warn. Both convention boundaries – cp = 1 under "left", cp = n under "right" – are valid and stay silent, and their opposites warn with the right range (2..200 for "right"). Twelve legitimate calls, including ci, fitted, index, multivariate and empty input, were checked to still be silent.

601. Two claims the release letter makes, checked and holding

  • cpt_test() never lets an unadjusted p-value pass for an adjusted one. 68 method/type pairs across every installed univariate engine: p_value inside everywhere, selection_adjusted a clean logical with no NA, and the warning firing on exactly the rows that are unadjusted – never on a fully adjusted result, always on a partly unadjusted one. Two of the 68 pairs are adjusted (the engines with their own test), 66 are not and say so. All three p.adjust corrections (holm, BH, bonferroni) were checked to be non-decreasing, bounded by 1, and order-preserving. Zero violations.

  • No engine fabricates changepoints on no-change data at a usable series length. NEWS records a 0.4.0 fix for “an ecp wrapper that fabricated changepoints on no-change data”, so the property is worth re-checking rather than assuming. Twelve pure-noise draws at , , per multivariate engine:

    engine draws reporting >=1 changepoint
    npmojo, inspect, geomcp, fastcpd, esac, pilliat, fmean 0 of 12
    kcp, var 1 of 12
    ecp, hdcov 2 of 12
    kwc 3 of 12
    fcov 4 of 12

    Ordinary Type-I error at nominal levels for the first eleven, and no fabrication anywhere near the ecp failure 0.4.0 fixed. The two functional methods are the loose ones and the measurement is not conclusive about them: fcov and kwc read the columns as a grid over a curve, so is a coarse grid rather than their design case, and ?fcov_wrapper already records that two columns fail outright while three or more return a fit. Re-running at and to separate “wrong regime” from “loose threshold” was started and abandoned – it had not finished either method at after forty minutes under load, and it is a refinement of a negative result rather than a blocker. Left open, and stated as open, rather than reported as either clean or broken.

602. §181.2’s transposed-matrix finding no longer holds

The roadmap recorded:

7 of 9 multivariate engines accept a transposed matrix; 5 fabricate changepoints

Re-measured on a 200 x 3 series against its 3 x 200 transpose, over the eleven multivariate engines that take a plain matrix:

behaviour count engines
refused, with a message naming the shape 5 kcp, npmojo, ocd, geomcp, var
warned (the degenerate-segmentation guard) 3 fastcpd, esac, pilliat
returned no changepoints 3 ecp, hdcov, fmean
returned a changepoint, silently 1 inspect

So the intervening rounds moved this from “5 fabricate” to one engine that returns a changepoint without comment, and the reason it is not guarded is worth stating rather than fixing:

a 3 x 200 input is not obviously wrong for a high-dimensional method. inspect, esac and pilliat exist for ; refusing more coordinates than time points would refuse their design case. And the existing degenerate-segmentation guard fires on k == n - 1, which at with one changepoint is correctly not triggered. Any threshold on alone would be arbitrary, and the false-positive measurement in §601 shows the engines are well behaved wherever a series is long enough to be one. Recorded as measured and deliberately not guarded, which is a different answer from §181.2’s and the one the numbers support.

603. The warning reached a caller it was not written for

test-050-registry.R went green with four new warnings, and two of them were the fix over-reaching. cpt_detect() routes a registered method’s bare-vector return through as_ggcpt():

res <- as_ggcpt(out, x, method = entry$method, ...)

so a user’s registered detector that emits a boundary index – or 80.4, or a repeat – now warned on every call, with a message telling them to “check the values against the series rather than relying on this normalisation”. That is advice about code they did not write. Here the indices come from a detector, not from a person transcribing published breaks, which is precisely the wrapper case §600 argued the dropping is right for.

The report is therefore a classed condition:

warning(structure(
  class = c("ggchangepoint_cp_dropped", "warning", "condition"),
  list(message = msg, call = NULL)))

and run_registered_method() muffles that class and nothing else, so any other warning as_ggcpt() raises still reaches the caller. Text-matching would have worked today and broken the first time the message was reworded.

Measured after: a registered detector returning c(0L, 80L, 500L), 80.4 or c(80L, 80L) is silent and still normalised to cp = 80 with registered = TRUE; the same three values through as_ggcpt() directly all warn. Both directions are tested, and the test also asserts the condition’s class, so a future rewrite to a plain warning() fails rather than silently un-muffling.

603.1 The other two were the tests, and they are better for it

test-050-registry.R already had a block named “as_ggcpt() drops what it documents and refuses what it cannot read” – so the dropping was a deliberate, tested decision, which is the strongest argument that warn-rather-than-refuse was the right scope call. Six assertions there and three more in two other blocks now use expect_warning() with the message, and the three that lose nothing (reordering, empty input, a numeric string) use expect_silent(). The file went from four warnings to none, and the assertions went from “the value is right” to “the value is right and the package said what it did”.

604. Verification

Full suite via testthat::test_local(): no failures; the standing two skips (mcp needs JAGS, TCPD is not downloaded) and the two upstream envcpt warnings are unchanged, and the four as_ggcpt warnings this pass introduced into the report are gone – asserted rather than emitted.

605. cpt_simulate() is right about everything it builds, and silent in one direction

cpt_power(), cpt_benchmark() and cpt_datasets() are all scored against what cpt_simulate() says it generated, so its arithmetic is load-bearing for every number the package reports about accuracy. Measured against the definitions rather than against a recorded value:

property asked realised
mean jump 0.5 / 2 / 5 error +0.0025 (se 0.017) at all three
sd ratio 2 / 4 2.039 (se 0.021) / 4.079 (se 0.041)
seg_id breaks 1, 2 and 4 changepoints exactly at the requested indices
AR(1) rho 0.3 / 0.7 0.301 (se 0.010) / 0.697 (se 0.008)
t(3) tail heavier kurtosis 20.2 against Gaussian 2.9

The sd-ratio numbers sit slightly high because sd() on 200 points is biased that way, not because the generator is. Nothing wrong with any of it.

605.1 The finding was in the direction nothing checked

k changepoints make k + 1 segments, and the two mismatch directions were treated differently:

cpt_simulate(400, changepoints = 200, params = c(0))        # warns
cpt_simulate(400, changepoints = 200, params = c(0, 3, 9))  # silent

Too few already warned, and the comment above it says why – the last value is recycled, so the trailing changepoints would be recorded as ground truth with no change behind them. Too many used the first two and dropped the 9: an ordinary two-segment series handed back to a caller who had plainly meant two changepoints, whose power or benchmark numbers are then scored against a truth they did not intend.

Now warns both ways, naming the changepoint count, the segment count and how many entries went unused, for every change_in rather than only "mean" – checked on var and meanvar as well. Silent when the counts agree, when params is left at its default, and when there are no changepoints at all.

The same shape as §600, one file over: a documented normalisation that is audible in one direction and silent in the other, where the silent one is the one a miscount lands in.

606. Why round 6 could not finish the fcov measurement

§601 left the functional methods’ false-positive rate open because the finer-grid run had to be abandoned. The reason turns out to be worth more than the answer. Timed one call at a time, against fmean_wrapper() on identical input so the comparison is the same package and the same data:

input fmean fcov
, 4.5 s 316 s
, 2.9 s 598 s
, 4.5 s not measured

fcov is five to ten minutes on a hundred-point series and roughly linear in – a factor of seventy to two hundred over fmean. So round 6’s twelve-draw sweep at was an hour of work before it reached , and round 7’s smaller retry (8 draws, ) was still unfinished at 43 minutes. That is not a defect in the sweep; it is the engine.

It is a documentation gap. Two wrappers already carry a cost section – ?taylor_wrapper’s “Series length, and why you cannot interrupt it” and ?ocd_wrapper’s “How long this takes” – and fcov is the third and by far the most extreme. Someone who picks it out of cpt_methods() and calls it on their data will conclude the session has hung. ?fcov_wrapper now says so, with the numbers, the linearity in , the fact that the cost is in the engine’s covariance-operator estimation rather than in anything this wrapper could tune, and the explicit advice not to put it in a loop (a twelve-replicate study at is two hours).

Interruptibility was deliberately not claimed. Both runs were killed from outside the session, which is not the same as testing whether setTimeLimit() is honoured – the experiment ?taylor_wrapper did do. Recorded as untested rather than asserted either way.

606.1 And the false-positive question stays open, now with a reason

fcov reported a changepoint on 4 of 12 pure-noise draws at and kwc on 3 of 12 (§601). Whether that is a coarse grid outside the methods’ design case or a loose threshold is still unresolved, and at roughly ten minutes a call the study that would settle it costs hours. Left open, with the cost documented so the next attempt can be budgeted rather than abandoned.

607. The three closed-form criteria are right, and one of three was reproducible

cpt_select()’s value column is what a user compares rungs by, so the first question is whether it is the number it claims. Checked against reference implementations written from the definitions, sharing no code with the package:

cost   = n log(RSS/n)
bic    = cost + (2K + 1) log n
aic    = cost + 2(2K + 1)
mbic   = cost + 3K log n + sum_i log(l_i / n)      (Zhang & Siegmund 2007)

Every rung of a seven-rung ladder, for all three criteria, at that rung’s own changepoint locations: exact agreement, 21 comparisons, no violations. The cost column is the Gaussian profile cost at those locations, exactly one row is marked chosen, and it is the argmin of value.

The behaviour is a bonus check on the docs. On a 300-point series with changes at 100 and 200:

criterion chose
bic K = 2
mbic K = 2
aic K = 6, the largest rung offered

which is precisely what ?cpt_select warns about – “its penalty does not grow with , so it over-selects changepoints, often taking every rung offered”. The prose was right and is now a test.

607.1 The gap was which formulas got written down

Inside one \describe block, "mbic" was given in full and the other two were not:

{"bic"}{Gaussian BIC over the ladder.}

{"aic"}{Gaussian AIC over the ladder. …}

“Gaussian BIC” does not identify a number. Both the cost convention ( against with its constants, against the raw RSS) and the changepoint parameter count (, , ) vary between authors, and the reader who wants to know why rung 3 beats rung 2 cannot get there from the page. Both formulas are now stated, with the parameter count spelled out as locations plus segment means, and a pointer that the first term is the cost column they can already see.

Same shape as §588: a returned number whose definition was not on the page. The test pins the formulas rather than recorded values, so a change to what a criterion means fails instead of passing with a new number.

608. The new warnings do not fire inside the package

Rounds 6 and 7 added warnings to as_ggcpt() and cpt_simulate(), which raises the obvious question of whether they became noise in the package’s own output. Every internal caller of the simulation machinery, checked:

cpt_datasets() whole and per-signal (blocks, fms, mix, teeth, stairs, step, ar1), signal_blocks(), signal_fms(), signal_mix(), signal_stairs(), signal_teeth(), rcpt(), cpt_scenarios(), cpt_power() and cpt_benchmark() – 17 call sites, all silent.

Confirmed independently by the check below: checking examples ... OK and re-building of vignette outputs ... OK with no new warnings, so the three conditions added across rounds 3, 6 and 7 fire for a caller’s mistake and never for the package’s own code.

609. Verification

R CMD check --as-cran on the tarball built after rounds 1-7:

checking installed package size ...              OK
checking R code for possible problems ... [21s]  OK
checking Rd files ...                            OK
checking examples ...                     [54s]  OK
checking examples with --run-donttest ... [122s] OK
  Running 'testthat.R'                    [334s] OK
checking re-building of vignette outputs  [116s] OK

Status: 1 ERROR, 2 WARNINGs, 3 NOTEs

The six are the same six this document has recorded since 0.4.0, and all six are the machine: no qpdf, no pdflatex (the WARNING and ERROR on the PDF manual plus the NOTE about the .tex it leaves), no tidy (the HTML manual NOTE), and rjags/mcp unavailable for want of JAGS. Rd files ... OK is worth naming this round because it covers the \tabular timing table added to ?fcov_wrapper and the \eqn formulas added to ?cpt_select.

Round 8’s own change is documentation plus a test; test-hardening.R passes standalone with it, and every other file is covered by the check above.

610. Three quantities that are right, and the one argument that is not

Round 9 measured four computed surfaces against their definitions. Three came back clean, which is worth recording so they are not re-swept.

cpt_delay() – seven hand-built alarm tables where the answer is known before the call, plus the matching rules and every summary:

case expected got
alarm 5 after the change delay 5, detected correct
alarm before the change miss + 1 false alarm correct
alarm exactly at the change delay 0 correct
two alarms after one change first wins, second is a false alarm correct
max_delay = 10, alarm at +20 miss + false alarm correct
max_delay = 10, alarm at +8 delay 8 correct
no alarms at all miss, 0 false alarms correct

and: one alarm cannot be claimed by two changes; an alarm past the next true change is not credited to the earlier one; alarms partition exactly into detections plus false alarms; mean_delay, median_delay, n_detected and arl = n_obs / n_false_alarms all equal their definitions; arl is Inf rather than NaN when nothing fired falsely. No violations.

cpt_label_error() – Hocking’s definition, region by region. All nine combinations of the three label types against 0, 1 and several changepoints inside; both window boundaries inclusive as documented; per region counting; and both guards refusing by name (an unknown change level, and end < start). No violations. This matters more than most: it is the objective cpt_learn_penalty() minimises, so an error here would propagate the way a wrong cpt_simulate() would.

cpt_report() – both text formats write a file and return the lines; markdown fences balance and headings exist; session = FALSE drops the section (78 to 40 lines) and confint behaves exactly as documented – skipped for an engine with no native intervals whether TRUE or FALSE, and a nine-line “Location intervals” section for smuce, which is the “uses the engine’s own intervals when it has them and skips the section otherwise” the help page promises. A no-changepoint result still produces 75 lines, and a path in a nonexistent directory is refused before the report is built.

611. min_votes had an unreachable setting and a boundary in the worst place

cpt_consensus()’s clustering is also correct – eight hand cases, including that the tolerance boundary is inclusive (100 and 105 merge at tolerance = 5, 100 and 106 do not), that clustering is by leader rather than transitive (100, 105, 110 gives two clusters, not one), that a single method contributing two nearby locations is still one vote, and that cp is the cluster median with spread its range.

The argument on top of it is where the two findings are.

611.1 A threshold nothing can reach

cpt_consensus(x, methods = c("pelt", "binseg"), min_votes = 3)

resolves to a threshold of 3 against two methods, keeps nothing, and returns an ordinary empty consensus. An empty consensus is a finding – it means the methods agreed on nothing – so returning one for an arithmetic impossibility spends the reader’s trust on the wrong thing. Now warns, and names the number of methods that ran rather than the number requested, because a method that errors is already excluded from the vote and that is exactly how someone lands here without having typed a silly number.

Same reasoning as round 1’s cpt_benchmark(methods = character(0)) guard.

611.2 The boundary is at “unanimous”

The rule is: strictly between 0 and 1 is a proportion, anything else is a count. Measured with three methods:

min_votes threshold means
0.5 2 half
0.99 3 all three
1 1 any one method
2 2 two
3 3 all three

So the two neighbouring values 0.99 and 1 mean opposite things – the strictest setting available and the loosest – and 1 is precisely what a reader thinking in proportions writes for unanimity. Nothing was wrong with the arithmetic; what was missing is that the page said only “pass a fraction in for a proportion”, which is true and does not warn anybody. @param min_votes now gives the table’s content in prose, names the trap, and says to pass the method count or a fraction just below 1 for unanimity. The new warning repeats it, since an over-large count is the likeliest way to discover the boundary the hard way.

Deliberately not changed: min_votes = 1 still means a count of one. A count of one is a legitimate request (“any method that saw it”), and reinterpreting it would break code that works.

612. The Demsar diagram cited nobody

autoplot(plot_type = "critical_difference") is documented as

the Demsar diagram: mean ranks with the Nemenyi critical distance, the standard way this literature says “method A beats method B”

which names a method, a diagram and a literature. grep for the citation:

$ grep -n "demsar" inst/REFERENCES.bib
$ grep -rn "insertRef" R/benchmark.R
54:  \insertRef{vandenburg2020evaluation}{ggchangepoint}
472:  \insertRef{vandenburg2020evaluation}{ggchangepoint}

Nothing. The metrics on the same page cite van den Burg and Williams; the statistical procedure the plot is built on cited no one. The package’s own standard is stricter than that – a test asserts that every \insertRef key in R/ resolves in inst/REFERENCES.bib, and another that every available method has a cpt_cite() entry – so the omission is against the house rule rather than merely thin.

612.1 The arithmetic was right, which is why this is the finding

nemenyi_cd() is three lines and correct:

q <- stats::qtukey(1 - alpha, nmeans = k, df = Inf) / sqrt(2)
q * sqrt(k * (k + 1) / (6 * N))

Checked against Demsar (2006) Table 5 rather than against a re-derivation, for :

k 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 10
published 1.960 2.343 2.569 2.728 2.850 2.949 3.031 3.102 3.164
computed 1.9600 2.3437 2.5690 2.7278 2.8497 2.9483 3.0309 3.1017 3.1637

Worst deviation , which is the table’s own rounding. The sqrt(2) – the constant most often dropped in reimplementations of this diagram – is there.

benchmark_ranks() is right too: rank 1 to the largest value for a higher-is-better metric and to the smallest for a lower-is-better one, NA taking the worst rank in both directions rather than being dropped, ties sharing the average, mean_rank averaging over datasets (hand-checked at 1.25 and 1.75 on a two-dataset grid with one tie), and an all-NA metric returning NULL instead of a table of ties.

612.2 What the section adds

A correct number that no one can interpret is not much use, and this one invites a conclusion. ?cpt_benchmark gains “Reading the critical-difference diagram”, covering the three things the picture cannot say:

  • what rank 1 means, and which way each metric is ranked – the lower_better set lives in the source and was nowhere on the page;
  • that NA takes the worst rank, so a method that failed on a dataset is penalised for it rather than quietly scoring on a smaller sample;
  • the formula for the bar, since round 8 established that a plotted or returned number should be reproducible from the page.

And the caveat the diagram structurally cannot show: Nemenyi is a post-hoc test. The convention is to run it only after a Friedman test rejects the null of equal ranks, and autoplot() does not run that omnibus test – it draws what it is asked for. With the handful of datasets cpt_datasets() supplies, is small and correspondingly wide, so the page says to read such a diagram descriptively. Left as a caveat rather than made into a gate: refusing to draw the diagram without a Friedman test would remove a feature, and running one silently would change what the function does.

613. cpt_stability(), and a fixed bug that stayed fixed

freq = hits / B where hits counts, per index, the replicates whose margin window covered it. The code carries a note about an earlier defect – incrementing once per changepoint double-counted a replicate wherever two detections’ windows overlapped, and the old pmin(hits / B, 1) clipped the excess out of sight, reporting 1.00 (“re-detected every time”) for indices only half the replicates covered.

The invariant that catches a regression is not the range but the granularity: if hits is a count of replicates then every frequency is an exact multiple of , and double-counting breaks that before it breaks . Measured at : every one of 240 frequencies is a multiple of 0.025, 1.00 at the true change and 0.00 in the quiet stretches. Now a test, phrased as the multiple rather than the bound.

614. Three surfaces measured, three correct – and the finding was in reading one

Round 11 took the remaining computed quantities. Recorded because after ten passes the informative result is increasingly which surfaces are clean.

cpt_penalty() – 96 comparisons against the documented formulas, across four series lengths and four changepoint counts:

BIC = SIC = k log n            AIC = 2k
MBIC = 0.5(k+1) log n + log C(n, k)
Hannan-Quinn = 2k log log n    sSIC = k (log n)^alpha

Exact at every point, None is 0, each penalty increases in , and the orderings the page asserts hold at all nine pairs tried: sSIC > BIC, MBIC > BIC, BIC > AIC. All six guards refuse by name – alpha <= 1 for sSIC (the definition needs ), k outside for MBIC (where lchoose would return -Inf and silently invert the penalty), for the penalties, and an unknown type – including the documented exemption that AIC is fine at because does not involve .

cpt_min_detectable() – the bisection holds its invariant. The trace opens on both range endpoints, adds at most max_iter midpoints, and every midpoint lies strictly inside the interval the earlier evaluations left (measured: final bracket around a reported 1.019 at achieved power 0.833). Both degenerate brackets are reported rather than returned as a number the search never found: an unreachable target gives jump = NA with “Even the largest change tried (0.05 sd) reached only 0 power”, and a target already met at the bottom gives jump = range[1] with “the answer is at or below it”.

cpt_annotate_events() – the matching is right in every direction tried. The tolerance boundary is inclusive on the position scale (offset 5 matches at tolerance = 5, offset 6 does not, offset 1 does not at tolerance = 0), and a Date column is read on the index scale rather than as a position: an event on the first date lands at position 1, not at the changepoint 100 positions away.

614.1 The finding: I misread the table while holding the source open

tidy() on a ggcpt_events flattens the object’s three slots into one table with a status column:

                   status  cp event position distance
1 unexplained_changepoint 100  <NA>      100       NA
2        undetected_event  NA     e      106       NA

so the row count is the number of changepoints plus the number of events, and – the part that matters – an unexplained_changepoint row carries a non-missing cp. The sweep for this round inferred “matched” from !is.na(cp) and reported seven false violations before the table was printed. That is the natural reading, and in a user’s hands subset(tidy(x), !is.na(cp)) returns the matched pairs and the changepoints no event explains – silently overstating how much the events account for, which is the whole question cpt_annotate_events() exists to answer.

@return documents the object’s three slots (matched, unexplained, undetected) thoroughly and never said what tidy() does with them, nor that the three status values exist. They appeared nowhere but two tibble::tibble(status = ...) calls in communicate.R. Now on the page, with which column is NA in each row shape and an explicit “filter on status, not on is.na(cp)”.

Same class as §588 and §607: a returned table whose values were not documented. The distinguishing feature of this one is that the evidence it was worth writing down is that it caught me.

614.2 What this round ships

No behaviour change. One documentation fix, and three previously untested contracts pinned: cpt_penalty()’s formulas, orderings and guards; cpt_min_detectable()’s bracketing and both degenerate reports; and the events table’s three statuses, tolerance boundary and index-scale handling. §232.4’s conclusion was to pair every documentation fix with the assertion that keeps it true, and the measured record is that checked surfaces stay complete while unchecked ones decay – so on a round that found the code right, the tests are the deliverable.

615. The penalty learner is right, and its coefficients do not mean what they look like

Round 9 verified cpt_label_error() – the objective. Round 12 takes the two pieces built on it, neither of which had a test.

target_interval() implements Hocking’s construction: the longest run of penalties achieving the minimum label error, open at whichever end of the grid the run touches. All seven grid shapes:

grid errors target
2 0 0 1 3
0 0 1 2
2 1 0 0
0 0 0
2 0 1 3 (single optimum)
0 1 0 0 0 1 (two runs) , the longer
NA NA NA

interval_regression() is the squared-hinge fit. Its reported loss equals the objective recomputed at the weights it returns, the search improves on the constant it starts from (2.500 to 0.501), a prediction comfortably inside every interval costs exactly zero, and an infinite bound contributes nothing on its side rather than Inf.

End to end, five labelled series: every learned penalty lands inside that series’ own target interval. And the model is genuinely a function of the series – four series of very different length and noise give four distinct predictions from eight non-zero feature weights, so the earlier observation that five near-identical series all got 63.036 was the right answer rather than a degenerate learner.

615.1 What the numbers looked like, and why that is a doc fix

       intercept            log_n        log_log_n           log_sd
         4.46931         -0.03716         -0.01238         -0.00985

Every non-intercept coefficient negative, so the predicted penalty decreases with :

  short_loud   n=80   64.88
  long_loud    n=800  59.35

A reader who knows BIC grows like will read that as the model having learned the opposite, and it has learned nothing of the kind. The labels did not pin the slope. Every one of those four target intervals is open above – – because the largest penalty on the grid still keeps the single changepoint the labels ask for. When every interval is open above, any sufficiently large prediction is optimal, the problem is under-determined in the slopes, and the term settles them near zero with whatever sign BFGS happened to reach. The predictions are all inside their targets, which is the only property the fit is for.

That is the common case, not a contrived one: a one-change label plus a generous penalty grid produces an open-above target nearly every time.

So ?cpt_learn_penalty gains two things. The @return now states that coef() is on the log-penalty scale and predict() on the natural one – previously it said only that both methods exist, which leaves a coefficient of looking additive when it is multiplicative. And a “Reading the coefficients” section says the signs are usually not interpretable, why (the open-above targets), and what to do if they need to be: widen penalties until the largest over-segments, so the intervals close above, with cpt_label_error_curve() to show whether they did.

A test pins the scale relation by rebuilding a prediction from coef() and cpt_features() by hand, so the two scales cannot drift apart silently.

615.2 The test asserted a property of the data, and the suite said so

The block written for §615 ended with

expect_gt(length(unique(round(preds, 6))), 1L)

– four series of very different length and noise must get four different penalties. It passed on the seed used while measuring and failed in the full suite, where a different seed produced four series whose targets are all open above. Then the fit is a constant, all four predictions are equal, and the assertion is false.

Which is the finding, stated more sharply than §615.1 had it: with open-above targets the model does not merely have uninterpretable slopes, it reduces to a constant – predict() returns the same penalty for every series. Both measured outcomes (slightly negative slopes on one draw, all-zero weights on another) put every prediction inside its target, which is the only property the fit is for.

The test now asserts the implication rather than the antecedent: if any feature weight is non-zero the predictions must differ, and if none is they must all be equal. That is a property of the model form, true whichever way the labels fall. ?cpt_learn_penalty gained the constant case explicitly, because a user who asked for a learned penalty and got one number back would otherwise reasonably think something had gone wrong.

Worth recording as my own instance of the mistake this loop keeps finding in the package: an assertion about what the data happened to do, in place of one about what the code guarantees.

616. 8d9df7b is green on every runner

Pushed to origin/master and watched to completion. Both workflows succeeded:

job R CMD check
ubuntu-latest (devel) Status: OK
ubuntu-latest (release) Status: OK
ubuntu-latest (oldrel-1) Status: OK
windows-latest (release) Status: OK
macos-latest (release) 1 NOTE
pkgdown (build + deploy) success

No testthat failure or error anywhere in either run.

The qpdf WARNING, the PDF-manual WARNING and ERROR, the HTML-manual NOTE and the leftover .tex NOTE that this document has recorded since 0.4.0 do not appear on any runner, which is the direct confirmation that all five were this machine’s missing pdflatex, qpdf and tidy rather than anything in the package.
